title: 60-year-old hiker stranded on icy mountain ledge rescued after standing in same spot for 7 hours, rangers say
text:
KEENE, N.Y. (WCAX/Gray News) — A 60-year-old Canadian hiker was rescued from an icy New York mountain ledge after spending seven hours standing in the exact same spot, according to state forest rangers.
The rescue unfolded on Wednesday, Oct. 21, along the Mount Colden Trap Dike in the Adirondack Mountains.
Rangers said the hiker triggered an emergency satellite beacon around 6:30 p.m. after losing his crampons, traction spikes attached to winter boots, while traversing an icy ledge.
Without traction gear, the climber was unable to safely move up or down, leaving him stranded.
Rescue teams reached the man around 1a.m. and began working to secure him.
“When I got out to him and was trying just to get him secured to me, the thought went through my mind: if we both slip before I have him clipped in and on my tether, he’s dead. He’s like, gone,” Forest Ranger Jenna Curcio said.
Officials noted the Trap Dike route is rated as a fourth-class mountaineering climb and has claimed multiple lives over the years.
Rangers urged outdoor enthusiasts to thoroughly research mountain routes and carry proper gear before heading into steep backcountry terrain.

title: Obituary: David Reed Robinson
text:
CRYSTAL – David Reed Robinson, 69, passed away unexpectedly at home on Oct. 10, 2026.
He was born in Bangor on Dec. 2, 1956. His father was a student at UMO, and Orono was his first home, along with his older brother.
After his father’s graduation, the family moved several times before settling in Falmouth, which David considered his hometown. He graduated from Falmouth High School in 1974.
He always had a love of music, and enjoyed putting on Beatles concerts for the family as a child.
He had a vast record collection containing hundreds of albums, and a disdain for today’s music technology. No “playlists” for him!
He was a talented athlete, playing baseball, basketball and golf, and had a great love for the family’s lakeside camp in Aroostook County, so much so, that he moved to the area in the late 1990s. At the time of his death, he was living in the town of Crystal, population 243.
David liked living a simple life. He was the quiet guy who would come out with a zinger at just the right moment.
He was honest, loyal, intelligent, and the life of the party when he wanted to be, and he will be deeply missed.
David was predeceased by his parents Jonathan C. Robinson, and Carolyn (Olsen) Robinson.
He is survived by siblings Mark Robinson of Winn and his family, and Kristen Robinson of Portland.

title: Early voting, competitive races: What to know about the 2026 midterm elections in 8 charts
text:
Early voting, competitive races: What to know about the 2026 midterm elections in 8 charts
Voters across the country will decide which political party will gain or retain control of the U.S. Senate and House of Representatives, as well as the governorships in several states.
The Get the Facts Data Team compiled a list of charts showing what to know about the 2026 midterm elections and the top issues voters are concerned about.
How many voters have cast an early ballot?
More than 52 million ballots were cast early this election, either in person or by mail, according to the latest data from the University of Florida Election Lab. Early voting data is not election results, and therefore it's not yet known which candidate will win their races.
Some states with competitive races, like Texas, Georgia, Tennessee and North Carolina, have seen high early turnout.
In Texas, early ballots cast in person or by mail already made up more than 80% of the total votes for the state's 2022 midterm election as of Friday. Texas has a close, competitive Senate race between Democrat James Talarico and Republican Ken Paxton.
The Cook Political Report’s CPR Race Ratings identified 76 competitive races as of Oct. 30: 11 for the Senate, 53 for the House and 12 for state governor.
The governor races in Kansas, Nevada and Georgia were rated as toss-ups, meaning the race could go either way.
The Cook Political Report rated 11 Senate races as competitive, with seven of those being toss-ups. In order to gain control of the Senate, Democrats need to flip a net of four seats held by Republicans.
Republicans currently hold a slim majority in the House of Representatives, with 218 seats. Democrats hold 214 House seats and would need a net gain of at least three seats to secure a majority.
Eighteen races in the House were considered toss-ups, including nine involving Republican incumbents.
Some of these House races became competitive after states redrew their congressional districts in mid-decade redistricting.
Florida’s 22nd district became an open seat after Democratic Rep. Lois Frankel’s district was redrawn as the 23rd district. Democrat Pia Dandiya and Republican Casey Askar are competing for the seat, which was rated a toss-up.
What concerns do voters have?
The economy, healthcare and the war in Iran were among the top issues voters said mattered the most in this midterm election, according to the latest Gallup poll.
A gallon of regular gas now averages $4.20 a gallon, up nearly 35% from when President Donald Trump took office. Diesel cost $3.63 a gallon at the start of Trump’s second term. It now costs $6.32, about 74% more.
The rise is partly due to higher oil prices amid uncertainty in the Middle East. The war in Iran has disrupted global oil supplies, affecting how much consumers pay at the pump.
With energy prices higher, inflation has increased in the U.S. The latest report showed inflation was up 3.7% in September compared with the year prior.
In April 2025, the stock market plummeted when Trump announced sweeping tariffs for all trading partners, but it has since bounced back. The Dow Jones Industrial Average has risen by 20% since Trump’s second term began.

title: Week Ahead in Washington: November 1
Obituary: Robert Wayne Collett Jr.
text:
SOUTH PORTLAND – Robert Wayne Collett Jr., 69, of South Portland, Maine, passed away peacefully on Oct. 18, 2026, at Springbrook Center after a courageous battle with liver disease.
Born on Oct. 3, 1957, Robert was the son of Elise Louise (Williams) Collett and Robert Wayne Collett Sr.
Robert attended schools in South Portland and began working at a young age. His early employment included Legion Square Market, Shaw’s Supermarket, The Salvation Army and Lilly Trucking. Following in his father’s footsteps, he later purchased a Pepperidge Farm Bread and Rolls franchise. Robert thoroughly enjoyed his years as a salesman, delivering products to local stores and building lasting friendships with customers and store receivers throughout the area. After selling his franchise, Robert earned his Class II driver’s license and continued his career in trucking. He worked for several transportation companies before joining Palco Air Cargo, where he found not only a job he loved but also a second family. Robert remained with Palco until a serious fall forced him to leave work, something he deeply missed in the years that followed.
Robert was predeceased by his father, Robert W. Collett Sr.
He is survived by his devoted mother, Elise Louise Collett; his sisters Debra Harris and her husband Rick Harris, Linda Theriault and her husband Michael Theriault, Donna Collett, and Laurie Briggs and her husband Theodore Briggs. He is also survived by his nieces and nephews, Melissa Siwik and her husband Chris Siwik, Jason Theriault, Christina Ouellette and her husband Jeff Ouellette, Shawn Theriault and his wife Erin Theriault, Evan Rench and his wife Tania Rench, Aaron Rench, Mitchell Briggs, and Alayna Briggs; several great-nieces and great-nephews; and his former wife, Lynne Collett.
One of Robert’s greatest passions was auto racing. He spent countless hours preparing race cars for weekend competition at Beech Ridge Speedway and was well known around the track as “Wrecker Boy” for his work driving the wrecker. Racing brought him tremendous joy, and he treasured the friendships he made through the sport. Recently, a close friend dedicated a race victory to Robert, a gesture that touched him deeply and brought him many heartfelt tears.
Robert was a beloved son, brother, uncle, and friend whose kindness, sense of humor, and genuine friendship left a lasting mark on all who knew him. His family is grateful for the many friends and loved ones who visited, called, and kept him in their thoughts during his final weeks.
A Celebration of Life will be held at a later date.
“Gone from our sight, but forever in our hearts.”
Condolences may be expressed online at http://www.hobbsfuneralhome.com.
In lieu of flowers, memorial donations may be made to: the American Liver Foundation in Robert’s memory

title: Man accused in crime spree with 17 victims, including three people stabbed
text:
TOPEKA, Kan. (WIBW/Gray News) - Ron Hubbard never expected fiction to become reality.
“I was thinking about a scenario I seen on TV where a delivery guy did the same when the police was chasing a guy who stole a car,” Hubbard said.
Hubbard said he was hanging with a friend Wednesday, Oct. 28, when they noticed something unusual.
“I happened to look up the street to my left, and I seen this strange guy,” Hubbard said.
The man, now identified as Adam Schwegman, also caught another bystander’s attention.
“We confronted him because the other guy had been up at the park, where this all took place,” Hubbard said.
Topeka police say an hour earlier, Schwegman stabbed two people along S.W. Fillmore. His booking charges also include an allegation of rape at that address.
TPD says Schwegman then moved up the same road, breaking into two homes -- four children were inside one of them, including a four-month-old. Officials say they were not hurt.
However, it didn’t stop there.
Police say a third victim was stabbed on a nearby street.
And finally, a 70-year-old woman was hurt when Schwegman attacked her at Ward Meade Park. Schwegman was running from there when Hubbard spotted him.
“I decided to step in, throw my leg out, trip him and he landed over here in the grass, and the knife fell in the grass,” Hubbard said.
Hubbard said he kicked the knife to the sidewalk, as the second person held Schwegman. He got away, but police soon caught him.
Schwegman was booked in connection with 16 charges, including aggravated battery and rape.
Hubbard says he was glad to step in to prevent further harm.
“Well, if you see something bad, try to help stop it. I wish we could have got to it before this happened,” Hubbard said.
Schwegman made his first appearance in court on Thursday, Oct. 29. The judge has set a total bond of $3 million.

title: Judge dismisses lawsuit seeking to block certification of Alaska Senate race if GOP incumbent loses
text:
JUNEAU, Alaska (AP) — A federal judge on Sunday dismissed a Justice Department lawsuit seeking to block certification of Alaska’s U.S. Senate race if Republican incumbent Dan Sullivan loses, the latest development in a ballot controversy that has roiled the final days of one of the nation’s most closely watched races.
Sullivan, an ally of President Donald Trump, faces Democrat Mary Peltola, a former congresswoman, in a race that is among a handful expected to determine which party controls the Senate for the final two year’s of Trump’s term.
Tuesday’s ranked-choice election also includes two candidates who have done little campaigning, one of whom shares the incumbent’s name. It was that candidate’s presence on the ballot that prompted Trump to push for the lawsuit out of fear he would siphon votes from the incumbent.
Shortly after the ruling, the Justice Department filed a notice saying it was appealing: “Alaskan voters deserve a fair election, not to be misled in an attempt to rig outcomes,” a department spokesperson said in a statement.
The lawsuit, filed less than two weeks before the election and as early voting was underway, called for an investigation into whether votes for retired teacher Dan J. Sullivan were intended for the senator. The state said the case lacked merit and argued there would be no way to determine that without violating voter privacy.
U.S. District Court Judge Sharon Gleason wrote in the order that the relief the federal government seeks is “infeasible” because many voters have already cast their ballots.
“More fundamentally, the United States provides no workable plan as to how it proposes to segregate ballots cast for Daniel J. Sullivan on Election Day and then conduct a court-ordered unspecified ‘investigation’ of those ballots in a manner that would preserve voter secrecy,” she wrote.
Peltola’s campaign and the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee argued that the case lacked any legal basis and amounted to election interference.
“Today’s ruling is a victory for democracy and a clear message to Donald Trump and Senate Republicans: No one, no matter how powerful, can toss out free and fair elections just because they don’t like the result,” said the committee’s executive director, Devan Barber.
The Justice Department, attorneys for the state and Peltola’s campaign did not immediately return messages seeking comment.
Senator says he expects ‘to lose a lot of votes’ to the other Dan Sullivan
The senator and his allies, including Trump, for months have portrayed Dan J. Sullivan as a sham candidate intent on confusing voters and helping Peltola.
Earlier Sunday, Sen. Sullivan told CNN that he thought the presence of the second Sullivan on the ballot would affect the election.
“I’m sure I’m going to lose a lot of votes to that trickery,” he said.
He also said he doubted claims by Peltola that she had no idea her top political aides were involved in recruiting Dan J. Sullivan to run as a way to confuse voters.
“There is no way this went on for a year that they weren’t informing her,” Sullivan told CNN’s “State of the Union.” “She got caught lying, and she’s still lying to the Alaskan people, the media, to all of us.”
The senator’s campaign did not immediately respond to a request for comment on the Sunday court ruling.
In the week before Election Day, The New York Times reported that Peltola’s campaign was involved in efforts to recruit the second Sullivan. Shortly after entering the race in June, Dan J. Sullivan said he’d had no contact with her campaign about running. He has not responded to multiple messages over the past few days.
His recent public absence prompted a social media post Sunday by the president: “The Fake Daniel J. Sullivan, Jr., has DISAPPEARED! Nobody can find him, including Law Enforcement.”
Peltola’s campaign responded to the Times story by saying it had no involvement in the campaigns for either Sullivan: “I am not interested in tricking voters,” Peltola said during a recent campaign event.
In its statement indicating its plans to appeal, the Justice Department said the federal judge dismissed the case on procedural grounds but did not dispute the government’s argument that Dan J. Sullivan entered the race “as a frivolous candidate to confuse voters.”
Multiple investigations look into whether Dan J. Sullivan was recruited as a decoy candidate
State courts, including the Alaska Supreme Court, rejected an earlier Republican-backed effort to block the retired teacher from the August open primary ballot on which he appeared as Daniel J. Sullivan Jr., with no party affiliation. The senator was listed as Dan S. Sullivan, Republican and incumbent.
Both Sullivans appear the same way on the general election ballot. Peltola placed first in the primary, followed by the senator. Dan J. Sullivan received about 2.5% of the primary vote, but that was enough to finish within the top four and qualify for the Nov. 3 ranked-choice election.
Attorneys for the Alaska Department of Law represented state elections officials in the case and asked Gleason, who was appointed by former Democratic President Barack Obama, to toss the lawsuit. They filed a scathing response to the federal government’s complaint, calling it “meritless.”
Alaska also said the state had taken “significant steps” to distinguish the two Sullivans on the ballot. Voters who still might be confused could ask for help or look up candidate biographies and other information in state-distributed election pamphlets.
Republicans, including ones working with Trump, also have a long history of backing decoy candidates in elections. The governor, a Republican, has ordered an investigation and suggested he may not certify a possible Peltola victory.
In her ruling, Gleason wrote that the Trump administration’s attempt to block certification ran counter to the Constitution, which gives states the authority to run elections. She also cited the Supreme Court’s Purcell principle, which holds that federal courts should generally not change election rules too close to an election.
Kristen Clarke, general counsel of the NAACP, which had filed a brief supporting the case’s dismissal, called the judge’s decision “a big win for the voters in Alaska.”
“The law is clear, and the DOJ’s case was a baseless, eleventh hour attempt to hijack this midterm election,” she said.
On Thursday, the Justice Department escalated a criminal investigation over the presence of Dan J. Sullivan on the Alaska ballot, issuing a raft of new grand jury subpoenas, a person familiar with the matter told The Associated Press. The FBI also has begun contacting people who donated to him, some of whom told the AP that the agents were asking if they had been misled about which candidate they were supporting.
___
Riccardi reported from Washington. Associated Press photographer Lindsey Wasson in Anchorage, Alaska, and AP writer Ali Swenson in Washington contributed to this report.

title: Heidi Klum reveals Halloween costume as her iconic party marks 25 years
text:
Heidi Klum reveals Halloween costume as her iconic party marks 25 years
Heidi Klum underwent a bloody transformation to become a giant, gruesome severed hand for her annual Halloween party in New York on Saturday, 25 years after she began hosting the much-anticipated event.
Klum was unrecognizable, with only her eyes and mouth showing, blood dripping from her mouth as she stuck her tongue out. The top of the hand ended in a gory assortment of dangling ligaments and tendons. She had an ensemble of helpers in blood-stained hazmat suits.
The idea came to her last year to be a giant hand — specifically her own left hand, with long red nails, a thumb ring, and her engagement ring and wedding band.
“I looked at my hand and I thought, ‘Hey, I think I could fit my body in this somehow,’” Klum said.
The supermodel-turned-TV personality went viral in 2022 when she arrived at the party on the end of a fishing line, encased in a slithering worm costume.
In past years, Klum has come dressed as the Greek myth Medusa, a peacock, an 8-foot-tall “Transformer,” a werewolf from Michael Jackson’s “Thriller” music video, a clone accompanied by several Klum-lookalikes, and Kali, the multiarmed Hindu goddess of death and destruction.
Klum said it took about five to six hours to get into her hand costume this year, but making it took a lot longer. She posted hints on her Instagram earlier in the day as bloodied prosthetics were applied to her face.
“Hands down, the hardest thing is carrying it,” Klum said. “It's quite heavy.”
Her husband, musician Tom Kaulitz, did not attend this year because he was on tour. But the details on her costume include a tattoo of his name on her ring finger, along with her palm lines and veins.
“A little bit of Tom is with me,” she said.

title: Halloween queen Heidi Klum deserves a hand for her costume in 2026
text:
(Gray News/AP) – Model and television host Heidi Klum has gone all out with her costume on Halloween year after year, and 2026 did not disappoint.
Klum revealed her masterpiece on social media late Saturday after much anticipation, having given clues throughout the day.
The supermodel defended her crown as Halloween queen by transforming into a severed version of her own hand.
Klum was unrecognizable, with only her eyes and mouth showing, blood dripping from her mouth as she stuck her tongue out. The top of the hand ended in a gory assortment of dangling ligaments and tendons. She had an ensemble of helpers in blood-stained hazmat suits.
The idea came to her last year to be a giant hand — specifically her own left hand, with long red nails, a thumb ring, and her engagement ring and wedding band.
“I looked at my hand and I thought, ‘Hey, I think I could fit my body in this somehow,’” Klum said.
She debuted the costume with a video post showing her actual fingers walking down the floor, and then halfway through the video, it transitions into her costume with her legs as two of her fingers.
Klum said it took about five to six hours to get into her hand costume this year, but making it took a lot longer. She posted hints on her Instagram earlier in the day as bloodied prosthetics were applied to her face.
“Hands down, the hardest thing is carrying it,” Klum said. “It’s quite heavy.”
Last year, Klum dressed up as Medusa, complete with moving snakes. The year before, she was an elaborate female version of E.T. that took a year of planning.
Her husband, musician Tom Kaulitz, did not attend this year because he was on tour. But the details on her costume include a tattoo of his name on her ring finger, along with her palm lines and veins.
“A little bit of Tom is with me,” she said.

title: Mexico comes alive during annual Day of the Dead celebrations
text:
Mexico comes alive during annual Day of the Dead celebrations
Bright orange marigolds, glowing candles and faces painted like the elegant skeletons known as catrinas fill the streets of Mexico every year during the country's Day of the Dead celebrations.
Festivities begin in October and lead up to Nov. 1 and 2, when the souls of deceased loved ones are believed to temporarily return to earth to reunite with their families.
No one knows when the first observance took place, but it is rooted in agriculture-related beliefs from Mexico’s pre-Hispanic era. Catholic traditions were incorporated into the celebration after the Spanish conquest in 1521.
Today, celebrations are marked by massive parades running along Mexico City's main avenue. Streets, businesses and markets are cloaked in orange Mexican marigold flowers, or cempasuchil, believed to light the path of the dead back to earth with their bright colors. Traditional pan de muerto, or bread of the dead, lines the display cases of bakeries.
Families decorate altars to their loved ones in their homes, placing treats, food and mezcal as offerings next to photos of their loved ones.
On the night of Nov. 1, families gather at cemeteries across the country to reconnect with their dead just as their ancestors have done for centuries.
But as the tradition and the Mexican capital have increasingly gained an international spotlight, and states like Oaxaca and Michoacan have seen an influx of tourists, some regions have experienced tensions around overtourism.
In Mexico City, many locals are skeptical of an annual parade featuring floats decorated with catrinas. The procession was created for the 2015 James Bond film “Spectre” and later incorporated into the city’s celebrations, though it was not previously part of the tradition.
In Janitzio, a small island on a lake in the central state of Michoacan, where celebrations were recognized by UNESCO as Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity in 2008, authorities closed the pantheon to tourists for the first time this year. The closure came after the island's community council reported the collapse of damaged tombs, crosses and parts of the cemetery's perimeter wall because of the flood of people.
Only local families and friends of those buried there would be allowed in.

title: Obituary: Roger Chase Downs Sr.
text:
WHITEFIELD – Roger Chase Downs Sr., 82, passed away unexpectedly at his home on Oct. 13, 2026, following ongoing cardiac and lung complications.
He was born on July 1, 1944, in Rochester, N.H., the second son of Pearl E. and Warren E. Downs. Roger grew up in Whitefield and attended the Alamo School, a two-room schoolhouse, from kindergarten through eighth grade. He then graduated from Gardiner High School in 1962, where he enjoyed playing football more than any academic class. It was there he met his wife, Rochelle. After marrying in 1961, they welcomed their children, Vicki, Roger Jr., and Daniel, over the next three years.
After graduating, Roger began working for Dessler’s Meat Market in Gardiner, honing his skills as a meat cutter. From there, he moved on to First National Stores, quickly becoming the regional meat manager. The family moved many times over the years as he climbed the ranks. In 1970, Roger and Rochelle moved their family to Freeport to open Downs Food Store. Together, they worked tirelessly over many years, making many friends and business acquaintances along the way. Thanks to Roger’s expertise, the store became known for its meat and fish department, also selling goods from local farmers and bakers. If you ever eat a country-style spare rib, you can thank Roger for contributing to its cut and design. Many years later, customers still remarked that they would only use Downs Foods clams for their clam chowder.
In 1982, Roger and Rochelle retired from the grocery business, becoming proprietors of several Freeport properties. This allowed them to move back to Roger’s childhood hometown of Whitefield, where he would pursue his longtime dream of becoming a farmer. They built their dream home on their 126-acre property, a former apple orchard, beginning many years of haying, gardening, and raising livestock. Over the years, he became a self-taught master of the fields, selling hay to local farmers and Agway for over four decades. He was a skilled gardener, harvesting countless crops of beautiful fruits and vegetables from White Heart Farm over the years, using them in the home-cooked meals, treats, and preserves he and Rochelle enjoyed preparing for family and friends. Countless memories were made on the farm: harvesting pumpkins for Halloween, picking apples, sleigh rides with the tractor, and many Thanksgiving, Christmas and Easter holidays spent together as a family enjoying each other’s company–and always, delicious food.
Following Rochelle’s passing in 2015, Roger was fortunate to meet his current partner of nearly five years, Mary Ellen Anderson of Nobleboro, at a cribbage event. She and Roger enjoyed many memories together, including gardening, baking and cooking, and playing many games of cribbage together at home and at the Wiscasset Community Center. Their last cribbage game was played the morning of Roger’s passing. As Roger’s health began to decline, Mary Ellen was instrumental in his care, allowing him to remain at home and continue to do many of the things he enjoyed. She became his eyes, his ears, his travel companion and confidante, and she became a beloved member of his family.
Roger was a jack of all trades, with many hobbies, passions, and interests, many of which he mastered. He was a skilled outdoorsman who enjoyed deer hunting, and participated in the Maine Moose Hunt three times. He traveled many places to fly fish, including Alaska, Labrador, and Nova Scotia, and wetted a fly in many ponds and lakes throughout Maine. Another hobby that he learned from his grandfather, Harry Chase, was the art of tapping maple trees. He was known for his famous black maple syrup, which he made by collecting sap and boiling it in the same evaporator used by Gramp Chase. He passed on this tradition to his granddaughters, Carly, Blair, and Grace, by collecting sap with them over many chilly afternoons and educating them on how to boil the perfect batch.
He was a lifelong football fan and remained loyal to the New England Patriots and Boston Red Sox through thick and thin. He was also a licensed pilot for many years, flying his beloved Cessnas throughout northern Maine and Canada. He was a true tinkerer, maker, and jury-rigger, always repairing broken farm equipment with whatever happened to be lying around. He loved sharing his passions with his family, whether it was explaining the mechanical structure of an engine or the timing of the first rain on a hay crop. He was a lifelong learner, attending mycology classes and business classes through Cornell University.
He was a passionate personal financier and follower of the stock market, and read many favorite books over the years (Benjamin Franklin was one of his favorite authors). He always enjoyed the daily paper every morning over a cup of black coffee with just a bit of milk. He was a voracious cribbage player throughout his entire life, with countless games and laughs over the years. He especially loved playing against his son-in-law, Claude, who became one of his best friends over the past several years. He was an active community member who cared deeply about giving back to the place he called home. He was a lifetime member of the Freeport Lions Club, served on the Whitefield Planning Board, and was a trustee of the Shin Pond Road Association. He contributed generously over the years to the Whitefield Historical Society, the Whitefield Cemetery Corporation, and the Sheepscot Valley Community Church. Due to his generosity, many historic sites and areas of Whitefield were maintained and refurbished. He will be remembered for his mischievous sense of humor, his generosity to the community, and his constant hospitality to friends and family.
He was predeceased by his wife, Rochelle Parlin Downs; their sons Roger Chase Jr. and Daniel Howard Downs; his brothers James Warren and Harry Leonard Downs, his sister, Sallie Ann Curtis; and their parents, Warren Edward and Pearl Emma Downs.
He is survived by his daughter Vicki L. Legere and her husband Joseph of Falmouth; granddaughter Blair E. Legere and her partner, Warren M. Blood, of Manhattan, N.Y., granddaughter, Grace V. Hawkes and her husband, Carter, of Norfolk, Va.; granddaughter, Carly M. Downs and her daughter, Elise Danielle, of Waltham, Mass.; son-in-law, Claude A. Castonguay of Biddeford; brother, John Haley Downs of Jefferson; and daughter-in-law, Peggy Flanagan of Whitefield. He is also survived by countless beloved cousins, nieces, nephews, and friends.
A service will take place at Sheepscot Valley Community Church in Whitefield on Saturday, Nov. 7, at 12 p.m. Arrangements and guidance are under the direction of Staples Funeral Home and Cremation Care, 53 Brunswick Ave., Gardiner. Condolences, photos and memories may be shared with the family by visiting the Staples Funeral Home website http://www.StaplesFuneralHome.com
In lieu of flowers, donations can be made to the Whitefield Cemetery Corporation, the Whitefield Historical Society or the Whitefield Union Hall in Kings Mills.

title: Jayson Tatum leads Celtics to 5th straight win
text:
ORLANDO, Fla. — Jayson Tatum scored 32 points — 15 of them from the free-throw line — and Paul George added 17 as the Boston Celtics won their fifth straight, 108-97 over the Orlando Magic Sunday afternoon.
Anthony Black and Tristan da Silva each scored 23 to lead the Magic (2-4), who dropped to 0-3 at home. Orlando forward Franz Wagner had 14 points and a career-high 12 assists.
Boston (5-1) also got a pair of critical blocks from Neemias Queta in the final two minutes, and George’s 3-pointer with 1:32 remaining gave Boston an insurmountable 11-point lead.
The Celtics built a 15-point lead by shutting out Orlando over the first four minutes of the second half. Orlando battled back on the strength of three of da Silva’s five 3-pointers, using a 12-0 run to cut Boston’s lead to 77-74 entering the final period.
And early in the fourth quarter, Black completed a 3-point play to tie it at 79, picking the pocket of George on an outlet pass. But on the following possession, Wagner couldn’t sink a layup to give Orlando the lead.
With Paolo Banchero (high-ankle sprain) missing his fourth straight game, Boston constantly keyed on Wagner.
Every time Orlando got close, Tatum slammed the door. Boston’s perennial All-Star made 15 of his 17 attempts from the free-throw line. Orlando as a team had just 19 free-throw attempts.
Tatum left late in the first quarter after the back of his head collided inadvertently with the forehead of Orlando’s Jamal Cain. Bleeding, Tatum visited the locker room but returned with 6:13 left in the first half.
Queta started in place of center Mitchell Robinson, who missed the game to rest. Luka Garza (12 points) and Baylor Scheierman (10) were in double figures for Boston, which leads the NBA in bench scoring.
Up next
Celtics: At Houston on Monday night.
Magic: Host Washington on Monday night.

title: Mamdani says Trump agrees to grant visa to mother of Ghanian teen killed in Bronx shooting
text:
Mamdani says Trump agrees to grant visa to mother of Ghanaian teen killed in Bronx shooting
New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani said on Saturday in a social media post that after talking to President Donald Trump, he has agreed to grant a visa to the mother of a 15-year-old immigrant from Ghana who was shot to death earlier this week.
The White House did not immediately respond to an email from The Associated Press confirming the administration would be issuing the visa.
Video above: Trump, Mamdani meet
The teen, Javits Frimpong, was on his way to school in a Bronx neighborhood shortly before 9:30 a.m. Thursday when he was shot in the abdomen, New York City police said. He was pronounced dead at a hospital later that day. No arrests have yet been made, and the killing remains under investigation.
“The murder of a child is a pain no parent should have to endure, let alone from thousands of miles away,” Mamdani wrote Saturday on X. “Javits Frimpong’s mother deserves to say goodbye to her son in person. I just got off the phone with President Trump and he has agreed to grant her visa immediately.”
“All of New York City is mourning this tragedy,” he said.
Frimpong arrived in the Bronx from Ghana a year ago to be with his father and begin a new life in the United States, according to U.S. Rep. Ritchie Torres, a Democrat from the Bronx.
Frimpong was on his way to school when he was shot, Torres wrote on X.
Video below: What could the rise of Democratic Socialism mean for the midterms?
“Our entire borough is mourning a young man who should have had his whole future ahead of him,” Torres said. “Every child in the Bronx deserves to walk to school without fearing for their life, and no parent should ever have to endure what Javits’s father, Thomas, is enduring now.”
Thomas Frimpong described his son as a quiet teen who spent much of his time on his cellphone. He told reporters that several days before the shooting he learned his son was being bullied at school.
“It was the principal who told me,” Thomas Frimpong said. “He said two guys are disturbing my son so he has suspended the two guys. My son is at school. He’s innocent, so I call him. I talk with my son, he said ‘dad, I’m OK.’ ”
Foreign Minister Sam Okudzeto Ablakwa said in a post on X that Ghanaian officials in New York are coordinating with local authorities and that the foreign ministry “will work tirelessly with U.S. authorities to ensure justice is secured.”
Trump has clamped down on immigration during his second term, including suspending the processing of visas from 75 countries.

title: Andreas Almgren wins men’s race in NYC in marathon debut, Sheila Chepkirui wins women’s race
text:
NEW YORK (AP) — Andreas Almgren of Sweden won the men’s race of the New York City Marathon in his debut in the event while Sheila Chepkirui of Kenya won the women’s race for the second time Sunday.
Almgren was making his debut at 26.2 miles after a successful career running half-marathons. He pulled away from Yemaneberhan Crippa of Italy in the final mile to take the victory in 2 hours, 6 minutes and 1 second. Crippa finished 13 seconds behind. Kamohelo Mofolo of Lesotho was third, edging out defending champion Benson Kipruto.
Chepkirui, who also won the race in 2024, pulled away from countrymate Hellen Obiri in the final 150 meters to seal the victory in 2:24:36. American Jessica McClain finished second, passing Obiri — a two-time winner — in the final few strides. It was the first time a U.S. woman finished in the top three since 2018. McClain was 6 seconds behind Chepkirui.
It was the 50th time that the race has run through all five boroughs of the city. There were just over 2,000 competitors in 1976, the seventh running of the race, including only 88 women. About 60,000 runners stepped up to the starting line Sunday, with nearly half of them women.

title: Rep. Haley Stevens switches endorsement to Mike Rogers in Michigan Senate race
text:
WASHINGTON (Gray DC) - Rep. Haley Stevens, D-Mich., withdrew her support for Michigan Democratic Senate nominee Abdul El-Sayed on Sunday and endorsed Republican candidate Mike Rogers, just two days before the midterm elections.
The reversal follows tense in-party fighting between Stevens, a moderate, and El-Sayed, a progressive, who often clashed while campaigning for the state’s Democratic Senate nomination. Stevens endorsed El-Sayed soon after she conceded the close August primary.
Stevens and Rogers were seen attending a church service together Sunday morning, which prompted questions about whom she supported.
Stevens answered in a video posted to social media, in which she officially switched her endorsement to Rogers. She said she felt what was coming out of the Democratic nominee’s campaign was “hate”.
“I don’t belong in Abdul’s campaign. I do not stand with Hasan Piker, who gets trafficked on our college campuses,” Stevens said, referencing a supporter of El-Sayed.
Top Democratic leaders were quick to respond on social media, calling the move “dangerous” and a “despicable betrayal.”
Meanwhile, President Donald Trump called Stevens “brave,” a thought echoed by Speaker of the House Mike Johnson. Trump later told reporters he would welcome her to the Republican Party.
Rogers held a gaggle with Stevens soon after the announcement and said he was honored to have her vote.
“This is more a statement about standing together against hate and the future of this state and this country than it is anything else,” Rogers said.
When asked about the change, El-Sayed said he “doesn’t think about Stevens” and is more focused on the issues leading his campaign.
The endorsement even led to a major switch up on the Hill: Stevens’ longtime congressional chief of staff issued a statement Sunday saying he and other members of the team resigned after the flipped support. He said he was shocked and heartbroken by the action, and ended the statement with his own endorsement of El-Sayed.

title: Election night in Maine: When will we know?
text:
Philip E. Mathieu is a data scientist at IDEXX Laboratories. He lectures part time at the Roux Institute and volunteers on the Executive Committee of Sierra Club Maine.
When will it be over?
For some of us, this question is almost as pressing as “who will win” the race for Maine’s Senate seat next week. But barring a blowout or a significant change in reporting practices, most major media outlets and the Associated Press probably won’t call the race until early Wednesday morning or later.
The logic is defensible: in Maine, many towns will not finish counting until Wednesday, so calling the race early risks a late “swing” as the final votes trickle in. Additionally, by nature of ranked-choice voting, a candidate has to both beat their opponent and clear the 50% threshold to “officially” win on election night, meaning that any close race is all but guaranteed to not get an official call until the following week.
For me, this uncertainty is a guarantee of anxiety on election night. So, as a data scientist trained at the Roux Institute and working full time for IDEXX, I decided to put my skills to work.
Drawing inspiration from the New York Times’ and Washington Post’s election models, I built a model that forecasts not who the winner is (the data says it’s a tossup) but when we’ll know with reasonable certainty the outcome, either way.
The model runs 3,000 simulations based on Maine general and primary election data from 2018-2026. For each town, it randomly selects a time for the town to report results based on previous reporting times. It also randomly assigns an actual percent for each candidate, based on current polling plus wide margins of error. This gives us 3,000 predictions spread across a range of possible results and a range of possible reporting times, which we can then use to figure out when we would know based on the final margin.
In about 7 out of 10 simulations, either Jackson or Collins wins by at least 2 points, and the model will be confident — 99.5% chance or better of the result not changing — by 11 p.m. On most of those nights, media outlets still won’t call the race until a few hours later, because they wait for more of the vote to be counted.
On close nights, when we don’t have a confident prediction by 11 p.m., 6 out of 10 simulations don’t reach a confident result until Wednesday midday or, for the closest races, until ranked-choice tabulation the following week. If it’s still too close to call by my model at 11 p.m., I’m going to bed.
What about the governor’s race, you ask? The answer there is a bit simpler. Because current polling shows Hannah Pingree with a significant lead, 9 out of 10 simulations favor a called race before 11 p.m. Additionally, there’s no ranked choice tabulation in that race, so chances are we’ll know by Wednesday morning at the latest, unless it is so close that it goes to a recount.
To explore more of this analysis and some other experiments looking at election modeling in Maine, visit philipmathieu.com/election-night-2026.

title: Trump administration has promised US farmers $15 billion in weeks before the midterms
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
SIOUX FALLS, S.D. (AP) — President Donald Trump’s administration has made $15 billion worth of promises to agriculture producers in the last few weeks of the midterm elections, initiatives intended to help offset higher costs for diesel and fertilizer that farmers have endured largely due to his tariffs and the war in Iran.
Whether that will motivate more voters to turn out in agricultural states where traditionally Republican seats are now seen as competitive is unclear. It may explain his increased attention on rural areas, including visits Sunday to Iowa and Kansas, two days before the election.
A look at the Republican administration’s pledges to farmers:
Who these efforts will help
Besides the more than $15 billion worth of payments and initiatives announced by Trump’s Department of Agriculture, the agency plans $13.8 billion in safety net program payments for eligible producers for the 2025 crop year, offsetting shortfalls for farmers who grow key crops such as corn, soybeans, wheat and rice.
Of the $15 billion, more than half will go toward an $8 billion one-time payment plan for farmers buffeted by soaring diesel prices. The USDA said it will release more details about the payments this month. It is not clear when the payments will go to farmers, who rely on diesel for trucks, tractors and combines.
Gregg Ibendahl, a farm management specialist at Kansas State University, said he estimates the payments to “more than cover the increase in fuel costs,” and that the money could help with high fertilizer prices.
At least $5 billion was announced in guaranteed loans for ranchers and fishermen. An additional $1.8 billion in payments is for producers and landowners who participated in conservation programs, $573 million will go toward fertilizer manufacturing projects and $57 million is for expanding meat processors. For specialty crop producers, $86.6 million in grants will be awarded to innovative projects.
On Thursday, the agency said it would purchase up to $472.5 million in agricultural commodities to support producers and give to charitable programs.
The USDA also announced other efforts, such as expanding sales of a diesel normally used only for off-road use, helping ranchers by making cattle sale data more transparent and strengthening wolf management policies to protect livestock.
Why farmers are struggling
It has been a frustrating year for farmers. Increased costs for fertilizer and fuel have made it difficult to turn a profit. Last year, tariffs drove up expenses for other equipment that farmers use, and the trade war with China resulted in a near boycott of U.S. agricultural goods.
On Friday, diesel was averaging $6.32 per gallon, down slightly from its peak in September but 70% higher than the price a year ago, according to motor club AAA. Filling up a 100-gallon tank now costs $260 more than it did one year ago.
“That input side risk, I think, is the thing that really has hurt farmers this year, as well as the fact that there has been a lot more uncertainty about what’s going to happen in the world,” Ibendahl said.
He said he expects these ad hoc payments to be a big help for farmers who otherwise would not make a profit this year, but they do not address the broader issues driving up prices.
“It’s hard to go to your lender in the next spring and say, ‘OK, well, we’re looking pretty good this year, but it’s all because of these extra temporary government payments, so how much can you make me a loan (for) next year for my crop?’” he said.
Alexandra Middlewood, an associate professor of political science at Wichita State University, said she has heard mixed reactions from farmers, who are happy their business will survive this year but see these programs as one-time bailouts rather than a long-term solution.
What farmers may vote on
Rural voters, including farmers and those who rely on the agricultural economy, have been an instrumental voting group for Trump.
Michael Smith, a political science professor at Emporia State University, said many rural voters like the president, but some of his policies have hurt the agriculture industry. Immigrant deportations have threatened the agricultural labor force, and cuts to foreign aid and SNAP food stamps hurt the market for agricultural products.
“Some people who admire Trump really just admire the person, the man,” he said. “But it doesn’t mean they necessarily like his policies. Well, Trump himself isn’t on the ballot this year. His policies are.”
Cost of living and access to health care are top issues for rural voters, Middlewood said. She added that there is a perception the administration has not done enough to address these issues, even as Trump boasts at campaign rallies about a booming economy.
Middlewood, who is based in Kansas, does not expect frustrated rural voters to shift to the Democratic Party, given how long the state has been a Republican stronghold. But some voters may decide to sit out of this election or vote independent, which would hurt Republican candidates.
“Independent voters make or break elections,” she said. ”And so that’s really what it’s going to come down to this year is those independent voters and who they’re breaking for.”

title: Mexico comes alive during annual Day of the Dead celebrations
text:
MEXICO CITY (AP) — Bright orange marigolds, glowing candles and faces painted like the elegant skeletons known as catrinas fill the streets of Mexico every year during the country’s Day of the Dead celebrations.
Festivities begin in October and lead up to Nov. 1 and 2, when the souls of deceased loved ones are believed to temporarily return to earth to reunite with their families.
No one knows when the first observance took place, but it is rooted in agriculture-related beliefs from Mexico’s pre-Hispanic era. Catholic traditions were incorporated into the celebration after the Spanish conquest in 1521.
Today, celebrations are marked by massive parades running along Mexico City’s main avenue. Streets, businesses and markets are cloaked in orange Mexican marigold flowers, or cempasuchil, believed to light the path of the dead back to earth with their bright colors. Traditional pan de muerto, or bread of the dead, lines the display cases of bakeries.
Families decorate altars to their loved ones in their homes, placing treats, food and mezcal as offerings next to photos of their loved ones.
On the night of Nov. 1, families gather at cemeteries across the country to reconnect with their dead just as their ancestors have done for centuries.
But as the tradition and the Mexican capital have increasingly gained an international spotlight, and states like Oaxaca and Michoacan have seen an influx of tourists, some regions have experienced tensions around overtourism.
In Mexico City, many locals are skeptical of an annual parade featuring floats decorated with catrinas. The procession was created for the 2015 James Bond film “Spectre” and later incorporated into the city’s celebrations, though it was not previously part of the tradition.
In Janitzio, a small island on a lake in the central state of Michoacan, where celebrations were recognized by UNESCO as Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity in 2008, authorities closed the pantheon to tourists for the first time this year. The closure came after the island’s community council reported the collapse of damaged tombs, crosses and parts of the cemetery’s perimeter wall because of the flood of people.
Only local families and friends of those buried there would be allowed in.

title: Ramblers end Seahawks’ season with 4-1 win
text:
The top-seeded Winthrop Ramblers defeated the visiting fourth-seeded Boothbay Region Seahawks 4-1 Saturday afternoon, Oct. 31 to advance to the Class C South field hockey championship game.
The semifinal matchup was the second time the teams met this season, with Winthrop edging Boothbay 2-1 at BRHS.
Addie Daigle scored twice for the Ramblers. Sophie Shuman gave Winthrop a 1-0 lead with a first quarter goal at 9:17. After Daigle made it 2-0 in the second quarter at 6:31, Boothbay cut the lead in half on a goal by Zuri Smith at 5:47.
With the score 2-1 at the start of the third quarter, Boothbay came out putting pressure on the Winthrop defense, getting four penalty corners in the second half of the quarter. A few shots were stopped by the Winthrop goalie. With just under a minute to play in the quarter, Winthrop got a penalty corner and Grace Folsom scored with eight seconds on the clock to make it 3-1.
Daigle’s second goal came with 3:34 to play and Winthrop kept Boothbay at bay the rest of the way.
Winthrop improved to 14-1 and Boothbay ends the season at 11-5.

Sunday will feature bright and beautiful sunshine with temperatures becoming slightly warmer than yesterday on Halloween. Conditions today will reach the mid to upper 50s, but much warmer weather is on the way.
Tonight will be fairly mild with temperatures in the low 40s and 30s, and by the afternoon on Monday, some areas will reach the upper 60s and even 70s. It will be partly cloudy tomorrow, but otherwise Monday will be a nice day for an outdoor lunch break.
Mountain and possibly inland areas may see showers on Tuesday evening as a cold front passes over Maine. Showers will stretch closer to the coast, but otherwise, Wednesday morning will be mostly dry.
This week as a whole will be warmer than average with highs reaching into the 60s on most days. Showers will make an appearance at the end of the week, but the timing and intensity still has time to change. Showers could arrive as early as Thursday evening and last into Saturday night.

title: Obituary: Jeffrey W. Somers
text:
GRAY – Jeffrey W. Somers passed away suddenly on Monday, Oct. 26, 2026 at his home in Gray, Maine.
He was born on May 20, 1957, in Portland, and lived a large portion of his life in South Portland before moving to Gray in 2005. Jeff was the younger son of William J. Somers and Katherine A. Somers (Arey). He grew up on Preble Street in South Portland and graduated from South Portland High School in 1975. He went on to earn two associate’s degrees, spent four years in the Air Force and had most recently retired from a long and rewarding career in the Maine Air National Guard (ANG).
Between his four years of active duty and career with the Air National Guard, he spent his first 20 work years at Business Equipment Unlimited in Portland as their lead service technician while also in the inactive reserves for the Air National Guard where he served one weekend a month in the 243rd Engineering Installation Squadron.
After his time at BEU, he secured a full-time position with the Maine Air National Guard where he worked for another 14 years as an engineering technician and airfield systems craftsman. Jeff was deployed to places like Germany and Curacao and was also sent on two separate tours into active war zones – first to Afghanistan in 2001 (Operation Enduring Freedom) and then into Iraq in 2011 (Operations Iraqi Freedom & New Dawn).
When not at work, Jeff always had a book in his hand and a spare book stashed everywhere. He was affectionately known as “Mr. Encyclopedia” when his daughters were young because he would insist on turning every question they had into a learning opportunity.
He would act tough about it, but he was a big softie when he was around cats. When his daughter gifted him a kitten that he “didn’t want” one day in 2008, Jeff slept on the couch that night specifically because he didn’t think the little kitten could get up the stairs and he didn’t want her to be scared or alone on her first night in the house. What was most appreciated about Jeff is that he made us all feel safe. Whether it was by providing a home to live in, providing financial or emotional support, or physically shielding us from danger, he was there to fix whatever it was that troubled us. If Jeff was around, it was going to be okay.
After retirement, he enjoyed working on his house and relaxing at home. In 2025, he went with his daughter to the Brunswick air show to see the Thunderbirds and it was like watching him turn into a kid again. He knew everything about every plane and every gadget and told stories about how he had flown on one of the planes that was being toured. It was a great day.
He was preceded in death by his parents William and Katherine; and his beloved cats Tommy, Sebastian and Ariel.
He is survived by his daughters Kimberly and Tracy; brother Scott, and their spouses and children.
A memorial service will be held on Nov. 9, at 10:30 a.m. at Hobbs Funeral Home (no visitation) followed by a procession to Highland Memorial Cemetery for a short graveside service. A reception will be held after at Hobbs Funeral Home.
In lieu of flowers, the family asks that donations be made in Jeff’s memory to the Animal Refuge League of Greater Portland, the place where he got Sebastian, his best little buddy.

title: What to know about the Affordable Care Act's open enrollment period now underway
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
WASHINGTON (AP) — People heading into the Affordable Care Act open enrollment period with plans to sign up for insurance should expect a variety of changes in 2027, including higher premiums and fewer coverage options.
The sign-up window for the marketplace, also known as Obamacare, starts Sunday in most states and runs through Jan. 15.
Big changes to the exchange include expiring financial assistance, rising rates, potential delays in working with a broker, new restrictions on immigrants, and stricter enrollment checks.
Financial help, including premium tax credits and cost-sharing reductions, is now restricted for many groups of people who were previously eligible.
Across the board, healthcare experts predict less coverage and higher prices, with the average price of health insurance purchased through the marketplaces expected to rise by 13% in 2027, according to analysis of new CMS data by the healthcare research nonprofit KFF.
Increases are driven by multiple factors
Cynthia Cox, a vice president and director of the ACA program at KFF, said the increase is primarily driven by rising healthcare costs, hospital market concentration, and potential factors such as the No Surprises Act, which took effect in 2022 and bans surprise billing, or the rising availability of GLP-1 drugs.
The people who will be most affected by the new increases are those who do not qualify for a subsidy.
“They may or may not be able to afford to continue to keep their coverage into next year,” Cox said, adding that “a lot of them have already moved into bronze plans, which are the cheapest plans.”
A CMS fact sheet about open enrollment that was distributed Friday says “Americans using HealthCare.gov will have robust access to low-cost plans.”
The price of ACA insurance has skyrocketed for many people during Trump’s second term after Republicans opposed extending COVID-era subsidies that had helped offset the costs of health insurance for most enrollees during Democratic President Joe Biden’s administration.
That resulted in 1.2 million fewer people signing up for coverage in the exchanges.
Nearly 20 million people in US are actively enrolled in ACA plans
As of February, roughly 19.2 million people in the United States were actively enrolled in ACA marketplace health plans, according to the Department of Health and Human Services website. The number of enrollees grew during the COVID-19 pandemic when enhanced subsidies became available through the American Rescue Plan Act and Inflation Reduction Act, both signed into law by Biden.
New regulations starting in 2027 will also limit tax credits for certain lawfully present immigrants, which could result in an additional 1 million uninsured individuals over time.
Meanwhile, the Trump administration has been removing ACA enrollees from the program as part of the ongoing campaign against what it characterizes as waste, fraud and abuse.
In September, Vice President JD Vance and other officials in the Republican administration announced plans to remove 760,000 ACA enrollees from public healthcare exchanges, alleging the individuals were fraudulently enrolled in the program or simply did not exist.
Vance said the discovery and canceled subsidy payments for hundreds of thousands of people from the exchanges, part of an administration-wide crackdown on fraud, would result in $2.2 billion in cost savings.
It’s unclear how many more people will drop off of ACA coverage in 2027, Cox said. But with higher premiums, immigration eligibility changes and the anti-fraud efforts, “I think there’s going to be fewer people enrolled in this market, but it’s going to be harder to understand why.”

title: 1 dead, at least 8 injured in shooting after largest HBCU football game, police say
text:
BIRMINGHAM, Ala. (WBRC/Gray News) – One person is dead and at least eight others are injured after two shootings Saturday night near the Magic City Classic in Birmingham, Alabama, authorities said.
The Magic City Classic is the largest historically Black college and university football game in the United States.
Birmingham Mayor Randall Woodfin confirmed Sunday that police were investigating two separate incidents that happened in the west city of the city.
Woodfin said the first shooting injured six people and happened outside of the Legion Field perimeter and outside of the Magic City Classic tailgate area. The mayor said the second shooting happened less than eight minutes later across the street from Legion Field in the Graymont Avenue area and had three victims. Police and fire and rescue responded to the scene around 7:50 p.m. Saturday night.
Investigators said multiple firearms were recovered at the scene.
Woodfin said a 17-year-old, who had a gun, is in custody in connection with the investigation; however, the teen is not the only suspect and the investigation remains ongoing.
Officials said seven people were taken to the hospital and the victims range in age from 19 to 30. Two are in critical condition and five are in stable condition, officials said.
More than 50 people were treated for minor injuries from the chaos of the shootings.
Birmingham Police Chief Michael Pickett described the shooting as a “senseless act of violence” and praised responding personnel.
“Everyone knows this is the largest event we have here in the city and it’s extremely taxing on our personnel. Other leaders in law enforcement recognize that and they quickly offered up support and we are grateful for that quick response,” Pickett said. “I’ll end with this.. our Birmingham police officer are true heroes. They are true heroes. Seeing the courage and resilience they displayed tonight, running alongside them in the direction of those gunshots, triaging people as we pass by them going in the direction of the shots to make sure they weren’t injured, or if they were injured rendering aid as we continue toward the gunfire.. that shows true courage, that shows the true dedication they have to actually saving lives. And I’m thankful that all of our police officers as well of others who were assistance are able to go home to their families tonight.”

Cost of living and access to health care are top issues for rural voters, Middlewood said. She added that there is a perception the administration has not done enough to address these issues, even as Trump boasts at campaign rallies about a booming economy.
Middlewood, who is based in Kansas, does not expect frustrated rural voters to shift to the Democratic Party, given how long the state has been a Republican stronghold. But some voters may decide to sit out of this election or vote independent, which would hurt Republican candidates.
“Independent voters make or break elections,” she said. ”And so that’s really what it’s going to come down to this year is those independent voters and who they’re breaking for.”

title: Sen. Chris Murphy hospitalized with stroke and expected to make full recovery, his team says
text:
Sen. Chris Murphy hospitalized with stroke and expected to make full recovery, his team says
Democratic Sen. Chris Murphy has been hospitalized after experiencing a stroke and is expected to make a full recovery, his team announced Sunday.
The 53-year-old experienced “numbness in his arm” on Saturday afternoon and was taken to a local hospital, where doctors determined he had had a stroke, according to a statement from his office.
He is at Johns Hopkins Hospital, and “the doctors are encouraged by his progress, he is awake and alert, and we are optimistic he will make a full recovery,” wrote his chief of staff, Allison Herwitt.
Murphy has served in the Senate since 2013. He previously represented Connecticut’s 5th Congressional District in the House of Representatives.
The Connecticut Democrat has emerged as a top progressive voice in Congress, championing causes such as affordable healthcare and gun safety, and his name has been floated as possibly joining a broad 2028 presidential primary field.
A stroke occurs when the blood supply to the brain is blocked or when a blood vessel in the brain bleeds. Immediate treatment can reduce the risk of brain damage or other complications.
Stroke is among the top causes of death in the United States. High blood pressure, high cholesterol, smoking, obesity and diabetes are leading causes of stroke, according to the U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. Symptoms can include trouble speaking or understanding others; numbness, weakness or paralysis in the face, arm or leg; problems seeing with one or both eyes; headache; and trouble walking.
Pennsylvania Democratic Sen. John Fetterman, who suffered a stroke during his 2022 campaign, said he hoped Murphy would enjoy “a full and speedy recovery.”
“As someone who survived a near-fatal stroke, I understand all too well how much this impacts your life,” Fetterman wrote in a post on X on Sunday.

title: Dozens injured, at least 6 dead in Halloween weekend gun violence at nightlife districts across US
text:
(AP) - Mass shootings over the Halloween weekend in nightlife districts across the U.S. left at least six people dead and dozens injured, officials said.
The deadliest violence occurred in Dallas, where a handful of shootings in the city’s Deep Ellum neighborhood, a center of music, restaurants and nightlife, killed four people and injured 15 others, police said.
Police in college towns like Fayetteville, Arkansas; Birmingham, Alabama; Newark, Delaware, and Bloomington, Illinois, also reported shootings in their nightlife districts.
Dallas Police Chief Daniel Comeaux said investigators were still trying to determine if three separate shootings Saturday night over the span of about an hour and 15 minutes were related, and it wasn’t immediately known why they started. Comeaux said some arrests were made but he didn’t specify how many or what charges were involved.
“This is a really big scene. It’s spread out,” Comeaux said.
The department had increased police presence in the district before the shootings. No police officers were injured.
One shooting happened after a football game in Alabama
In Birmingham, one person was killed and eight others were wounded in two separate shootings just outside Legion Field after the annual ‘Magic City Classic’ football game on Saturday night, Mayor Randall Woodfin said at a news conference Sunday.
Two were listed in critical condition Sunday, fire officials said.
Alabama State and Alabama A&M are archrivals whose annual contest has been played for more than 100 years. Nearly 70,000 fans attended Saturday’s game, won by Alabama A&M 31-28. The event draws some of the largest crowds in the country for games played in their college football division.
Michael Pickett, chief of the Birmingham Police Department, said most spectators and families had left the stadium property after the game. The first shooting happened nearby, where vendors were set up along Graymont Avenue.
The circumstances of the shootings were unclear, and it was also unclear where the fatality occurred.
Police spokesperson De’Rell Freeman said one person had been detained and that “multiple weapons” were found.
Shootings in other nightlife districts
In Newark, Delaware, six people were shot late Saturday near the University of Delaware campus, Newark police Lt. Greg D’Elia said.
All six were transported to hospitals for treatment and their conditions were not available. A university spokesperson said they would provide updates on the investigation online as they become available.
Video shared on social media showed people running for safety from the scene. One stretch of the city’s Main Street was closed for several hours after the shooting, police said.
A shooting early Sunday in Bloomington, Illinois, left a 19-year-old woman dead and another woman in critical condition. Six others had injuries of an unknown nature that were not life-threatening. The shooting happened near the campus of Illinois Wesleyan University. Bloomington is about 135 miles (217 kilometers) southwest of Chicago.
In Fayetteville, Arkansas, six people were taken to hospitals with gunshot wounds from a shooting early Sunday near the University of Arkansas. No arrests have been made, police said in a news release. A preliminary investigation indicates an altercation preceded the shooting.
Halloween stores were the scene of two attacks
On Friday, two people were killed in separate shootings at Spirit Halloween stores in California and Michigan.
Police said a shooting inside a store in Fairfield, California was a targeted attack. Family members told police that the 31-year-old woman who died was pregnant. Six other people were wounded, police said. There were no immediate arrests.
In Madison Heights, Michigan, just north of Detroit, a 21-year-old man was fatally shot Friday afternoon. A man who was assaulted by bystanders as officers took him into custody was hospitalized with injuries that were not life-threatening, police said.
___
Raby reported from Charleston, West Virginia. AP reporter Claudia Lauer in Philadelphia contributed to this report.

title: Somali pirates seize Iranian fishing vessel, raising fears of attacks on cargo ships
text:
Somali pirates seize Iranian fishing vessel, raising fears of attacks on cargo ships
Somali pirates have seized an Iranian fishing vessel carrying 23 people, the Maritime Security Center Indian Ocean said, warning that the ship was approaching a commercial shipping lane and could become a floating base for further attacks.
The Azini was hijacked Thursday between the coastal towns of Bandar Bayla and Hafun in northeastern Somalia, a maritime security officer with the Puntland Maritime Police Force said Sunday.
Related video above: How the recent spike in Somali piracy is related to the US-Iran war.
The officer told The Associated Press that 12 pirates seized the vessel, which was carrying 21 Iranian crew members and two Somali security guards. He spoke on condition of anonymity because he wasn't authorized to speak with the media.
The crew’s safety was unknown, the center said in an alert dated Saturday. In an updated warning, it said that pirates could use the vessel as a “mother ship” to support attacks on commercial vessels.
The European Union’s naval Operation Atalanta was investigating. The center urged ships in the area to remain vigilant and report suspicious activity.
The seizure follows a resurgence of Somali piracy across the Gulf of Aden and western Indian Ocean. By August, pirates had hijacked six commercial vessels since April, with some attacks taking place far from Somalia’s coastline. The captures included the oil products tanker Sibu 1, seized about 136 nautical miles (252 kilometers) east of al-Mukalla, Yemen.
In September, Puntland authorities said pirates killed five crew members of the tanker MT Honour 25 before security forces recovered the vessel. The tanker had been held since April. Authorities said that 16 suspected pirates were detained.
The renewed piracy adds another danger for shipping in a region already disrupted by the Iran war. Attacks in the Strait of Hormuz and threats by Yemen’s Iran-backed Houthi rebels against Saudi-linked shipping through Bab el-Mandeb have complicated routes used to move oil to world markets.
Those disruptions have lengthened voyages and driven up tanker costs. The AP reported in September that some oil shipments diverted around Africa faced journeys up to a month longer, while daily spot charter rates for tankers transiting the Strait of Hormuz had reached $1 million.
International naval patrols and improved maritime security sharply reduced Somali piracy over the past decade. The latest seizures have renewed concerns about the threat to vessels off the country’s long coastline.

title: Beware those peddling untested fixes to public safety
text:
Matthew Guariglia is a senior policy analyst at the Electronic Frontier Foundation working on issues of surveillance, privacy, AI and government use of technology. Beryl Lipton is a senior investigative researcher at the Electronic Frontier Foundation, working on government transparency and law enforcement surveillance technology.
There’s a debate happening in Maine and every other corner of this country about whether automated license plate readers (ALPRs) have any place in our communities.
For the compelling but very complicated problem of “public safety,” ALPRs and other police surveillance technology have become easy, lucrative “solutions” to sell. Despite their capacity to obliterate privacy and facilitate abuse, these devices can now be found in every state in the country, spurred by marketing and police spending.
Fortunately, the public has become more aware of just how dangerous this technology is, and people across the country are responding with successful calls to end this technology in their communities.
These AI-powered cameras monitor roads in the U.S., and the details of the cars and people who pass them are logged in databases shared with police and government agencies nationwide. They make it easy to search for a person’s past locations or get an alert when someone enters a particular city.
In towns with ALPRs, it can be as simple as a search for your license plate number, vehicle type or bumper sticker to get a report on the places you’ve driven today, this month, or all year — no warrant necessary. There are now hundreds of thousands of ALPR cameras, many connected to a nationwide data sharing network accessible to thousands of government employees, in and out of state.
Abuse of these extensive networks is well-documented. ALPR platforms have facilitated nationwide high-tech police stalking. They have helped Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) harass our immigrant neighbors. They have been used to track and spy on abortion seekers across state lines.
During ICE raids in Maine, agents ran license plate information through government databases to threaten and follow protesters (it’s not clear whether ALPRs were also used). There are real dangers posed by government actors who can access personal information and use these surveillance systems for intimidation and harm.
Even though the tech’s big claims of success are backed, at best, by a dubious track record of lowering crime rate, surveillance salespeople remain just that: salespeople, eager to take the credit when crimes go down, sell you more products when it goes up and keep you locked into a subscription in the meantime.
Flock Safety, one of the largest ALPR companies, has grown fabulously wealthy convincing people that we need to live under constant surveillance to combat crime both large and small. “There are 18,000 cities to go after,” CEO Garrett Langley has said of Flock’s rapid expansion, referring roughly to the total number of policing agencies in the country, each one a sales target. The company is now worth billions of dollars across a portfolio of products that also includes drones and AI analysis.
Should tax dollars go to indiscriminate surveillance? Should we be paying to help some police officer in Texas pull up your last drive down the coast or up to camp? Mainers have the opportunity and the responsibility to ask their community leaders to do more with their money than install mass surveillance on our telephone poles and in our forests.
It’s not news that people in this state understand that doing the right thing and doing the established thing can be very different. Your privacy is a priceless resource, one almost
impossible to renew or restore once it’s gone.
York, Auburn and South Portland recently decided to pause their use of ALPRs. They are
among the approximately 400 towns and cities across the country that have canceled their contracts with Flock this year.
ALPRs are just one of the surveillance technologies being used, and Flock is just one company peddling surveillance. Drones are being deployed as flying cameras. Advanced AI systems are using data from police and data brokers to map out networks of friends and family. Predictive policing is making insinuations about who might commit crimes, undermining our right to a fair criminal justice system.
As the mega-corporations of the world race to extract and monetize every personal detail, cloaking unbridled surveillance as a necessity for public safety, now is not the time to let sales speak be a substitute for common sense. Crime is a real societal problem that requires thoughtful, empathetic and evidence-backed action, not surveillance-as-a-solution.
In our city councils, our budgets and our streets, let’s focus on the genuine needs of our communities and remain skeptical of anyone trying to sell dangerous technology as a one-size-fits-all fix for public safety.

title: Here’s the salary it takes to live comfortably in each US state in 2026
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
(SmartAsset) - As housing, grocery, transportation and other essential costs pressure household budgets, earning a six-figure salary no longer guarantees financial comfort in much of the U.S. A single adult now needs at least $80,000 a year to live comfortably in every state, while the threshold exceeds $100,000 in nearly half of states. For a family of four, the income needed to live comfortably is as much as $329,000.
SmartAsset used MIT Living Wage Calculator data to analyze the living wage in each state — what a full-time worker must earn to cover minimum basic needs — and adjusted it using the 50/30/20 budgeting rule. Under the rule, 50% of income goes to necessities like housing and utilities, 30% to discretionary spending and 20% to savings for retirement and emergencies. The resulting estimate represents the annual, pre-tax income needed to live comfortably in each state.
Key Findings
- In most states, a family of four needs at least $200,000 a year to live comfortably. That threshold applies in 40 states for households with two working adults and two children.
- Massachusetts and Hawai‘i are the most expensive states to live comfortably. Massachusetts is the most expensive state for a family of four, with an income requirement of $329,555. Hawai‘i is the most expensive state for single adults, who need $129,002.
- Montana had the largest increase in the income needed to live comfortably. For a single adult, that threshold rose 8.6% since 2025, the largest increase in the study.
- Mississippi and West Virginia are the least expensive states to live comfortably. Mississippi is the least expensive state for a family of four, with an income requirement of $187,533. West Virginia is the least expensive state for single adults, who need $81,245.
- In six states, the income needed to live comfortably has declined since 2025. Those states are Tennessee, Maryland, Louisiana, North Carolina, Mississippi and Texas. In each, a single adult needs less income in 2026 than in 2025.
