Gabby Williams leads Valkyries to WNBA championship
text:
Gabby Williams leads Valkyries to WNBA championship in second season
Gabby Williams scored her team's final 11 points of the third quarter and dazzled through the fourth on the way to 30 points, and the Golden State Valkyries captured a championship in just their second season by beating the Atlanta Dream 68-63 in a sensational first WNBA Finals Game 7 on Saturday night.
Video above: LSU star Flau'jae Johnson headed to Bay Area, picked by Golden State in WNBA Draft
Jordin Canada scored 18 points, Allisha Gray 16 and Angel Reese had eight points and 12 rebounds for the Dream, denied another championship in the franchise's fourth try.
Gray made two free throws with 11 seconds left then Atlanta forced a jump ball — Gray against Williams — and Veronica Burton corralled it and converted two free throws with 5.1 seconds to go.
“I'm just so blessed, this is insane!” said Burton, cut by Dallas two years ago.
Rhyne Howard's layup tied it at 57 with 2:41 left only for Williams to answer once more with a clutch 3-pointer. She converted two free throws with 1:40 remaining, then Kiah Stokes scored a late basket. Stokes pulled down 13 rebounds and blocked two more shots to cap her spectacular postseason.
Williams left Seattle with a great feeling about joining Golden State and its close-knit culture, returning to the Bay Area where she played youth basketball to build something special with the Valkyries — and she’s now done that. Fans chanted “Gabby! Gabby!” throughout the fourth quarter.
“All it took was good people,” she said. “All we heard last year was we don’t have no stars. We don’t have no talent. Yeah right! We got good people. We got good people. We got winners. We got people who are ready to put their bodies on the floor to win a game.”
When the final buzzer sounded, the violet-clad sellout crowd at Chase Center went into a frenzy as players sprinted onto the floor to hug and celebrate as confetti fell from the rafters.
“Ballhalla” had become “Boohalla” for this far-but-haunted Halloween night in the raucous arena. Now, with a women's championship to its name right alongside the one earned by the Golden State Warriors in 2022.
“We gotta build a bigger trophy case,” co-owner Peter Guber said.
The team that led at halftime in the first six matchups had won every game so far, and the Dream were ahead 30-24 at the break. Atlanta also had been 16-0 this season when Reese made at least one 3. The Dream's DeWanna Bonner became the first player in WNBA history to reach 600 career postseason defensive rebounds.
Valkyries coach Natalie Nakase changed her starting lineup in a move that paid huge dividends after Golden State fell behind 2-1, inserting Kaila Charles and Tiffany Hayes and bringing Kayla Thornton and Cecilia Zandalasini off the bench.
The 37-year-old Hayes, who came out of retirement two years ago and spent 10 seasons with the Dream, scored 11 points in the winner-take-all Game 7 and brought energy all series that made Nakase want to win for the veteran guard as much as anybody.
Valkyries owner Joe Lacob guaranteed a championship within the first five years for this franchise three years ago when the Bay Area was granted an expansion team, and in improbable, joyful fashion, his team accomplished it in Year 2. That was after becoming the first expansion organization to reach the playoffs in its inaugural year in 2025.
During the victory ceremony, Lacob shouted out the team and its leaders, while Nakase, general manager Ohemma Nyanin and President Jess Smith hugged. And Lacob thanked the fans who have sold out Chase Center for every game since Day 1.
“Ballhalla!” Lacob hollered.

title: Presque Isle, Fort Kent and Fort Fairfield Punch Tickets to Regional Soccer Finals
text:
Presque Isle, Fort Kent and Fort Fairfield Advance to Northern Maine Soccer Championships
Aroostook County is going to be well represented when the Northern Maine regional soccer championships get underway this week.
Saturday brought three more County teams into the championship picture, with Presque Isle's girls rolling to a shutout victory, Fort Kent's boys surviving a dramatic penalty-kick finish, and Fort Fairfield's girls winning a one-goal battle against Central Aroostook.
Not every County team was able to keep its season going, though. Presque Isle's boys fell to top-seeded John Bapst, while Madawaska's girls saw their tournament run end against Penobscot Valley.
With the semifinal round now complete, here's how Saturday's games played out and what's coming up on Championship Wednesday.
Girls Soccer
Class B North: Four Different Scorers Send Presque Isle to Regional Final
(3) Presque Isle 4, (7) Cony 0
Presque Isle's girls are heading to the Class B North championship after an impressive 4-0 victory over Cony on Saturday.
The third-seeded Lady Wildcats got goals from four different players, with Hailey Plant, Carrlyn Buck, Bridgid Schupbach and Willow Bugbee each finding the back of the net.
Cony came into the game after knocking off second-seeded Gardiner in the quarterfinals, but Presque Isle made sure the Rams wouldn't pull off another upset.
The shutout sends the Lady Wildcats into Championship Wednesday, where they'll face top-seeded John Bapst.
The Crusaders earned their spot with a 3-2 semifinal victory over Hermon, overcoming a halftime deficit to advance.
It's a matchup between the top seed and a Presque Isle team that's coming off back-to-back playoff victories, including Saturday's four-goal performance.
One more win would give the Wildcats the Class B North championship and send them to the state final.
Class D North: Fort Fairfield Edges Central Aroostook
(2) Fort Fairfield 1, (3) Central Aroostook 0
Fort Fairfield's girls are headed back to the Class D North championship after a hard-fought 1-0 semifinal victory over Central Aroostook.
It was another close game between two familiar County opponents, with the second-seeded Tigers finding the goal they needed and keeping the Lady Panthers off the scoreboard.
The shutout sends Fort Fairfield into Wednesday's regional championship, where the Tigers will face top-seeded Penobscot Valley.
Class D North: Penobscot Valley Ends Madawaska's Run
(1) Penobscot Valley 1, (5) Madawaska 0
Madawaska's tournament run came to an end Saturday with a narrow 1-0 loss against top-seeded Penobscot Valley.
The fifth-seeded Owls had earned their semifinal berth with an overtime victory over Ashland earlier in the week.
They gave the top seed a close game, but Penobscot Valley came away with the one-goal victory.
That sets up a Class D North championship between Fort Fairfield and Penobscot Valley on Wednesday at 4:15 p.m. in Presque Isle.
Both teams advanced through the semifinals with 1-0 shutouts, setting the stage for an interesting championship matchup.
Boys Soccer
Class B North: John Bapst Ends Presque Isle's Season
(1) John Bapst 5, (4) Presque Isle 0
Presque Isle's boys saw their postseason run come to an end Saturday against top-seeded John Bapst.
The Crusaders defeated the fourth-seeded Wildcats 5-0 to advance to the Class B North championship.
Presque Isle had reached the semifinals with a 4-1 quarterfinal victory over Erskine Academy, but couldn't find the same offensive success against the top seed.
While the boys' season comes to an end, Presque Isle will still have its girls team competing for a regional championship Wednesday.
Class C North: Fort Kent Survives Penalty Kicks at George Stevens Academy
(3) Fort Kent advances over (2) George Stevens Academy, 4-2 on penalty kicks following a 1-1 draw
Fort Kent's boys are headed to the Class C North championship, but they certainly had to earn it.
The third-seeded Warriors traveled to Blue Hill on Saturday to face second-seeded George Stevens Academy, and the semifinal turned into one of the closest games of the day.
James Wilson scored Fort Kent's regulation goal, with Dominic Cyr providing the assist.
The teams remained tied at one through regulation and overtime, sending the game to penalty kicks.
That's where Wyatt Daigle delivered the deciding kick for Fort Kent.
The Warriors won the shootout 4-2, securing their place in the regional championship.
And there's a pretty interesting storyline waiting for them.
Both the Fort Kent boys and girls will face Orono in their respective Class C North championship games.
The Lady Warriors advanced Friday with a 5-0 victory over Houlton, while the boys needed Saturday's penalty-kick finish to get past George Stevens Academy.
Now both Fort Kent teams are one win away from Northern Maine titles, and both will have to get past the Red Riots to bring those championships home.

title: All 9 people aboard a jet that crashed in Florida have died, transportation secretary says
text:
WEST PALM BEACH, Fla. (AP) — A business jet carrying nine people nose-dived into a South Florida neighborhood Sunday and erupted into a giant fireball that appeared to just miss homes before crashing near a busy roadway. All passengers on board were killed, U.S. Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said.
Duffy posted on X on Sunday that the Learjet 60 crashed in Palm Beach County at 12:50 p.m. and called it a “horrific tragedy.” The Federal Aviation Administration is sending a team to support the National Transportation Safety Board’s investigation into the cause, he said.
It was not immediately known if anyone on the Learjet 60 or on the ground in the Palm Beach County neighborhood was injured or killed.
The aircraft had departed Austin-Bergstrom International Airport in Texas and was headed to the Bahamas, according to the Federal Aviation Administratio. Authorities did not immediately say what caused the jet to go down or who was on it.
Jim Reynolds, a spokesperson for Austin-Bergstrom International Airport, said it was a private aircraft. He could not immediately provide details about who was on the flight.
“This is definitely a tragedy,” he said.
He said the tail number for the flight was N722BD.
Video shot from people inside their cars captured the terrifying moment the aircraft plunged from the sky, before striking near the roadway and exploding. Flames flickered around chunks of pavement lining the crater as people milled about, expressing shock it landed only feet from homes and only inches from passing vehicles. Thick black smoke engulfed the crash site.
It was unclear if the crash caused any damage to homes.
The crash occurred near Military Trail and 10th Avenue North. The Palm Beach County Sheriff’s Office closed roads in both directions and urged motorists to avoid the area. Firefighters and other emergency personnel rushed to the scene.
A woman working nearby said electricity in the area had been out for approximately two hours following the crash.
The circumstances of the crash remained under investigation.

title: 60-year-old hiker stranded on icy mountain ledge rescued after standing in same spot for 7 hours, rangers say
text:
KEENE, N.Y. (WCAX/Gray News) — A 60-year-old Canadian hiker was rescued from an icy New York mountain ledge after spending seven hours standing in the exact same spot, according to state forest rangers.
The rescue unfolded on Wednesday, Oct. 21, along the Mount Colden Trap Dike in the Adirondack Mountains.
Rangers said the hiker triggered an emergency satellite beacon around 6:30 p.m. after losing his crampons, traction spikes attached to winter boots, while traversing an icy ledge.
Without traction gear, the climber was unable to safely move up or down, leaving him stranded.
Rescue teams reached the man around 1a.m. and began working to secure him.
“When I got out to him and was trying just to get him secured to me, the thought went through my mind: if we both slip before I have him clipped in and on my tether, he’s dead. He’s like, gone,” Forest Ranger Jenna Curcio said.
Officials noted the Trap Dike route is rated as a fourth-class mountaineering climb and has claimed multiple lives over the years.
Rangers urged outdoor enthusiasts to thoroughly research mountain routes and carry proper gear before heading into steep backcountry terrain.

title: Obituary: Sherrill M. Cressman
text:
LOGANVILLE, Ga. – Sherrill M. Cressman, lovingly known as “Sherry”, passed away on Oct. 9, 2026, in Loganville, Ga. She was born on May 3, 1939, in Porter, the daughter of the late Ira and Gwendolyn Clark.
Sherry was raised in Maine and attended local area schools in Cornish. She graduated from Portland High School. Throughout her life, she was devoted above all to her family, embracing the roles of wife and mother with deep love and steady care. A dedicated wife, mother, and grandmother, she truly enjoyed taking care of her family, and that devotion shaped the life she lived each day.
She also found happiness in the simple and meaningful pleasures of home. Sherry enjoyed crafts and sewing, pursuits that reflected her creativity and care. She also took special joy in tending to her flowerbeds, where her patient attention and love of beauty could be seen in full bloom.
She was preceded in death by her husband, John Cressman and her sons, Adron Baughman and Brian Baughman.
Sherry is survived by her children, Leisha Dicenso, Kevin Baughman and his wife Lisa, Kendra Clement, and Shanna Ross and her husband Bryan. She is also survived by her sister, Suzanne Hume, and by her brother, Reginald Clark and his wife Dawn. In each of them, and in the family, she cared for so faithfully, her love and example will continue to live on.
Sherry will be remembered for the warmth she gave so freely, for the care she poured into her home and family, and for the quiet, lasting ways she made life more beautiful for those around her. Her memory will be treasured by all who knew and loved her.
Relatives and friends are invited to attend a celebration of life on Monday, Nov. 9, from 11 a.m. to 1 p.m., at Dolby, Blais & Segee Funeral Home, 434 River Rd., Windham.

title: Nearly 6 million Bodum French press coffee makers under recall
text:
(CNN) - Bodum is recalling nearly six million French press coffee makers...sort of.
It’s not a traditional recall.

Bodum said it happens when consumers use metal spoons to stir the coffee.

title: Harper’s Critique Falls Flat: Addressing the ‘Atlantic’ Article as a Black First-Year
text:
Let me start off by saying that I am a native New Yorker, born and raised, and I strangely relate to Harper. We’re both Black, come from first-generation college backgrounds, and I also can’t say that I’ve ever experienced overt racism aside from a dirty look or two. I assume this is the case for Harper, as he makes it a point to disapprove of his colleague “Ava” having a seemingly paranoid fear of white locals, as he grew up in a town similar to Lewiston.
However, my experience stems from growing up somewhat sheltered in a historically Black neighborhood, going to a majority Black school for most of my life, and the fact that I am currently listening to “Sexy Soulaan” as I write this line. So naturally, the first thing to tick me off about the article is Harper’s reference to New York City as a place of “money lust and voguish pop-ups and puffy-vested financiers and pandemic chaos,” because the city that shaped my love of directionless walks, churros on the beach, and block parties is so much more than that. I believe this sentiment encapsulates the primary issue that I have with the article: Harper’s tendency to oversimplify complex issues and reduce them to personal experiences.
It feels like Harper constantly dismisses or misinterprets the feelings of his colleagues, specifically “Ava,” and completely misses his own mark on what is to blame for the tokenization and problematic practices he describes. Frankly, regardless of the controversial nature of the word “cracker,” Harper presents as an untrustworthy character in my eyes. Ava’s drastic concerns of being hated, or even killed, for simply being Black are not unfounded in this day and age, especially as a woman in a year when racially motivated crimes were considerably highlighted.
It reminds me of my own family’s warnings to be prudent because that is just the reality we live in. I question why he didn’t just share his perspective, as it certainly would have made for an interesting conversation between two reasonable adults. He displays this attitude of quiet objection again when a colleague mentions avoiding a restaurant because of a student’s experience there. Instead of expressing his reproach and perhaps learning more about why his Black colleagues feel this way, he dismisses them as classist and paranoid. The worst part is that he does this while leading them to believe he’s a safe space to be given the benefit of the doubt. It feels two-faced and exploitative to disclose these private conversations.
This may have been an important conversation, but it was certainly not a productive one. If this article were to come out mid-year, let’s say April, one could argue that he’s giving students a genuine consideration to think about when choosing colleges. But this was released in August, when students are literally gearing up to move in. It feels like he just wanted to shake things up without caring who’s affected.
All this article does is leave Harper’s colleagues to the wolves and plants seeds of doubt in students of color like myself. Because now, I’m wondering who else is thinking like this? When I enter the workforce, will there be colleagues who feel I was hired because of my race? Was I hired because of my race? Logically, I know I shouldn’t be doubting myself because all of these competitive opportunities come from audacity and the ability to walk into a room confidently. Self-doubt won’t solve a hard equation, get me an internship, or raise my hand in class, but it is hard to ignore and not return to this spiral when it is highlighted. Frankly, these questions are distractions.
Harper is not here to clean up whatever he created, and that feels cowardly, because things like this break trust in the community. People stop being vulnerable because there’s people like Harper who go out and put them on blast later on. It is terrible because minorities, especially Black people, have historically been silenced and gone unbelieved. Harper himself is using race as a shield. It is so hard to shut down Harper because we have built up a society that holds these personal anecdotes with race to a certain significance and value. Who wants to be the hypocrite that discredits yet another Black man? Irony lines this story like glue, it’s ridiculous.
His reference to an incident where a white student was accused of attempting to “lynch” his roommate by calling the police on him seems…incomplete. I genuinely do not feel comfortable commenting on this because details are clearly missing. But, it is worth saying a white person’s participation in “progressive politics” does not make it impossible for them to act in a prejudiced manner. Regardless of whether the claims were true, Harper’s apparent belief that having class privilege as a Black student somehow bars you from racism and his immediate reflex to defend the white students involved is troubling, and consistent with his judgement towards his coworkers.
Now, I’m not saying that we should believe and rally behind every Black person who makes an accusation, or that Harper should have believed the allegations, but I find his reasoning for doubt to be deeply flawed and dangerous. Because, again, have you seen the state of this country? In the same way that Harper was shocked and offended by the issues that he only saw once he was hired, why would it be impossible for a “woke” white student to be covertly racist? He should know better than anyone that not everything is what it seems.
Harper’s concerning positions are extremely frustrating because they distract from the validity of the main point he makes: many elite institutions praise inclusive policies whilst harming minorities. I truly feel for him as I get further into the article. It must have been jarring to see the institution he worked for try to undermine the people who run it and for his work to be overshadowed by close-minded assumptions. The several microaggressions Harper experiences are extremely upsetting, and he is right to be angry. In particular, the “oops” and “ouch” solution that Professor “Sandra” suggests in response to Harper’s concerns about unqualified teachers teaching about race, not only trivializes the topic of race, but also puts too much attention and responsibility on students of color.
This misguided proposal not only assumes all students of color hold the same opinions about race, a flaw that Harper also points out, but it could also pit two valid expressions and experiences against one another by relying on personal validation as academic merit. Also, students of color may have an opinion about a comment, but not be able to articulate their rationale on the spot, which could discredit genuine concerns or put them in an uncomfortable spotlight that they’d rather avoid. Long story short, Harper is valid in his outrage at rampant tokenization because he’s right. It’s everywhere. It’s the disposable Black girlfriend trope that you won’t stop noticing once you pick it up. It’s using a Black model to misleadingly promote makeup products that don’t actually work on darker skin tones (looking at you YSL). It’s being placed on a MLK Day planning committee even though your work doesn’t substantially deal with race.
I’m not going to dismiss his feelings around being a “DEI hire,” because that is his experience and what right do I have to call it wrong? But I am not going to validate them either, because a lot of Harper’s evidence feels like a misdirected blame of progressive and inclusive values, rather than the paradoxically racist mechanisms elite institutions use to try to employ them. Harper ironically falls into the trap of using DEI, and the very idea of inclusion, as a scapegoat for the actions of the privileged. His disdain towards Bates’ incoming Race, Power Privilege, and Colonialism (RPPC) requirement also does not land well. Why would it be insane to take required classes on race in a country basically built on it? This proposed initiative makes sense considering Bates’s history as one of the first colleges to admit Black students. The concept of race is embedded in our society and influences everything, from the way neighborhoods are built to the food we eat.
Nobody raises eyebrows at Columbia requiring swim classes or the numerous Catholic colleges that require theology. During my first few weeks here, I’ve met people from all over the country, out the Deep South to as far west as California, as well as international students who live around the world. I seriously doubt that everyone was taught about US race relations and the lasting influences of American colonialism beyond a few pages in a textbook.
In fact, I know this is true because several states made laws limiting the instruction of Critical Race Theory (CRT), the idea that racism is systemic rather than individual or isolated, in the past few years. As a first-year student who’s had to sit through at least two hours of the school’s new Perspective dialogues and pre-orientation workshops, I sincerely doubt any racist will suddenly change their mindset or that teenagers will stop making stupid decisions because of these lessons. However, the effort to move towards a more equitable and safe space is necessary. It is quite literally the school’s responsibility to take claims of racism seriously, so the idea of a racism self-audit seems completely reasonable.
My issue with Harper is not that he calls out Bates. It’s that he misdirects his anger towards progressive values and I can’t help but ask what the point of writing this was or, at the very least, why he wrote it in this way. He ironically gives himself over to conservative voices as apparent proof that schools should not have more inclusive policies, becoming a token for discriminatory causes that harm marginalized groups even more.
But don’t let my views become evidence for the “right” position. I don’t want to be the “last Black person talked to.” In an attempt to answer my own question, I suppose a good thing to come out of this article is that it prompts students to ask questions about higher education that they are often too scared to face. Yes, academia is deeply racist at times. Now, are we going to continue ignoring it or are we actually going to do something about it?

title: Villanova, Notre Dame open college basketball season following papal audience
text:
Villanova, Notre Dame open college basketball season following papal audience
They’ve been blessed by the pope. And now it’s finally time for some hoops.
The Villanova and Notre Dame men’s and women’s teams are meeting in a doubleheader in Rome on Sunday to open the college basketball season.
The event, dubbed the Eternal City Tip-Off, was created to honor the first American pope.
Chicago-born Pope Leo XIV received all four teams in an audience at the Vatican on Saturday.
Related video: Notre Dame coaches reflect on meeting Pope Leo while in Rome
Leo told the teams from his alma mater Villanova and fellow Catholic university Notre Dame that in matters of sport, the pontiff is neutral.
Then the pope, who was born Robert Prevost, said his former self might disagree.
“Prevost has another opinion, but we won’t do that now,” he said to laughs during a whooping, cheering audience of 7,000 people from both schools — players, coaches, fans and their families — in the Vatican audience hall.
The games are being played at the 11,000-seat Palazzo dello Sport, which is located about a half-hour drive from the Vatican.
While Leo, who underwent lung cancer surgery last month, was not expected to attend the games, a contingent of cardinals and other Vatican officials was expected at the arena.
The schools also brought their team chaplains to Rome.
The men’s game starts at 3:30 p.m. local (9:30 a.m. ET) and is being shown on Fox with Bill Raftery as the analyst. The women’s game, which features the only ranked team of the day in No. 13 Notre Dame, is slated for 6 p.m. (noon ET) on FS1.

title: Trump administration’s social media posts ahead of elections criticized for being inflammatory
text:
(AP) - The Trump administration’s online accounts are circulating images of a pumpkin carved with a sombrero design and a fake Halloween-themed background around a Black man apparently accused of food assistance fraud, in social media posts slammed by critics as inflammatory rhetoric.
Only days before the midterm elections, the posts coincide with the government’s sweeping campaign to show its aggressive immigration enforcement, and highlight efforts to crack down on fraud to save taxpayers money when rising healthcare costs and other economic stressors have made affordability a top voter concern.
Agriculture Secretary Brooke Rollins posted Saturday on the social platform X a photo of the Black man standing in front of stacks of what appear to be U.S. currency with the headline, SNAP FRAUDSTER, an apparent reference to the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program, formerly known as food stamps.
He is holding aloft what appears to be a bill set aflame.
“Some costumes come with a price tag. This one comes with a prison sentence,” it says to the backdrop of fake Spirit Halloween costume packaging.
Another photo posted by the White House on X on Thursday showed a pumpkin with the shape of a sombrero carved across it and the words “Spooky szn is here.”
The post by Rollins, who was nominated by Trump to serve as the U.S. Secretary of Agriculture in November 2024, appears to be taken from an Instagram post from September 2025 by an account under the name Shawty Dred.
Earlier this month, Mercedes Reshard New, identified by the Justice Department as a social media personality also known as “Shawty Dred,” was arrested on federal charges for fraudulently obtaining more than $4 million in Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program benefits in Georgia.
It’s not the first time the White House has been accused of posting inflammatory images on official government social media accounts.
Just over a year ago during the government shutdown, the White House revived a deepfake video posted by Trump of House Democratic leader Hakeem Jeffries in a fake mustache and sombrero to accuse the Democrats of acting on behalf of illegal immigrants instead of U.S. citizens. Jeffries described the meme as bigoted. They played it on repeat in the White House briefing room, though Vice President JD Vance promised that the “sombrero memes will stop” when Democrats agreed to end the shutdown.
The NAACP did not respond to an email seeking comment, nor did the White House or Rollins.
The Trump administration in recent weeks has ratcheted up its anti-immigrant rhetoric and accusations of fraud, including against U.S. Rep. Ilhan Omar whose Washington, D.C., home was searched by federal agents earlier this month. Federal authorities are investigating potential fraud in her family’s immigration paperwork. Omar, who was born in Somalia, is a naturalized U.S. citizen.
It also has taken a series of punitive steps linked to allegations of fraud in mostly Democratic-led states, including California and Minnesota whose governors accused the federal government of targeting their states for political reasons.
Federal prosecutors said in a news release Oct. 21 that the influencer, New, controlled more than 350 fraudulent SNAP accounts under stolen identities between January 2020 and July 2026. He allegedly applied for his company, Shawty Dred LLC, to become an authorized SNAP retailer and used EBT debit cards to extract about $4 million from the accounts.
New’s Instagram account, which has more than two million followers, has flaunted his extravagant lifestyle, federal prosecutors said. Posts depict him flying on private jets, posing with Rolls-Royce vehicles in front of his “super mansion,” and handling massive stacks of cash.
“Instead of this money feeding families in need, New, the social media personality known as ‘Shawty Dred,’ allegedly used the cash to bankroll a life of luxury,” Special Agent in Charge of FBI Atlanta Marlo Graham said in the release.
New was indicted by a federal grand jury Oct. 7 on dozens of counts of mail fraud and aggravated identity theft, and one count each of SNAP fraud and illegal transactions with access devices. He was arrested Oct. 13 and remains in federal custody.
According to Fulton County jail records, New has been arrested multiple times on suspicion of crimes including identity theft, insurance fraud, financial transaction card fraud, forgery and simple assault.
A federal defender listed in court records as representing New, Joseph Austin, did not return a phone message.

title: Is it a grouse or a partridge? Maine hunters weigh in
text:
This was originally published Nov. 3, 2025.
If you’re high-stepping through brush and second-growth bushes following a birdie pointer, listening to an electronic caller beep and carrying an expensive double-barrel 20-gauge at port arms, you are likely hunting grouse.
If you are slowly driving a backwoods road or stalking an old skidder trail, you are probably hunting partridge. You might carry a well-worn single shot or your grandfather’s rattling corn-shucker pump, keeping an eye out for a bird on a stump or sunning on a bank.
Veteran upland bird gunners would argue that the difference between grouse and partridge mostly depends on your location: Aroostook County or southern Maine.
Many waterfowl and upland enthusiasts won’t fire their scattergun unless the target is in the air. I’ve hunted for several decades and shot Ol’ Pat sitting, running and flying. I guarantee you can’t tell the difference once the bird is in a savory stew or frying pan.
Ruffed grouse populations are cyclic and often weather-dependent during the spring hatching. Some years a hunter can drive or walk all morning and spot only a bird or two. Some autumns, a limit can be bagged in an hour or so.
During these years of plenty, I like to up the challenge by occasionally using my Thompson Contender .410 single-shot handgun.
Greg Palm of Presque Isle, a longtime hunting companion and recently noted for accomplishing a rare big game Grand Slam two years in a row, increases the challenge by using a five-shot .410 Ruger Judge revolver.
Over the years, I’ve met dozens of hunters who favor a .22 rifle with a low-power scope. Their theory: a headshot ruins no meat, and if they miss, there’s likely another partridge down the road.
Veteran sportsmen who have harvested plenty of upland birds, waterfowl and big game often switch weapons to increase the challenge. When birds are plentiful, it evens the odds a bit.
Another common practice is replacing semi-auto or pump shotguns with double-barrel or single-shot models. I often carry my aging break-action Stevens over-under .22 and 20-gauge combo that dates back to my early teens. It limits my range a bit, and I figure one bird at a time is fine during plentiful years, so accuracy becomes more important.
There’s an elite cadre of grouse gunners who raise the odds by using only a .410 or the more unique 28-gauge. Many of these aficionados utilize a well-trained dog to locate and hold their feathered quarry for a flush, which further boosts the challenge by only shooting at flying birds. Every flush is an adventure. Add uneven ground, thick cover and fewer pellets in the small-gauge shell, and each opportunity boosts the adrenaline level.
Last fall, I met two grouse hunters who had really amped up their tactics to bag a brush chicken. One was armed with a compound bow, and two weeks later, a second sport I happened upon was using a crossbow. Each had birds in their vests and had missed a couple of chances.
Other than a boomerang, slingshot or rock and sling — all of which surely don’t fit current regulations — archery precision is a tough endeavor. But for many longtime hunters, changes in tactics, techniques, weapons and ammunition keep each outing more exciting and adventurous.
Thus far this partridge season has yielded above-average results, and we have until the end of December to enjoy more action.
Hopefully, a number of the more experienced hunters will be inclined to up the challenge a bit, understanding for most that the “how” is far more important than the “how many.”
Just a few alterations in gear and technique can shine a whole new light on the enjoyment and excitement of an old, treasured pastime. There’s still lots of time to perk up your outings for partridge, or grouse if you prefer.
On the ground or in the air, it’s all fair — gear up and get out there soon and often.

title: Obituary: Suzanne Lausier
text:
SAN MATEO, Calif. – Suzanne Lausier, 76, of San Mateo, Calif., died peacefully on Tuesday, Oct. 20, 2026, in Burlingame, Calif. Born in Danforth, Maine in 1949, the sixth of nine children, she was a quiet observer in a large family and loved music all her life, playing saxophone and guitar and always singing.
She studied history in college and found her calling in caring for those with developmental disabilities, first at the Pineland Center in Maine, then as a special education teacher in Durham, N.C. She earned a Master of Education at UNC and retired near family in Rhode Island and California.
She is survived by her daughter, Annie (Michael) Chrien; grandchildren Owen and Olivia; sisters Joan, Annette, and Evangeline; brother Conrad (Marie); and many nieces and nephews.
She was preceded in death by her parents, Conrad and Marguerite (Cropley) Lausier; and siblings Julie, Joe, Charles, and David.
A private family viewing was held Friday, Oct. 23. A celebration of life will be announced.

title: Halloween queen Heidi Klum deserves a hand for her costume in 2026
text:
(Gray News/AP) – Model and television host Heidi Klum has gone all out with her costume on Halloween year after year, and 2026 did not disappoint.
Klum revealed her masterpiece on social media late Saturday after much anticipation, having given clues throughout the day.
The supermodel defended her crown as Halloween queen by transforming into a severed version of her own hand.
Klum was unrecognizable, with only her eyes and mouth showing, blood dripping from her mouth as she stuck her tongue out. The top of the hand ended in a gory assortment of dangling ligaments and tendons. She had an ensemble of helpers in blood-stained hazmat suits.
The idea came to her last year to be a giant hand — specifically her own left hand, with long red nails, a thumb ring, and her engagement ring and wedding band.
“I looked at my hand and I thought, ‘Hey, I think I could fit my body in this somehow,’” Klum said.
She debuted the costume with a video post showing her actual fingers walking down the floor, and then halfway through the video, it transitions into her costume with her legs as two of her fingers.
Klum said it took about five to six hours to get into her hand costume this year, but making it took a lot longer. She posted hints on her Instagram earlier in the day as bloodied prosthetics were applied to her face.
“Hands down, the hardest thing is carrying it,” Klum said. “It’s quite heavy.”
Last year, Klum dressed up as Medusa, complete with moving snakes. The year before, she was an elaborate female version of E.T. that took a year of planning.
Her husband, musician Tom Kaulitz, did not attend this year because he was on tour. But the details on her costume include a tattoo of his name on her ring finger, along with her palm lines and veins.
“A little bit of Tom is with me,” she said.

title: Shooting at Spirit Halloween store in California leaves pregnant woman dead and 6 wounded
text:
(AP) - A targeted shooting inside a Spirit Halloween store in Northern California left a pregnant woman dead and six other people wounded, police said.
Gunfire rang out at about 8:30 p.m. Friday inside the store, which sells Halloween costumes and decor, at the Solano Town Center in Fairfield, the city police department said Saturday in a statement on Facebook.
The shooting “stemmed from a targeted incident involving one suspect,” police said.
The woman who died was identified by police as Constance Hages, 31, and family members told authorities she was pregnant.
Three male victims, ages 16, 19 and 32, were in critical condition, and a 23-year-old man was hospitalized in critical but stable condition.
Two other men, ages 19 and 43, were treated for gunshot wounds and released from the hospital.
No arrests have been made. Authorities said they were reviewing video and other evidence “to identify the individual responsible for this heinous act of violence.”
The department said no additional information would be released at this time.
“We recognize the concern and uncertainty this incident has created throughout our community, particularly with the many Halloween events and celebrations planned for today,” the department said. “We understand that an incident of this nature is frightening and deeply unsettling. We encourage everyone to remain vigilant, look out for one another, and report any suspicious activity.”
Solano Town Center, which has 130 stores and restaurants, remained open but said it was canceling its planned trick-or-treating event scheduled for later in the day “in light of last night’s event.”
“We appreciate your patience and understanding during this time,” the mall said in a statement.
The FBI’s Sacramento office said it was assisting Fairfield police in the investigation.
Fairfield, a city of some 120,000 residents, is about 37 miles (60 kilometers) southwest of Sacramento and halfway between there and San Francisco.

title: Mild stretch returns to Maine ahead of rain chance
text:
Mild stretch returns to Maine ahead of rain chance
Whether or not it's a manic Monday, it will be a mild one!

Whether or not it's a manic Monday, it will be a mild one!
Skies will be mostly clear tonight, with lows in the upper 30s and light, variable winds. Monday will be partly sunny, with highs in the upper 60s and southwest winds around 10 mph. Monday night will be partly cloudy during the evening before becoming mostly cloudy, with lows in the mid-40s and light, variable winds.
Tuesday will be partly sunny in the morning before becoming mostly cloudy, with highs in the mid-60s and light, variable winds. Tuesday night will be cloudy, with lows in the mid-40s. title: Obituary: John S. Patchell
text:
ST. AUGUSTINE, Fla. – John S Patchell, 81, passed away peacefully on Oct. 3, 2026, at his home in St. Augustine, Fla. after losing his battle to cancer.
John was born in Portland, Maine, to parents Joseph and Helen Patchell. He graduated from South Portland High School in 1963 and attended SMVTI majoring in Electronics. He then became a computer technician for Burroughs, working at Casco Bank in Portland for many years and continued his career working for Unisys Corporation. John was a jack of all trades, building and repairing with family and friends.
John moved to Florida with his wife, Diane, of 37 years, where they lived for more than 20 years. He ran a small repair service for local musicians repairing amplifiers. John loved coming back to Maine and spending time on Sebago Lake and visiting family and friends.
John was predeceased by his father, Joseph Patchell, his mother, Helen Patchell; and his sister Joan Coyne.
John is survived by his brother, Donald Patchell of South Portland, Maine, his sister Virginia (Patchell) Frederick of Scarborough, Maine; his wife Diane Patchell of St. Augustine, Fla.; his four daughters Wendy Miles of Freeport, Maine, Kimberly Hibbard of Pownal, Maine, Susan Harlow of Yarmouth, Maine, Deborah Cates of Auburn, Maine, and his stepson Jerry Bridgham of St. Augustine, Fla. His family included nine grandchildren; 11 great-grandchildren; and 10 nieces and nephews.
Due to John’s request, there will be no formal services. He will be dearly missed by all.
In lieu of flowers,
donations can be sent to:

title: Andreas Almgren wins men’s race in NYC in marathon debut, Sheila Chepkirui wins women’s race
text:
NEW YORK (AP) — Andreas Almgren of Sweden won the men’s race of the New York City Marathon in his debut in the event while Sheila Chepkirui of Kenya won the women’s race for the second time Sunday.
Almgren was making his debut at 26.2 miles after a successful career running half-marathons. He pulled away from Yemaneberhan Crippa of Italy in the final mile to take the victory in 2 hours, 6 minutes and 1 second. Crippa finished 13 seconds behind. Kamohelo Mofolo of Lesotho was third, edging out defending champion Benson Kipruto.
Chepkirui, who also won the race in 2024, pulled away from countrymate Hellen Obiri in the final 150 meters to seal the victory in 2:24:36. American Jessica McClain finished second, passing Obiri — a two-time winner — in the final few strides. It was the first time a U.S. woman finished in the top three since 2018. McClain was 6 seconds behind Chepkirui.
It was the 50th time that the race has run through all five boroughs of the city. There were just over 2,000 competitors in 1976, the seventh running of the race, including only 88 women. About 60,000 runners stepped up to the starting line Sunday, with nearly half of them women.

title: Nobleboro Planning Board Approves Cell Tower Proposal
text:
The Nobleboro Planning Board approved the application for a cellphone tower from Blue Sky LLC with conditions at its meeting on Oct. 15.
The approval comes after months of back and forth between the town and the Massachusetts company for over a year.
In June 2025, Blue Sky Towers LLC, in partnership with Verizon, submitted an application to the Nobleboro Planning Board to discuss the installation of a wireless communication facility after discovering a “coverage gap” in Nobleboro.
In November 2025, Blue Sky Towers LLC withdrew the application from the planning board and submitted an application to the appeals board due to the town’s land use ordinance that restricts the location of what the town identifies as facilities. The appeals board denied the variance on Jan. 27. The board determined the application did not involve traditional dimensional standards such as lot size, frontage, lot coverage or yard setbacks.
The company requested a dimensional variance that would allow applicants to build the tower outside of the selected location to fill an identified coverage gap identified by Verizon.
Blue Sky filed a federal lawsuit against Nobleboro in February stating its belief the town’s land use ordinance, along with the appeals board’s decision not to grant a dimensional variance for a proposed cell tower, violates federal telecommunication laws and that federal law prevents the town from applying a provision that requires a 300-foot setback from Route 1.
The lawsuit is currently on hold pending the completion of findings of fact.
“Right now the case is on hold and it would probably be dismissed by agreement between the parties once the process is finished,” town attorney lawyer Jeffrey Thaler said.
The plans approved on Oct. 15 are for a 176-foot telecommunications tower with a 6-foot lightning rod at 29 Starter Drive. The property is owned by Anthony and Rebecca Baldwin, according to the application. The owners of the property declined comment when reached by phone on Monday, Oct. 26.
As part of the conditions of approval, Code Enforcement Officer Evan Pothier is to make sure the tower is at least 600 feet from the high water mark for the larger pond on the abutting property.
Nobleboro Planning Board Vice Chair Marianne Pinkham said that if the code enforcement officer thinks the property needs a second look, Nobleboro will provide a survey at the expense of Blue Sky.
“To figure out whether it’s 600 feet from the pond, there would have to be access permitted by an abutting landowner for part of the survey, or access for the code enforcement officer,” Thaler said. “The code enforcement officer will talk with the abutting landowner to see if he will allow him to walk the land.”
According to Blue Sky engineer Jesse Moreno, the abutting property owners have not given permission to Blue Sky to go on their property to conduct a survey. Alternate planning board member Matthew Benner suggested that if the abutters do not allow access on their land to conduct a survey, the code enforcement officer will base the measurements on the best of his ability.
Discussing the light mechanism, the board made sure the lights on the tower will not be distracting to passersby and will only be pointing downward. The tower will be a muted gray color to “match the sky,” according to planning board Chair Matthew Lewis.
At the Oct. 15 meeting, Blue Sky’s real estate lawyer Mark Beaudoin, a partner at Nixon Peabody LLP, said it has been undecided when construction will start.
The Nobleboro Planning Board will meet next at 5:30 p.m. on Thursday, Nov. 19 at the town office, at 192 Route 1. For more information, call 563-8816 or go to nobleboro.maine.gov.

title: Selma Blair says ‘I am so sorry’ after arrest in alleged flight attendant assault
text:
(CNN) - Actress Selma Blair apologized Friday on social media for the alleged actions that led to her arrest last month.
Blair is accused of striking a flight attendant and biting another crew member during a flight. She also allegedly kicked a nurse who was involved with her transport.
In an Instagram post, Blair addressed the incident.
“Not one day ever have I intended to hurt or frighten anyone a day in my life,” Blair said. “And so to the people that I disappointed, that I hurt, that I frightened, alarmed, I am so sorry.”
Blair also spoke about what comes next.
“Right now, I’m going to be taking care of my health. And my son. And thinking of you all with gratitude and love,” she said.
Blair pleaded not guilty to assault on Oct. 12 and was released on bail.

title: Connecticut man arrested for OUI after police pursuit ends in crash in Naples
text:
Connecticut man arrested for OUI after police pursuit ends in crash in Naples
A Connecticut man is facing multiple charges, including operating under the influence, after leading Maine State Police on a pursuit that ended in a crash at a Naples restaurant early Sunday morning.
Stuart John McClure, 32, of New London, Connecticut, was arrested near the crash scene and charged with operating under the influence, eluding an officer, aggravated driving to endanger and criminal speed.
According to Maine State Police, a trooper spotted a 2015 Jeep Cherokee speeding and driving erratically on Route 302 in Bridgton at about 12:30 a.m. Sunday.
The trooper initiated a traffic stop, and McClure initially pulled over before accelerating away at a high rate of speed.
The trooper, who suspected McClure might be impaired, pursued the vehicle for several miles before it crashed as it entered the causeway in Naples.
Police say the Jeep struck the awning and porch support beams at Rick's Café.
McClure then ran from the crash scene but was found hiding in shrubbery along the causeway shoreline, according to state police.
He was taken by ambulance to Maine Medical Center, where he is being treated for injuries that are not considered life-threatening.
The Cumberland County Sheriff's Office and Bridgton Police Department assisted Maine State Police with the incident.

title: Connecticut man charged with OUI after chase ends in crash into Naples restaurant
text:
NAPLES, Maine (WABI) - A Connecticut man faces multiple charges after leading Maine State Police on an early morning vehicle pursuit that ended when his SUV crashed into a local restaurant, according to authorities.
Stuart John McClure, 32, of New London, Connecticut, was arrested and charged with Operating Under the Influence, Eluding, Aggravated Driving to Endanger, and Criminal Speed.
Police said a state trooper initiated a traffic stop around 12:30 a.m. after spotting a Jeep speeding and driving erratically along Route 302 in Bridgton.
According to police, the driver initially stopped, but allegedly sped away as the trooper approached, prompting a pursuit that stretched for several miles.
The chase ended when McClure lost control of the Jeep entering the Naples causeway, crashing into the awning and porch support beams of Rick’s Café.
Police said McClure fled the vehicle on foot but was located shortly after hiding in shrubbery along the shoreline.
McClure was taken by ambulance to Maine Medical Center for treatment of non-life-threatening injuries. The Bridgton Police Department and Cumberland County Sheriff’s Office assisted in the incident.

title: Trump's rallies in Iowa and Kansas come as Republicans fight to keep Senate and House control
text:
WASHINGTON (AP) — President Donald Trump is closing out the final days of a turbulent midterm campaign with rallies in two states he has handily won in the past, underscoring the defensive posture his Republican Party is taking as the elections become a referendum on his White House second term.
His first stop is scheduled for Sunday afternoon in Dubuque, Iowa, where Republicans are battling to hold onto a critical Senate seat along with the governor’s office. The 2nd Congressional District, which includes Dubuque, has also become competitive as the GOP works to protect its fragile majority in the House.
Trump plans to close out the last weekend of campaigning before Election Day on Tuesday with a visit to Salina, Kansas. Adam Hamilton is mounting a robust bid to become the first Kansas Democrat to win a Senate seat in 94 years.
With more than 52 million votes already cast, the trips mark Trump’s return to his trademark rallies after taking a one-day break on Saturday. Republicans initially canceled the Iowa and Kansas stops only for them to be abruptly rescheduled as Trump works to preserve a Senate majority at risk of slipping away.
The travel is a reminder of how starkly the political environment has changed since Trump’s last campaign. In 2024, he worked to flip states that had previously backed Democrat Joe Biden in 2020. This year, Trump has focused largely on states he has dominated before as voters, including previous supporters, question the economic fallout of his decision to impose tariffs and launch the war in Iran.
While those dynamics have helped Democrats in their bid to regain congressional majorities, they face challenges of their own, including holding on to a crucial Senate seat in Michigan. The Democratic nominee, Abdul El-Sayed, is spending the final days of the campaign in an increasingly public feud with one of his primary opponents, Rep. Haley Stevens, that threatens to divide the party heading into the election.

title: Enrollment down, scores at record high for Lewiston’s multilingual students
text:
Multilingual student enrollment in Lewiston schools has declined by about 200 students this year, even as the program reports a record improvement in an annual English proficiency test for those students, officials say.
Lysa McLemore shared the data with the Lewiston School Committee last week as she celebrated the success of the annual WIDA Access Test, which measures English proficiency in multilingual learners. The scores were the highest she’s seen in her 14 years with the district, she said, with 143 students scoring high enough to exit the multilingual student program.
While proficiency is up, enrollment is lower this school year after climbing steadily over the previous four years to a high of more than 2,000 students, McLemore said.
The trend is not unique to Lewiston: multilingual student enrollment has also decreased in Portland at the same time that it has increased statewide.
It’s unclear if the drop in the state’s two biggest cities is related to the uptick in U.S. Immigration and Custom Enforcement agents there, McLemore said, because families relocate for a variety of reasons that are not often disclosed or shared with school officials.
“The majority of students who have left or enrolled (in the Lewiston schools this year) have relocated to, or from other school districts, both within Maine and out of state,” she said.
A student can be considered a multilingual student if English isn’t their first language.
Recently, President Donald Trump’s Administration repealed an order created under former President Barak Obama that provided universal guidelines to school districts on their obligations to teach English learners. Maine has its own guidance that school districts follow.
WHAT DOES DATA SHOW?
In the state’s two largest school districts, multilingual enrollment has fluctuated over the years.
Portland reached a high of about 2,000 students in 2023-24, with the number declining to 1,629 this year. In Lewiston, the number increased since 2021 to a high of over 2,000 students last year, before dropping by about 200 this year to 1,796.
The number of multilingual students can fluctuate for numerous reasons.
Portland’s superintendent, Ryan Scanlon, talked about the trend this winter when building the current year’s school budget, as overall enrollment across the district continues to decrease. For multilingual students, it could be because of a decrease in immigrant migration to Maine, he said.
“We had the influx of students in the 2023-2024 school year where students were new to Maine and new to Portland. That flow stopped. There’s been a significant reduction in immigrant movement to Maine and to the United States as a whole,” Scanlon said at a school board meeting.
In Portland, students speak a total of 61 languages. In Lewiston, students speak 39 different languages. The most common among both districts are Somali, Portuguese, Arabic, Swahili, Kinyarwanda and Spanish.
The most recent state immigration data is only through 2023, so it’s difficult to tell if Maine has seen a reduction in immigrants in the years since, like Scanlon suggested. But nationally, the U.S. Census reported earlier this year that there’s been a historic decline in international migration to the United States. A spokesperson from the Center for New Mainers did not respond to multiple attempts for a comment.
But statewide, the number of multilingual students has increased.
In 2016, there were 5,145 multilingual students across the state. Now, there are 8,004. They make up 4.7% of Maine’s overall student population, which has decreased since 2016.
Data suggests that multilingual speaking families are moving out of Lewiston and Portland and heading to the areas nearby, like Biddeford, Westbrook and South Portland, as those school districts continue to see a steady increase yearly with multilingual students.
A spokesperson from the Maine Department of Education said they do not know what is causing the shift in Maine’s enrollment numbers because they do not have the ability to survey families.
WIDA ACCESS TEST
As multilingual student enrollment goes up stateside, so do the WIDA Access Test scores.
The annual multi-day test is given to English learners in kindergarten through 12th grade. It measures a student’s English progress through reading, listening, writing and speaking. The goal is to “exit,” showing that a student has demonstrated they no longer need to take the test or be in the program.
Just after the pandemic in 2021-2022, the state had an average exit rate of 8.9%. It decreased to 7.8% in the 2023 school year, then to 7.5% in 2024 before increasing to 8.8% in 2025, state data shows.
McLemore first shared the scores in June, but reflected on the success at last week’s school committee meeting. In June, she mentioned that it’s difficult to compare Lewiston’s 7% exit rate to the state average of 8.8% because some districts may only have a few students taking the test.
“That’s the most students we have exited in as long as I can remember. Maybe ever,” McLemore told the school committee. “Through data analysis, we learned the average scale score growth —the amount of growth in the four domains of reading, writing, listening and speaking — is up.”
McLemore thinks two factors may have contributed to the student’s high test scores.
The district has implemented a new curricula in the multilingual department and the staff have had a “significant amount” of professional development on the most successful ways of teaching to multilingual learners.
“We’re doing a good job in making decisions about curriculum and resource adapting so it aligns with the needs of multlingual and English speakers,” she said.

title: Experienced outdoorsmen still make mistakes. I made one recently in western Maine.
text:
Summer is long in the rearview mirror, and the autumn foliage has come and gone. Winter is a ways off, but the telltale signs — brisk winds, cold temperatures and gray skies — are here. The woodpile outside the back door is piled high, and the last of the kindling has been split and stored. I’d like to say I’m ready for the snow, but are we ever really?
As I sit at the dining table with a steaming cup of tea, I’m reflecting on what was one of the best summers in a long time. Backpacking, hiking, camping, sea kayaking and carousing hither and yon. It was a real memory-maker of good fun.
One summer trip in particular stands out. A short sojourn to the mountains had me both chuckling and shaking my head, two things I’m doing right now as I think back on the silliness of it all. Everything worked out, but jeez, where was my foolish head at the time?
It was mid-August, and I had a few blank days on the calendar. Blueberry Mountain in the Weld area of western Maine had been on my to-do list for quite some time. I’d last climbed the 2,958-foot peak two decades ago, so I was overdue to tag it again. I could also get a revised description for the next edition of the “Maine Mountain Guide” out of the effort.
I informed my wife of my plans. She, of course, shook her head and returned to preparing the camper for the Lubec trip. I hastily — too hastily, as you will soon see — packed my camping and hiking gear into the truck.
The next day I was off to Mount Blue State Park, where I’d reserved a couple of nights at the campground.
That’s when things started to go south, so to speak.
Campsite No. 72. I popped up the screen tent and secured it in place. Then I took the big air mattress, which I’d inflated at home, and put it inside. Looking down at the mattress, I immediately got a sinking feeling. I went to the back seat and, lo and behold, there was no green stuff sack with my sleeping bag inside. And no pillow.
Yup, I had no sleeping bag. With two nights in the low 50s forecast.
Great! You knucklehead. Fortunately, there’s always a fleece blanket covering the back seat, so I grabbed that and spread it on the mattress. I took my duffel bag of clothes, wrapped it in my beach towel and threw it down for a pillow. Then I piled on the puffy jacket, fleece hoodie and whatever else I could find. It would have to do. Yikes.
On the way to the beach on Lake Webb, I stopped at the ranger station and asked whether they had any “spare” sleeping bags for such occasions. They had none, but suggested Walmart in Farmington or Mexico.
Returning to the campsite, it was time to kindle a campfire, crack a beer and get started on dinner. It would be a simple affair of boiled hot dogs, a can of Spaghetti-O’s (yes, you read correctly — the kid in me is still there), Hannaford potato salad and sliced tomatoes and cucumbers with Italian dressing.
I looked for the camp stove. And looked. And looked. Nada.
I found a fuel canister, the pots and utensils but no stove. Goodness gracious, what the heck is wrong with me, I thought?
The blaze was now going well, so I filled a pot with water, tossed in a couple of dogs and put it on the grate. Maybe 20 minutes and a whole lot of head-scratching later, the dogs were done.
I ate my meal but couldn’t relax. The entire time, I was fretting about whether I should go to Mexico or not. As if there was really a choice.
The Mexico Walmart was open until 8 p.m. Google Maps said 25 minutes. It was 6:30 p.m. I cleared the picnic table, secured all my gear and the cooler and jumped into the truck.
I was going to Walmart, darn it.
I found the camping aisle and pulled a red sleeping bag off the shelf. On sale for $15 and good to 50 degrees. I’ll take it.
Then I spied a cheap backpacking stove knockoff. $18. It’ll do, I thought. To be sure, I also snagged a can of fuel. Not taking any chances, this camper.
I was back at my campsite by dark and settled in. I rekindled the fire, opened another beer and, for the first time in about four hours, actually relaxed.
At 10 p.m., I retired to my bed and slept like a baby in my new Walmart bag. Go figure.
Morning. When there must be coffee. I set up my new stove rig, got water boiling and dug out the coffee, creamer, coffee filter, cup and spoon. But alas, I couldn’t find the coffee filter thingy that sits on top of the cup. Sigh.
I put the filter into my mug, folded the edges over the lip and poured. With a smattering of grounds in my cup, I had coffee, and my day could begin.
Sleeping bag, camp stove, coffee filter holder. My brain has gone soft.
Oh yeah, about Blueberry Mountain. After breakfast, I headed up the road a few miles to the trailhead and started up the mountain. It was a steep and sweaty ascent, with nearly 1,400 feet of elevation gain over 1.4 miles on an eroded, rocky and rooty trail. I took notes along the way for the next guidebook edition, which currently lists the trail as 0.2 miles shorter. Check.
The open ledges on Blueberry’s summit yield extraordinary views. I felt like I could reach out and touch the slopes of Big Jackson Mountain. The distinctive hump of Little Jackson could be seen just to Jackson’s left. Tumbledown was hidden behind Little Jackson. There was Sugarloaf, too, along with Mount Abraham, the Bigelows, Saddleback and the Horn. Amazing!
The descent wasn’t any easier than the climb, but I kept a steady pace. All the while, I was smiling and laughing to myself about my forgetfulness. I never, ever forget the principal equipment on any trip. Little stuff, maybe, but not a sleeping bag or stove. But hey, it all worked out. Thanks to Walmart, I guess.
I had the afternoon free at the state park, so I took my kayak to Lake Webb and paddled around for a few glorious hours. The pyramidal form of Mount Blue took center stage, and as I floated around to the northeast, I could view all the great peaks of the Tumbledowns, including Blueberry Mountain, where I’d been just a few short hours earlier. Sweet.
The lake was bathwater warm, so I reveled in a refreshing swim at the beach afterward.
To be sure, I’m a list maker. Probably you are, too, when planning your trips. The key, though, is to actually check things off as you’re loading up. Otherwise, well, you’re gonna forget stuff. Sometimes even the important stuff, don’t you know.

title: Dozens injured, at least 6 dead in Halloween weekend gun violence at nightlife districts across US
text:
Dozens injured, at least 6 dead in Halloween weekend gun violence at nightlife districts across US
Dozens of people were injured and at least six people died in mass shootings as gun violence broke out at nightlife districts in half a dozen cities across the country over the Halloween weekend.
Related video above: Scene after shooting near University of Delaware campus on Halloween
Police in Dallas, the site of the deadliest violence, said four people are dead and 15 others were injured following a handful of shootings in the city's Deep Ellum neighborhood, a center of music, restaurants and nightlife in the city. Police in college towns like Fayetteville, Arkansas; Birmingham, Alabama; and Newark, Delaware, also reported shootings in their nightlife districts this weekend.
Dallas Police Chief Daniel Comeaux said investigators are still trying to determine if the shootings Saturday night over the span of about an hour and 15 minutes were related.
Comeaux said three separate shootings occurred, and it wasn't immediately known why they started. Comeaux said some arrests were made but he didn’t specify how many or what charges were involved.
“This is a really big scene. It's spread out,” Comeaux said. “We are interviewing some individuals right now that we have arrested, still trying to figure out exactly how it ties into all the shootings out here.”
The department had increased police presence in the district before the shootings. No police officers were injured.
Separately, one person was killed and eight others were wounded in a mass shooting just outside Legion Field in Birmingham, Alabama, after the annual ‘Magic City Classic’ football game on Saturday night, police said.
Michael Pickett, chief of the Birmingham Police Department, said most spectators and families had left the stadium property after the game, but the shooting happened nearby, where vendors were set up along Graymont Avenue.
He said he was “very grateful that more people weren’t injured.”
The circumstances of the shooting were unclear.
Police spokesperson De'Rell Freeman said one person had been detained and transported to police headquarters for questioning, and “multiple weapons” had been found and secured.
Alabama State and Alabama A&M are historically Black universities and archrivals whose annual contest has been played for more than 100 years. Nearly 70,000 fans attended Saturday's game, won by Alabama A&M 31-28. The event draws some of the largest crowds in the country for games played in their college football division.
The Magic City Classic has such a deep history that Alabama State coach Eddie Robinson Jr., a former NFL linebacker and alumnus of the school, proposed creating a Hall of Fame for the game.
In Newark, Delaware, six people were shot late Saturday near the University of Delaware campus, Newark police Lt. Greg D’Elia said. All six were transported to hospitals for treatment, police said early Sunday. No updates on their condition were available as of Sunday afternoon. A university spokesperson said they would provide updates on the investigation online as they become available.
Video shared on social media showed people running for safety from the scene. One stretch of the city's Main Street was closed for several hours after the shooting, police said.
A shooting early Sunday in Bloomington, Illinois, left a 19-year-old woman dead and another woman in critical condition. Six others had injuries that were not life-threatening, but it was unclear from a statement by the city's police department and McLean County Coroner’s Office if those people had gunshot wounds. The shooting happened near the campus of Illinois Wesleyan University. Bloomington is about 135 miles (217 kilometers) southwest of Chicago.
And in Fayetteville, Arkansas, six people were taken to hospitals with gunshot wounds from a shooting that happened early Sunday. No arrests have been made, police said in a news release. A preliminary investigation indicates an altercation preceded the shooting.
On Friday, two people were killed in separate shootings at Spirit Halloween stores in California and Michigan.
Police said a shooting inside a store at an indoor shopping mall in Fairfield, California was a targeted attack. Family members told police that the 31-year-old woman who died was pregnant. Six other people were wounded, police said.
In Madison Heights, Michigan, just north of Detroit, a 21-year-old man was fatally shot Friday afternoon at a Spirit Halloween. Another man who was assaulted by bystanders as officers took him into custody was hospitalized with injuries that were not life-threatening, police said.

title: Traps don’t distinguish between pets and predators
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
The Oct. 19 article “Interest in trapping grows in Maine” was very concerning. Not only for all the wild animals, as well as pets, that unknowingly step into a cruel trap that causes immense suffering, injury and ultimate death, but also for the misinformation it spreads about how to successfully control predator populations that commonly prey on backyard chickens and small livestock.
If predators are killing people’s chickens, their coops, runs or yards are insecure. The neighborhood dog could just as easily kill their chickens. People must fortify their coops, not try to kill every fox or coyote — they’ll never win.
The key to reducing predators is all about layers of protection — coop in the middle, wire or electrified netting for the chickens yard, and then a simple perimeter fence beyond that to disrupt predator travel-ways and make them reroute for good, avoiding people’s yards altogether. Keep the most vulnerable livestock in the center, surrounded by larger livestock accessing the outermost pastures. Provide trees or shrubs for protection from sky predators.
I’ve had chickens for over a decade, with fox, coyotes, hawks, eagles, fishers and weasels seen regularly, and have had no livestock lost to predators and zero predators killed.
Responsible animal keeping is achievable and doesn’t need to be expensive — it just takes a bit of understanding of how predators think and ways to keep them at bay naturally, without cruelty or killing. Hunting or trapping of predators to address a predator problem is a fool’s errand.
Arielle Cousens
Readfield

title: Taiwan accuses China of harassment after standoff between coast guard ships
text:
Taiwan accuses China of harassment after standoff between coast guard ships
Taiwan’s coast guard accused China of harassment after a Chinese vessel entered restricted waters near a disputed coral island administered by Taiwan in the South China Sea.
China claims democratically ruled Taiwan as its own breakaway province and has not ruled out the use of force to annex it. Beijing sends warships and military jets near the island almost daily, and in recent months has stepped up coast guard patrols, especially in waters east of Taiwan, raising alarm in Taipei.
The Chinese coast guard vessel entered waters near the Pratas Islands, southwest of Taiwan’s main island, early on Saturday, Taiwan’s coast guard said. It added that a Taiwanese coast guard vessel confronted the Chinese ship and asked it to leave.
At the height of the standoff, the two ships came within just 1 nautical mile (1.9 kilometers) of each other, Taiwan’s coast guard said.
Beijing says the waters it patrols fall under its jurisdiction.
Taiwan’s coast guard called on Beijing “to immediately cease these pointless acts of harassment.” It said that the incident was the 13th such intrusion near the Pratas Islands this year, involving 16 vessels.
Also on Saturday, China’s coast guard announced it had sent a group of vessels to conduct a “routine law enforcement patrol” in waters east of Taiwan.
“The China Coast Guard will continue to intensify its law enforcement patrols in waters under its jurisdiction, firmly upholding the nation’s territorial sovereignty and maritime rights and interests,” its statement read.
In June, France, Germany and Britain issued a rare joint statement expressing alarm over Chinese activities east of Taiwan, saying they endangered regional stability.
