title: AP Top 25 live updates: Poll shakeup looms after USC stuns Ohio State
text:
No. 1 Miami dug deep to hold off North Carolina and keep its undefeated record intact, but No. 2 Ohio State wasn’t as fortunate. The Buckeyes fell to USC in the biggest upset of the week, setting up another major shakeup in the AP Top 25.
Seven ranked teams lost, potentially creating a domino effect in the latter half of the rankings. South Carolina, USC and Iowa all made strong cases to enter the poll.
Plenty of changes could be in store when the latest poll drops at 2 p.m. Eastern. And this poll could set the table for the initial College Football Playoff rankings coming out Tuesday night!
Stick around for projections, voter Q&A and live updates.
Poll predictions
By ERIC OLSON
Miami escaped North Carolina 38-35 and should hang on to the No. 1 ranking for a third straight week.
With Ohio State going down, No. 6 Utah is in line to crack the top five for the first time since 2019 by virtue of its 49-25 win over Cincinnati.
Major changes probably are coming toward the bottom of the poll. Six teams between Nos. 17 and 25 lost. Iowa, which shut out Wisconsin 30-0 at home, should return to the rankings after a one-week absence. USC also could return after its first top-five win since the 2017 Rose Bowl against Penn State and its highest-ranked win since it beat Oklahoma in the 2004 season’s national championship game.
A Maryland student wins just by showing up
By EDDIE PELLS
Another under-the-radar winner Saturday was mechanical engineering major Bryce Hartle.
Who’s he?
Well, attendance-challenged Maryland football (which fired coach Mike Locksley last week) was offering free spring tuition to the winner of a raffle for students who stayed through the fourth quarter of Saturday’s Big Ten showdown against Illinois.
Hartle won. Maryland lost (20-17).
And, if snapshots of the stadium at kickoff are any indication, the Terps might need to up the ante for the next game.
UCLA is undefeated but are the Bruins for real?
A Power Four team quietly takes care of business and improves to 8-0 on the season in a so-called paycheck game.
Sounds like a team destined for a No. 1 or No. 2 ranking, right?
But that team is UCLA — a program that hasn’t won 10 games since 2013 or won its conference since 1998. That makes it hard to see the Bruins more than a spot from No. 7 during a week in which Ohio State was the only team ahead of them to lose.
But what will the CFP selection committee think? Their evaluation of UCLA could be as good a sign as any as to whether they agree with the AP poll voters or are looking at completely different factors.
There’s reason for doubt: UCLA is playing without its starting quarterback, Nico Iamaleava. Then again, backup Ty Dieffenbach is avoiding mistakes, throwing for a modest three touchdowns since taking over in a 17-15 win over Oregon on Oct. 10.
How will the CFP committee view Indiana with an injured QB?
Indiana squeaked out another victory this week. Its last three wins have all been fourth-quarter or overtime affairs decided by a touchdown or less. It also lost 19-15 to Ohio State.
One factor the selection committee will look at in deciding where the defending champions belong in their first rankings is the health of Hoosiers quarterback Josh Hoover.
Hoover came into Saturday’s game against Minnesota at less than 100% with an arm injury. He left at halftime and Indiana was nothing near dominant in getting past the Gophers 23-16 in overtime.
At 8-1, the Hoosiers still carry the resume of a top-six team into Tuesday’s bracket reveal, but the committee has the latitude to dock (or elevate) teams based on player availability.
Big 12 gets back to ‘normal’ with wins from Utah, BYU, Texas Tech
All of the top four contenders in the Big 12 were in action Saturday and the results left us where we were a few weeks ago — with Utah, BYU and Texas Tech the top contenders for the title.
No. 13 Texas Tech’s 34-26 victory over No. 22 Arizona not only righted the ship in Lubbock but probably knocked the surprising Wildcats out of contention for the conference title and the automatic playoff bid that will come with it.
No. 8 BYU beat Arizona State 27-20. Like the Red Raiders, the Cougars rebounded from an upset the previous week.
Utah, after beating Cincinnati to improve to 5-0 in the conference, has a one-game lead over both teams with its game against BYU — the “Holy War” — set for next Saturday.
Halloween horrors strike lower half of the Top 25 (and No. 2 Ohio State)
Even a relatively calm Halloween in college football didn’t spare everyone in the upper reaches of the AP Top 25. Ohio State looks like it may be headed for a tumble.
The second-ranked Buckeyes, playing without starting quarterback Julian Sayin, fell hard at USC on Saturday, 30-18. They were the only team in the Top 10 to lose in the final week of games before the College Football Playoff releases its first ranking. That happens Tuesday.
Today, the latest Top 25 figures to be fairly stable — quite a difference from the last two weeks, when chaos reigned from top to bottom in the poll.
This week No. 1 Miami survived a scare from coach Bill Belichick’s North Carolina Tar Heels, but persevered 38-35. No. 3 Georgia rolled over No. 17 Florida 27-8. No. 6 Utah and No. 7 UCLA both won to join Miami as the only remaining undefeated teams in the FBS.
Most of the turnover would likely happen toward the bottom of this week’s rankings, where six teams between No. 17 and 25 lost: Florida, No. 19 SMU, No. 20 Northwestern, No. 22 Arizona, No. 24 Oklahoma State and No. 25 Wisconsin.
Who decides the rankings?
By THE ASSOCIATED PRESS
AP Top 25 voters are writers and broadcasters who cover college football.
AP employees do not vote, but they do choose the voters, and they seek wide representation from all over the country. This season, there are 69 voters.
The focus begins with voter representation in states with a Bowl Subdivision school, and the total number of voters from each state increases with the number of FBS teams. There are also spots reserved for national voters.
The AP allows broad latitude for voters to determine their rankings. They are urged to base their votes on performance, not reputation or preseason speculation (except, of course, for the always provocative preseason poll); to avoid regional bias, for or against; to pay attention to head-to-head results; and to make significant changes if desired.
Down goes Ohio State
By ERIC OLSON
For the fourth straight week, a No. 1 or 2 team lost to an unranked opponent, and a total of seven Top 25 teams lost in Week 9.
The biggest loss Saturday belonged to No. 2 Ohio State, which was without injured quarterback Julian Sayin and went down 30-18 at Southern California. The Buckeyes lost for the second time this season and may take a big fall.
Oregon heads to Columbus next Saturday.

title: Hannah Pingree up big in Maine governor’s race, final NYT/Press Herald/Siena poll shows
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Hannah Pingree maintained a double-digit lead in the Maine governor’s race, the final New York Times/Portland Press Herald/Siena poll showed, a strong showing just days before Election Day.
Pingree, a 50-year-old Democrat from North Haven and the daughter of U.S. Rep. Chellie Pingree, faces Republican Bobby Charles and independent Rick Bennett on the ballot this Tuesday in the race to succeed Gov. Janet Mills. If Democrats hold the governor’s office, it would be the first time since 1959 that Maine voters elected successive executives from the same party.
The poll of 714 likely voters, surveyed by the Siena Research Institute between Oct. 27 and Nov. 1, showed Pingree with the support of 49% of respondents. Charles polled at 37%, and Bennett pulled 8%. The governor’s race will not be subject to a ranked-choice runoff.
Charles, a 66-year-old lawyer from Leeds, has sat in a distant second place throughout the campaign after winning a bruising Republican primary this summer. Each of the previous two Times/Press Herald/Siena polls has shown Charles with the support of 36% of voters.
Bennett, 63, a state senator and former Maine Republican Party chair, has struggled to gain traction, sitting at 8% in each of the two prior polls.
Relatively few voters remained undecided, the poll showed, with 6% refusing to answer or saying they didn’t know whom they’d choose.
The campaign has largely focused on affordability, with heating oil prices at record highs due to the Iran war and housing prices continuing to rise due to a lack of supply.
Pingree, the race’s front-runner since she won her primary this summer, has mostly avoided major slip-ups. She’s sought to connect Charles to his party’s leader, President Donald Trump, who remains deeply unpopular in Maine.
Pingree has solidified her base of support among Democrats, and is also supported by 51% of unenrolled voters — 26 percentage points more than Charles, and 35 more than Bennett. About 10% of those who said they plan to vote for Republican Sen. Susan Collins also said they plan to vote for Pingree.
Charles, meanwhile, has hoped to tie Pingree to Mills, the outgoing governor he blames for high energy prices, low hospital reimbursement rates, alleged MaineCare fraud and more. He often uses the term “Mills-Pingree administration” to slam the past eight years of Democratic trifecta governance in Augusta.
While Republicans were slow to coalesce behind Charles after their expensive, bruising primary, he has solidified his support among Maine GOP voters in the past month and a half, according to the Times/Press Herald/Siena poll. In September, Charles only had the support of 73% of Republicans; he now has the support of 86%.
Bennett remains a distant third place. Fewer unenrolled voters are supporting Bennett — who has openly criticized the two-party system — than Charles.
With slim paths to victory for both Charles and Bennett, Pingree appears poised to keep the Blaine House in Democratic hands, while the party fights to maintain its tight Maine Legislature majorities.
In addition to leading in most major polls — one Marist poll from last month showed Pingree and Charles tied — Pingree has also enjoyed a comfortable fundraising advantage and has raked in about $5 million during her campaign.
The New York Times/Portland Press Herald/Siena poll of Maine voters was funded with support from the Maine Trust for Local News.

title: 3 firefighters resign after drinking at a bar while on duty, police reports says
text:
NASHVILLE, Tenn. (WSMV/Gray News) - Three Nashville firefighters have resigned after they were seen ordering drinks at a Broadway bar while on duty, according to a police report.
Mayor Freddie O’Connell is calling for accountability after the incident happened around midnight on Monday night.
The police report said officers were called by the manager at Dierks Bentley Whiskey Row when a bartender reported she was concerned they were drinking alcohol on duty.
It identifies the three firefighters as Athams Davis, Griffin Hunter and Daniel Wrenn. They were wearing Nashville Fire Department T-shirts and carrying bright yellow radios while at the bar, police said.
Police report outlines reported bar visit
When police approached the firefighters, they told officers they were on duty but all denied drinking alcohol inside Whiskey Row, according to the report.
Officers continued to interview the bartender who served the group and other bar staff. They said the three ordered two vodka-Red Bulls and a water just after midnight.
While the bartender said she did not personally see the firefighters drink the alcoholic beverages, she provided officers with a receipt signed by one of them for the mixed drinks.
Police said they notified the area’s fire commander, who came to the scene and immediately placed the three on administrative duty.
The bar’s manager said they were working to obtain video footage to provide additional context.
Fire department launches investigation
The firefighters were placed on administrative leave before they resigned on Wednesday. It’s not clear if the internal investigation is still ongoing after their resignations.
The Nashville Fire Department simply said it was aware of an incident involving three employees, but would not release details of what happened or the names and positions of the firefighters.
The department said it would not provide any additional information because this is a personnel matter. A spokesperson did not respond to requests for a copy of the NFD employee rules and regulations for firefighter conduct.
“The Nashville Fire Department holds all personnel to the highest standards of professionalism, accountability, and conduct,” the department said in a statement. “Actions that compromise those standards are taken seriously and addressed accordingly.”
Mayor calls for accountability
The incident on Broadway comes just months after a firefighter was found unresponsive at his station with drug paraphernalia. The autopsy report said he died from cocaine toxicity.
O’Connell said he talked with Chief William Swann and was speaking with other leaders to make sure people know it is not acceptable for Metro employees to drink or do drugs on the job.
“I think (Swann) has demonstrated, within the fire department, that there is a zero-tolerance approach to this,” O’Connell said. “They are delivering internal accountability. But, I think also, what I am looking for is the assurance that we are doing the appropriate amount of retraining updates to ensure that all personnel are there.”
O’Connell said he is also working with the firefighter union, IAFF Local 140, to hold people accountable. The union said they do not have any comment about this incident at this time.
“Early indications are that our IAFF Local is wanting to ensure that a popular, successful fire department retains the confidence of Nashvillians, and their ability to execute on all fronts,” he said. “We have been having those conversations throughout the year. I think we will be looking to leadership in the Nashville Fire Department to give the public signs of the ongoing confidence we all need to have in them.”

title: Pierce Gorneault Wins State Title as County Cross Country Teams Shine
text:
Caribou’s Gorneault Wins State Cross Country Class B Title as County Runners Shine in Augusta
Aroostook County had plenty to celebrate at Saturday's Maine State Cross Country Championships in Augusta.
Caribou's Pierce Gorneault captured the Class B boys individual state championship, Emma Graves finished second in the Class B girls race, and the Houlton/GHCA boys came within 19 points of defending their Class C state title.
But the results went beyond individual performances.
Caribou earned both the boys and girls Class B Sportsmanship Awards, recognizing the Vikings for the way they represented their school and community.
Presque Isle also had strong performances in Class B, while individual runners from Houlton, Washburn and the Maine School of Science and Mathematics represented the County in Class C girls.
Here's how the local teams and runners finished at the state championships.
Class B Girls: Graves Takes Second as Caribou and Presque Isle Finish in the Top Six
Caribou sophomore Emma Graves was among the fastest runners in Maine on Saturday, finishing second in the Class B girls championship.
Graves covered the 5,000-meter course in 19 minutes, 28.70 seconds, finishing behind Lincoln Academy senior Karen Higgins, who won the state championship in 18:58.41.
Graves was joined in the top ten by Caribou freshman Jenna Strid, who finished ninth in 20:06.27.
That gave the Vikings two runners among the top ten finishers in the state.
Presque Isle also had a strong showing near the front of the field.
Junior Aleah Rideout finished 11th in 20:21.32, while freshman Lillian Johnson placed 13th in 20:31.24.
Caribou finished fifth in the team standings with 135 points, while Presque Isle was right behind in sixth with 144.
Freeport won the Class B girls team championship with 67 points, followed by Mount Desert Island with 81 and Yarmouth with 87.

Class B Boys: Pierce Gorneault Brings Home State Championship
Caribou sophomore Pierce Gorneault delivered one of the biggest performances of the day, winning the Class B boys individual state championship.
Gorneault finished the 5,000-meter race in 16:26.85, nearly ten seconds ahead of Yarmouth's Jackie Chalmers, who took second in 16:36.41.
His time was also the fourth-fastest among all classifications at the state championships.
It was a tremendous performance for Gorneault, who had already established himself as one of Northern Maine's top runners throughout the fall season.
Caribou also had two more runners finish inside the top 20.
Freshman Peyton Gorneault placed 17th in 17:57.08, while senior Tewolde Stewart finished 18th in 18:03.61.
Those performances helped the Vikings finish third in the Class B boys team standings with 121 points, just one point ahead of fourth-place Cape Elizabeth.
Yarmouth won the team championship with 27 points, followed by Freeport with 92.
Presque Isle finished ninth as a team with 225 points.
Junior Paxton Darrell led the Wildcats with a 16th-place finish in 17:55.52, while sophomore Jeremy Charette placed 38th in 18:52.53.

Caribou Sweeps Class B Sportsmanship Awards
Beyond the race results, Caribou received another major recognition Saturday.
Both the Vikings boys and girls teams were awarded the Class B Sportsmanship Awards.
It's an impressive accomplishment for one school to receive both honors at the same state championship meet.
The awards recognize sportsmanship, respect and the way athletes represent their teams throughout competition.
For Caribou, the honors add another highlight to a day that included an individual state championship, a runner-up finish and two top-five team performances.
Class C Boys: Houlton/GHCA Finishes State Runner-Up
Houlton/GHCA came into Saturday's Class C boys championship looking to defend its state title.
The Shires had won their second consecutive Northern Maine regional championship the previous weekend, putting four runners among the top five finishers.
At states, Houlton once again put together an impressive team performance, finishing second with 66 points.
Winthrop captured the state championship with 47 points, while George Stevens Academy finished third with 105.
Senior Malachi Witmer led the Shires with a sixth-place finish in 17:17.24.
Sophomore Logan Witmer placed 12th in 17:39.52, followed by Wyatt Quint in 16th at 17:52.74.
Nathan Brady finished 18th in 17:57.26, and Brayden Drake was right behind in 19th at 17:57.76.
That gave Houlton five runners among the top 20 finishers in the state.
Stephen Cormier and Lucas McPhee rounded out the Shires' seven-runner lineup.
Although Houlton wasn't able to repeat as state champion, a runner-up finish capped another outstanding season for the program.

Class C Girls: County Runners Represent Houlton, Washburn and MSSM
While there were no County teams in the Class C girls team standings, four local runners earned the opportunity to compete individually at the state championships.
Houlton/GHCA freshman Charlotte Estabrook led the County contingent, finishing 51st in 25:08.59.
Sadie Wigmore, a freshman from the Maine School of Science and Mathematics, placed 54th in 25:26.70.

title: 8-year-old girl attacked by wolf in a German zoo
text:
An 8-year-old girl was attacked by a wolf in a German zoo
An 8-year-old girl was attacked by at least one wolf inside a German zoo's enclosure and suffered serious injuries, officials said.
The attack occurred Wednesday during a special event for children at the Johannismühle Wildlife Park south of Berlin, Teltow-Fläming district officials said in a news release.
Video above: Otter 'pumpkin dunkin'' at Oregon Zoo
The girl was flown to the hospital, the news release said. A zookeeper intervened before two other girls also in the Arctic wolf enclosure were attacked. The wolves had been given water at the time.
The zoo is closed until further notice as an investigation takes place.
A wolf bit a woman in a shopping area in Hamburg earlier this year, authorities said, in what is believed to be the first such attack since wolves returned to the country in 1998.

title: BU men’s hockey rallies with 3 unanswered goals to beat UMaine in OT
text:
After getting blown out on Friday night, 7-2, the determined University of Maine men’s hockey team jumped out to a 2-0 lead against Boston University in Saturday’s series finale and took that advantage into the third period.
But it turned into another nightmarish evening at BU’s Agganis Arena for the Black Bears as Tynan Lawrence scored a pair of third-period goals to tie it, the second one coming with just 2:12 remaining, and Caleb Malhotra scored 1:35 into overtime as the Terriers extended their Agganis winning streak to 10 games over the Black Bears, 3-2.
UMaine hasn’t won at Agganis Arena since 2018.
BU improved to 6-2 overall and 4-2 in Hockey East while UMaine fell to 4-4 and 0-2.
Mikhail Yegorov finished with 34 saves for the Terriers while Albin Boija made 24 saves for UMaine.
Rowan Calvert and Max Scott had staked UMaine to its 2-0 lead, and the Black Bears outshot the Terriers 21-8 in that initial period.
But Lawrence scored a power play goal at the 6:56 mark of the third period to cut the lead in half off a Conrad Fondrk assist. It was his team-leading sixth goal of the season.
His equalizer came off a three-on-three rush. Jack Harvey skated down the middle of the ice and found an open Lawrence in the left faceoff circle. Lawrence took a stride and beat UMaine goalie Albin Boija with a wrist shot from the faceoff dot.
Harvey also set up the game-winner, with a pass to Malhotra in the right side of the Maine zone.
Malhotra cut to his left, skated through a UMaine stick check and made a nifty move to maneuver around another Black Bear before snapping a wrist shot into the short side corner for his second goal of the season.
“You can’t have a bad gap when you play against players like that. They make plays,” said UMaine head coach Ben Barr.
Freshman Calvert opened the scoring with his first career goal.
He scored from the low slot with Jaden Lipinski earning an assist.
Scott expanded the lead with his second in as many nights.
Lee Parks fed him a pass, and Scott scored with a quick wrist shot from between the faceoff dots at the 14:45 mark.
UMaine outshot BU 8-6 in the scoreless second period, but BU had a 12-6 advantage in the third. Each team had one shot in the three-on-three overtime.
“The guys played hard, but there were just too many guys at the end of the game that you couldn’t put out there and it killed us,” Ben Barr said. “We had some discipline issues at the end, which is unacceptable.”
He was irritated by an unsportsmanlike conduct penalty on Lukas Peterson at the 5:50 mark of the third period because BU’s Jax Wismer had been whistled for boarding, which would have put UMaine on the power play with a chance to go up 3-0. Instead, it was a four-on-four and then Scott was called for slashing 16 seconds later, which set the stage for Lawrence’s four-on-three power play goal, jumpstarting the rally.
BU had three power plays in the final period.
“When you have to kill that many penalties and shorten the bench at the end, that’s just not sustainable, especially against a team like that,” Barr said.
He said his team has to learn from its mistakes.
“We’ve got to move on from it. It is what it is,” said Barr, whose Black Bears will entertain UMass on Friday and Saturday.
BU will visit Michigan State for a pair of games the same nights.

title: 'I am so sorry': Selma Blair issues video apology after plane assault arrest
text:
'I am so sorry': Selma Blair issues video apology after plane assault arrest
Actress Selma Blair posted a video on social media apologizing for her actions weeks after she was arrested for an alleged assault on a plane.
In an Oct. 30 video shared on Instagram, Blair, 54, said she has been advised by her attorneys to not share much about the case, further saying she did not mean to injure or cause harm to anyone.
“What I can tell you, though, is very simple, and the truest thing I know about myself, and that not one day ever have I intended to hurt or frighten anyone a day in my life,” she said. “And so to the people that I disappointed, that I hurt, I frightened, alarmed: I am so sorry.”
Related video:
The "Legally Blonde" and "Cruel Intentions" actress was arrested on Oct. 11 after she allegedly punched a flight attendant and bit another after attempting to open the plane door while in the air, multiple media outlets reported.
When the plane—which was heading to New York from Los Angeles
Later, a nurse moving Blair said the actor kicked her in the chest, causing substantial pain.
A day following the incident, Blair was released from custody on $20,000 bail.
According to Variety, the 54-year-old is due back in court in Queens, New York, on Jan. 19, 2027.

title: JD Vance has some explaining to do
text:
Since he has been very public about his conversion to Catholicism, it would be interesting to hear how Vice President JD Vance reconciles his professed newfound faith with his slanderous lies about Haitian immigrants in Ohio eating pets, his support of the despicable campaign of his friend Vivek Ramaswamy, his personal attacks on his political opponents and the brutal treatment of immigrants by this administration. That is not even including his support of war and capital punishment.
Maybe instead of trying to profit on his “faith” by selling a book, he could consider some quiet introspection to align his words and actions with the true message of Christianity.
Peter Watko

title: Obituary: Jennifer (Chouinard) Vella
text:
RAYMOND – It is with great sadness that we announce the unexpected passing of Jennifer (Chouinard) Vella on Oct. 20, 2026. Jennifer graduated as valedictorian of the Deering High School Class of 1988 in Portland, Maine.
Her love of music led her to Los Angeles, Calif. where she worked in the music industry. It was during this chapter of her life that she formed some of her most cherished lifelong friendships, including those with her seven “Cali Angels.” After also living in Arizona, Jennifer eventually returned home to Maine, settling in Raymond to raise her beloved sons, Nicholas and DJ.
Jennifer loved her family unconditionally and her friends fiercely. Gentle and kind, she had a special place in her heart for animals, particularly German Shepherds, her all-time favorite. Her beloved German Shepherd, Ember, was always by her side, along with her adoring cat, Cinder.
Jennifer also cherished summers spent at her family camp, where she found peace and happiness surrounded by the family she loved. It was a special place for her and one where many treasured family memories were made.
Music was a lifelong passion for Jennifer. One of her greatest joys was seeing her son Nicholas develop that same love of live music. She was incredibly proud of him, and their shared passion gave them something special that was uniquely theirs. Going to concerts together brought Jennifer great joy and created memories she deeply treasured.
Jennifer was equally proud of her son DJ and the hardworking, dependable man he had become. DJ was always there to lend a hand and help take care of things around the house. He was someone she could count on whenever something needed to be done. She admired his strong work ethic and was proud of his willingness to always lend a hand.
Jennifer was preceded in death by her father, Peter Chouinard.
She is survived by her mother, Karen Beauchesne Chouinard; her brother, Paul Chouinard and his wife Tricia Duchesneau Chouinard; her sons, Nicholas and DJ; her former husband, Todd Vella; and many aunts, uncles, cousins, and dear friends.
Jennifer will be remembered for the depth of her love, the gentleness of her spirit, and the fierce loyalty she showed to the people and animals she held dear. May the music she loved, the friendships she treasured, and the memories she created bring comfort to all who knew and loved her.
“We breathe the light, we breathe the music, we breathe the moment as it passes through us.”
— Anne Rice, one of Jennifer’s favorite authors

title: Man driving to Canada detained by ICE was the son of a Maine state senator
text:
Man driving to Canada detained by ICE is the son of a Maine state senator
Denise Tepler said she does not know why her adopted son was recently detained by ICE, calling it a waste of time, energy, and American taxpayer dollars.
Man driving to Canada detained by ICE is the son of a Maine state senator
Denise Tepler said she does not know why her adopted son was recently detained by ICE, calling it a waste of time, energy, and American taxpayer dollars.
A man who was driving to Canada to start a new life was detained by Immigration and Customs Enforcement in New Hampshire.
Jessie Laurel Tepler-Mujambere, a 28-year-old originally from Burundi, had been living with his adoptive family in Maine for the past decade. His adoptive mother, Denise Tepler, is a state senator in Maine representing District 24.
Tepler-Mujambere had a pending asylum status in the United States, and earlier this week he received the paperwork for his Canadian citizenship.
"His car was packed, completely packed, totally ready to go. He's like, I'm moving to Canada. I'm 28 years old now to start my life," his adoptive mother, Tepler, said.
On his way to Canada, Tepler-Mujambere was pulled over by police near Colebrook.
According to the Department of Homeland Security, Tepler-Mujambere was pulled over for speeding, and it was determined he was illegally present in the U.S.
Tepler-Mujambere's family said he was not told why he was pulled over.
DHS said that "Tepler-Mujambere first entered the United States at the Dulles International Airport on November 10, 2014, with permission to stay until May 5, 2015. Against our nation’s laws, he overstayed his welcome and failed to depart once his legal permission expired."
In that same statement to News 9, a DHS spokesperson said, "A pending application does NOT confer legal status in the United States," a DHS spokesperson wrote in a statement to News 9.
Tepler-Mujambere's family told News 9 his work permit was not renewed by the federal government in June.
They said his Canadian citizenship was approved in July, but the paperwork came the last week of October.  
Tepler-Mujambere was detained by ICE until he was eventually brought to Canada.
During that time, his family said he was driven from Colebrook to the Strafford County Jail in Dover to spend the night. The next morning, they said he was brought down to Manchester, then back up to the Strafford County Jail for a second night. On Friday morning, his family said he was driven by officers to the Canadian border in Vermont, where he was ultimately released.
Tepler called this situation a waste of time, energy, and American taxpayer dollars.
"He almost was in Canada, and he had his Canadian citizenship papers with him," she said. "And yet they put him in jail for two nights. That means we're paying to house him and feed him for two nights."
Tepler said that her son's car was towed to a New Hampshire garage with a $150 towing fee and a $100 per day fee.
The Department of Homeland Security is encouraging people who are not in the United States legally to self-deport.

title: Loneliness isn’t the lonely person’s problem
text:
Jeffrey S. Barkin, MD, DLFAPA, is a practicing psychiatrist in Portland and the former president of the Maine Medical Association. He co-hosts “A Healthy Conversation” on WGAN.
As a psychiatrist, one of the more poignant and frequent things I hear from single people is also one of the simplest: “I would love to meet someone. I just don’t know where to meet them.”
I hear versions of this from people in their 20s and 30s, but also from people in their 40s, 50s, 60s and beyond. Some have never married. Others are divorced or widowed and assumed they would eventually meet someone again. Many are educated, successful and interesting, with friends, careers and otherwise full lives. They haven’t given up on romance.
They simply cannot figure out where everyone went.
“Michael” is 31, educated, employed, funny and thoughtful. He wants to marry and have children but hasn’t been on a date in almost two years. Dating apps became demoralizing after months of swiping produced few meaningful encounters, while approaching a woman at work, the gym or a coffee shop seemed increasingly awkward. His evenings gradually migrated online.
“Susan” is 62, divorced for six years, with grown children and a successful career. She has close friends, exercises, travels and genuinely enjoys her life. She would also very much like someone to share it with. After numerous first dates arranged through apps began feeling like job interviews, she finally deleted them.
What she missed most, she said, wasn’t sex or even romance. It was having someone who would notice the small things that happened during her day.
Both eventually asked essentially the same question: “Where am I supposed to meet somebody?”
Their experiences reflect something larger happening in American life.
Pew Research Center found that 47% of Americans under 30 were single in 2022, including 63% of men under 30. Yet being unattached doesn’t necessarily mean rejecting relationships, marriage or children. Many young people still want those things but struggle with getting from wanting a relationship to actually having one.
Sexual activity has declined as well. An analysis of the General Social Survey published in JAMA Network Open found that among men ages 18 to 24, the percentage reporting no sexual activity during the previous year increased from 18.9% from 2000–2002 to 30.9% from 2016–2018.
Dating apps were supposed to solve the problem of finding one another, and for millions of people they have. Pew found that 1 in 5 partnered Americans under 30 met their current partner through a dating site or app.
Yet the same technology can be discouraging. Online dating can transform courtship into something resembling a marketplace, with hundreds of people available for inspection and rejection in minutes.
Pornography illustrates a related technological paradox. It didn’t create loneliness, and it would be simplistic to blame it for declining dating, sex or fertility. But like social media and dating apps, it demonstrates how technology can deliver pieces of experiences that once required interaction with another human being. Convenience can remove not only inconvenience, but vulnerability.
We have therefore created an extraordinary paradox: perhaps the largest romantic marketplace in human history exists at precisely the moment when so many people say they cannot find anyone to meet.
Maybe the problem isn’t that we have too few potential partners. Maybe we have too few places to encounter them naturally.
There is evidence that those places really are becoming scarcer. A 2024 national survey by the Survey Center on American Life found that Americans are participating less often in organized activities, joining fewer community groups and spending less time with friends, neighbors and family. Only 17% belonged to a hobby or activity group, 15% to a neighborhood association and 10% to a sports or workout group.
In other words, some of the social infrastructure through which strangers once became acquaintances — and acquaintances sometimes became partners — has weakened.
Earlier generations, despite social constraints of their own, more often encountered potential partners through the infrastructure of ordinary life: workplaces, neighborhoods, religious institutions, civic organizations, clubs, extended families and circles of friends. These weren’t necessarily places people went looking for dates.
That was precisely the point. People encountered one another repeatedly while doing something else. Attraction had time to develop.
Someone who might be dismissed after three seconds on a dating app could become appealing after three conversations. You could watch someone tell a funny story, help a friend, behave kindly toward a waiter or laugh at themselves. People arrived with context. Friends could vouch for them. Familiarity could become friendship, and friendship could become something else.
Much of that social infrastructure still exists, of course. But enormous portions of our lives have migrated onto screens.
A 25-year-old can spend Friday night looking at hundreds of potential partners without meeting a single person. A 55-year-old can communicate with dozens of online friends while eating dinner alone.
Being single, of course, isn’t synonymous with being lonely. Many single people have rich, connected lives, and plenty of married people experience profound loneliness. Nor does everyone want a romantic relationship.
The problem is more specific: people who genuinely want companionship increasingly describe difficulty finding the ordinary circumstances in which relationships can begin.
Technology introduces another complication: seemingly unlimited choice. Someone can be kind, intelligent, attractive and interesting while still losing to the possibility that someone even more appealing might appear with the next swipe. There will always appear to be someone “better” out there — richer, smarter, funnier, thinner or more attractive.
But successful relationships don’t require discovering the objectively best person available. They require two imperfect people eventually deciding to stop searching and begin knowing each other.
The consequences can extend beyond loneliness.
America’s fertility rate has generally been declining for years for many reasons: economics, later marriage, changing opportunities and priorities and the fact that some adults simply don’t want children. Dating technology cannot plausibly explain something so complex.
Still, hidden inside all those statistics is an elementary biological and social fact: Most children begin with two people finding each other.
If fewer people form durable partnerships, that eventually affects family formation. Demography moves slowly, which makes its consequences easy to overlook.
But demographics aren’t what concern me most.
Human beings learn intimacy through other human beings: through faces, voices, touch, humor, irritation, disappointment and forgiveness.
Technology can offer partial substitutes for those experiences. The danger comes when the substitute becomes easier than the human experience it was supposed to facilitate.
Because real people are inconvenient. They misunderstand us, interrupt us, sometimes bore us and occasionally hurt us. They also surprise us, comfort us, challenge us, laugh with us, grow old beside us and hold our hands when life becomes frightening. No algorithm can eliminate the vulnerability required to obtain those things.
Perhaps we also need to stop treating the difficulty of finding companionship entirely as the single person’s responsibility.
For generations, matchmaking was part of ordinary community life. Friends invited two single people to dinner because they thought they might like each other. Cousins made introductions. Neighbors knew neighbors. Religious communities, clubs and workplaces allowed people to encounter one another repeatedly without declaring in advance that they were searching for a romantic partner.
We have largely outsourced that function to algorithms. Maybe we should take some of it back.
When a friend says, “I can’t meet anyone,” those of us who are married or partnered shouldn’t simply suggest another app. We should ask ourselves a different question: “Whom do I know?”
For someone in middle age, finding a relationship may require overcoming the fear that the opportunity for love has passed. It hasn’t.
For younger people, it may require remembering that courtship was never supposed to resemble an online marketplace in which human beings are sorted by photographs and preferences. For everyone else, it may require recognizing that communities have a role in helping people find one another.
The encouraging news is that our desire for one another remains remarkably durable. Beneath all our astonishing technology remains the ancient human longing to know another person and to be known in return. We haven’t lost that capacity. Perhaps we have simply become less practiced at creating the circumstances in which it can happen.
Loneliness isn’t only the lonely person’s problem, and helping people find one another shouldn’t be either.
Introduce two friends. Invite someone along. Put away the phone and look around the room. Take the chance of being rejected, or give someone a chance you might otherwise have overlooked.
Because an entire marriage, a family, perhaps even generations of people who don’t yet exist, can still begin with one person looking at another and saying the most ordinary word imaginable: “Hello.”
Sometimes an entire future begins there.

title: Rep. Haley Stevens switches endorsement to Mike Rogers in Michigan Senate race
text:
WASHINGTON (Gray DC) - Rep. Haley Stevens, D-Mich., withdrew her support for Michigan Democratic Senate nominee Abdul El-Sayed on Sunday and endorsed Republican candidate Mike Rogers, just two days before the midterm elections.
The reversal follows tense in-party fighting between Stevens, a moderate, and El-Sayed, a progressive, who often clashed while campaigning for the state’s Democratic Senate nomination. Stevens endorsed El-Sayed soon after she conceded the close August primary.
Stevens and Rogers were seen attending a church service together Sunday morning, which prompted questions about whom she supported.
Stevens answered in a video posted to social media, in which she officially switched her endorsement to Rogers. She said she felt what was coming out of the Democratic nominee’s campaign was “hate”.
“I don’t belong in Abdul’s campaign. I do not stand with Hasan Piker, who gets trafficked on our college campuses,” Stevens said, referencing a supporter of El-Sayed.
Top Democratic leaders were quick to respond on social media, calling the move “dangerous” and a “despicable betrayal.”
Meanwhile, President Donald Trump called Stevens “brave,” a thought echoed by Speaker of the House Mike Johnson. Trump later told reporters he would welcome her to the Republican Party.
Rogers held a gaggle with Stevens soon after the announcement and said he was honored to have her vote.
“This is more a statement about standing together against hate and the future of this state and this country than it is anything else,” Rogers said.
When asked about the change, El-Sayed said he “doesn’t think about Stevens” and is more focused on the issues leading his campaign.
The endorsement even led to a major switch up on the Hill: Stevens’ longtime congressional chief of staff issued a statement Sunday saying he and other members of the team resigned after the flipped support. He said he was shocked and heartbroken by the action, and ended the statement with his own endorsement of El-Sayed.

title: Gabby Williams leads Valkyries to WNBA championship in second season, beating Dream 68-63 in Game 7
text:
SAN FRANCISCO (AP) — A fresh WNBA CHAMPIONS T-shirt over her uniform, Gabby Williams cradled the shiny MVP trophy in one arm and gave it a kiss. She held up a No. 1 with her left hand, then hugged and high-fived her supporters all the way to Golden State’s locker room where she pulled on some goggles for the celebration.
Williams made her way back to the Bay Area where she cherishes so many youth basketball memories exactly for a chance to do something like this — to win it all and be part of building something special.
And she has done that all right.
“I just walked into a group full of love,” Williams said. “And that just changed the entire trajectory of my career.”
Williams scored her team’s final 11 points of the third quarter and dazzled through the fourth on the way to 30 points, and the Valkyries captured a championship in just their second season by beating the Atlanta Dream 68-63 in a sensational first WNBA Finals Game 7 on Saturday night.
“Gabby is our closer she stayed patient, she stayed with it,” coach Natalie Nakase said. “Closing with 30, that is incredible!”
Williams joined Penny Taylor in 2007 for Phoenix as the only players in WNBA history to score 30 or more points in a winner-takes-all Finals game.
Jordin Canada scored 18 points, Allisha Gray 16 and Angel Reese had eight points and 12 rebounds for the Dream, denied another championship in the franchise’s fourth try.
Gray made two free throws with 11 seconds left then Atlanta forced a jump ball — Gray against Williams — and Veronica Burton corralled it and converted two free throws with 5.1 seconds to go.
“I’m just so blessed, this is insane!” said Burton, cut by Dallas two years ago.
Rhyne Howard’s layup tied it at 57 with 2:41 left only for Williams to answer once more with a clutch 3-pointer. She converted two free throws with 1:40 remaining, then Kiah Stokes scored a late basket. Stokes — now a four-time WNBA champion — pulled down 13 rebounds and blocked two more shots to cap her spectacular postseason.
Williams left Seattle with a great feeling about joining Golden State and its close-knit culture, returning to the Bay Area determined to prove herself as a WNBA star after all her international success — and now she’s a postseason icon. Fans chanted “Gabby! Gabby!” throughout the fourth quarter.
“All it took was good people,” she said. “All we heard last year was we don’t have no stars. We don’t have no talent. Yeah right! We got good people. We got good people. We got winners. We got people who are ready to put their bodies on the floor to win a game.”
When the final buzzer sounded, the violet-clad sellout crowd at Chase Center went into a frenzy as players sprinted onto the floor to hug and celebrate as confetti fell from the rafters.
“Ballhalla” had become “Boohalla” for this far-but-haunted Halloween night in the raucous arena. Now, with a women’s championship to its name right alongside the one earned by the Golden State Warriors in 2022.
“We gotta build a bigger trophy case,” co-owner Peter Guber said.
The team that led at halftime in the first six matchups had won every game so far, and the Dream were ahead 30-24 at the break. Atlanta also had been 16-0 this season when Reese made at least one 3. The Dream’s DeWanna Bonner became the first player in WNBA history to reach 600 career postseason defensive rebounds.
Nakase told Williams at halftime the game would open up for her.
“Nat told me to stay patient, I trust her with my life,” Williams said. “I stayed patient.”
Nakase changed her starting lineup in a move that paid huge dividends after Golden State fell behind 2-1, inserting Kaila Charles and Tiffany Hayes and bringing Kayla Thornton and Cecilia Zandalasini off the bench.
The 37-year-old Hayes, who came out of retirement two years ago and spent 10 seasons with the Dream, scored 11 points in the winner-take-all Game 7 and brought energy all series that made Nakase want to win for the veteran guard as much as anybody.
Valkyries owner Joe Lacob guaranteed a championship within the first five years for this franchise three years ago when the Bay Area was granted an expansion team, and in improbable, joyful fashion, his team accomplished it in Year 2. That after becoming the first expansion organization to reach the playoffs in its inaugural year in 2025.
During the victory ceremony, Lacob shouted out the team and its leaders, while Nakase, general manager Ohemma Nyanin and President Jess Smith hugged. And Lacob thanked the fans who have sold out Chase Center for every game since Day 1.
“Ballhalla!” Lacob hollered.
“These ladies deserve all the credit in the world for the incredible resilience, every last one of them, and our coach,” he said later. “I can’t even say how proud I am. I don’t care men, women, whatever, it doesn’t matter, that is an incredible year, an incredible performance, not only tonight but the whole playoffs.”

title: Former UMaine quarterback Joe Fagnano makes NFL debut for Ravens
text:
Former University of Maine quarterback Joe Fagnano made his National Football League debut for the Baltimore Ravens in Sunday’s 36-10 loss to the Buffalo Bills in Orchard Park, New York.
Starting quarterback Lamar Jackson, who returned to the lineup after missing the previous three games due to a high ankle sprain, suffered a thumb injury on his first throw of the game, and backup Tyler Huntley sustained a toe injury early in the second quarter.
Jackson will need surgery and will be placed on injured reserve by the Ravens.
Fagnano, who transferred from UMaine to the University of Connecticut, completed his first two passes for 28 yards and engineered a third-quarter drive that produced a field goal to pull Baltimore within 16-10.
He finished the game completing 10 of 21 passes for 91 yards. He was sacked three times and threw an interception at the end of the first half that resulted in a Bills field goal. He also had a four-yard run.
Fagnano, an undrafted free agent, earned a roster spot as the No. 3 quarterback by having an impressive preseason for the Ravens.
He led the NFL in passing yards with 509, and he completed 74.7% of his passes (56-for-75). He threw three touchdown passes and was intercepted just once.
In his last preseason game, he completed 19 of 27 passes for 162 yards in a 41-3 win over the Washington Commanders. He threw a touchdown pass and ran for another.
The 25-year-old Fagnano played at Football Championship Subdivision UMaine from 2019-22 and completed 59.7% of his passes (461-for-772) for 5,655 yards and 46 touchdowns. He was intercepted 12 times. He also ran the ball 229 times for 535 yards and five TDs.
He then transferred to Football Bowl Subdivision UConn, where he completed 64.7% of his passes (423-for-654) for 48 TDs and six interceptions. He carried the ball 93 times for 223 yards and four touchdowns.
Last fall, he threw for 3,448 yards and 28 TDs with only one interception. He completed 69% of his passes.
Fagnano signed a three-year deal with the Ravens worth $3.1 million.

title: ‘You were called, you served, you are one of us.’
text:
Allen Wicken lives in Rangeley.
“You were called, you served, you are one of us.”
As an honorably discharged Maine veteran (1970-72), I was invited to be one of 66 mostly Vietnam-era and Korean War veterans to participate in Honor Flight Maine this past Oct. 16-18. Those words, spoken to me by Diane Carlson Evans, RN, in Hanoi, Vietnam, in January 1998, loomed large in my mind during those three days.
Honor Flight Maine has proven to be a powerfully positive experience for Maine’s veterans in the years since its inception in 2014.
Its main mission is to provide a cost-free trip to the Washington, D.C., area to visit the many national memorials dedicated to U.S. veterans of various conflicts from WWI up to the present. Its mission can be stated in its belief: “It is essential to express our gratitude and recognition for their service, and we are here to make that experience memorable and meaningful.”
Diane was a combat nurse during the Vietnam conflict, and is the veteran most responsible for bringing the Vietnam Women’s Memorial into being. It is a moving statue of three nurses and a wounded soldier located in a grove of trees not far from the well-known Vietnam Veterans Memorial (“the Wall”) near the National Mall in Washington, D.C. I made a special effort to again visit that memorial as well during our Honor Flight Maine weekend.
What were Diane and I doing in Hanoi, Vietnam, in 1998 you might ask? It was because of an impressive nonprofit called World T.E.A.M. Sports (WTS), organized in the late 1980s to provide challenging events, such as cycling and handcycling, for those with physical disabilities to demonstrate the abilities rather than disabilities of the participants. I first participated on an earlier project as a staff member with WTS in 1996 and three more through 2010.
Diane and I were among those asked to be staff members on WTS’ most ambitious project to date: Take a number of combat-wounded American Vietnam veterans to Vietnam and cycle the length of the country from Hanoi to Saigon (now Ho Chi Minh City) 1,200 miles in 16 days along with a number of disabled North Vietnam Army (NVA) veterans as teammates as well.
It’s was no surprise that it proved to be a powerful experience on many levels. As a Maine-licensed physical therapist (MS, Duke University ’74) cycling with, and available to assist the disabled riders as needed, and a Vietnam era veteran experienced with WTS’ mission as well, I was invited to be a part of the “Vietnam Challenge” team.
After two days in Hanoi, we got to know each other, attending special events organized for our benefit, getting used to our Cannondale hybrid bikes and visiting Hanoi’s Bach Mai Hospital. The evening before the celebrated start of the ride near the tomb of Ho Chi Minh, many of our Vietnam veterans became upset by a request made by the local communist government officials. A meeting was scheduled among the veterans to discuss how we would respond.
As the veterans were heading toward the meeting, Diane Carlson Evans noticed that I was walking in the opposite direction.
When she asked about it, I told her that I didn’t actually serve my time in that war-torn country after a low lottery number resulted in my two years (1970-72) of active duty at a U.S. Army medical research facility in Massachusetts. That’s when she said, “You were called, you served, you are one of us.”
The feeling of guilt that had curiously been with me since I received my post-basic training orders at Fort Knox, Kentucky, in 1970 instantly left me.
I sensed similar evolving feelings among many of my Maine veteran colleagues on Honor
Flight Maine, most all of whom served dutifully and honorably but were never on the front lines.
I ask that this fine project continue well into the future.

title: Kimi Antonelli becomes youngest Formula 1 champion in history
text:
Kimi Antonelli becomes youngest Formula 1 champion in history
Mercedes-AMG F1 driver Andrea Kimi Antonelli has become the youngest Formula 1 champion in history — with four races still to go in the season.
Related video above: IndyCar Freedom 250 races through DC in historic first
At 20 years and 2 months old, Antonelli has officially taken the title of youngest F1 champion from Sebastian Vettel, who first became champion when he was 23 years old.
Antonelli is also the first Italian driver to win the series since Alberto Ascari in 1953 — a 73-year gap.
It was a busy season for the young Mercedes driver. He's won nine grands prix so far this year, with a total of 15 podium finishes, scoring 365 points. The driver currently in second — Antonelli's Mercedes teammate George Russell — trailed him at 242 points going into this weekend.
Last year's drivers' champion, McLaren driver Lando Norris, has struggled for much of this season. He entered this weekend in sixth place, with four-time drivers' champion Max Verstappen in fourth.
Antonelli just had to finish today's race in at least ninth place to secure the drivers' championship. He ended up in third. The race itself was won by Red Bull’s Max Verstappen.
The series will continue next weekend in São Paulo, Brazil, with the Brazilian Grand Prix.

title: The Case for the 8 A.M.
text:
Nothing unites college students more than their collective disdain for 8 A.M. classes. As a sophomore at Bates, I’ve never gone a semester without one. I doubt that will change.
I certainly understand the opposition. After late nights studying for an exam, spending time with friends, and extracurricular activities, most college students dread waking up early. When the Maine winter rolls around, waking up before 7 A.M. to trek though snow certainly isn’t ideal. So when course registration comes, it’s not a surprise that most students avoid the early time slot.
While many see an 8 A.M. as a reason to reconsider taking a class, I see it as a chance. An 8 A.M. is a chance to get into some of the most sought after classes, with the most inspiring faculty. I’ve found that being open to early mornings has allowed me to consistently get my first choice of courses. At a small college where course registration is already a competitive process, I view the 8 A.M. as a tradeoff that can increase my odds of an ideal courseload.
Two of my favorite classes in my freshman year at Bates were Chemistry 107: Atomic and Molecular Structure with Professor Geneva Laurita and Sociology 235: Global Health: Sociological Perspectives with Professor Heidi Taylor. Both of these courses met at 8 A.M., and they were both classes I looked forward to attending. I found both professors’ teaching styles to be very engaging and the course material was certainly some of my favorite. While I may have had a few frantic mornings rushing from Frye Street because my alarm clock didn’t go off, I mainly remember enjoying the classes, and having my whole day ahead of me after.
These experiences reinforced the idea that, for me, the course material and professor’s teaching style matter far more than the time of the class. Additionally, the consistency of having an 8 A.M. every semester has helped me maintain my morning routine from high school. While I don’t always love waking up early, it was never an adjustment that I had to make. There is also a feeling of camaraderie in an 8 A.M. class. The shared early mornings, eating a to-go breakfast, and the occasional spilled coffee make for stronger bonds.
An underrated part of taking early classes is lunchtime. This semester, I have no class after noon for four days of the week. This allows me to enjoy a long lunch in Commons, catch up with friends, and always have time to get dessert. Additionally, this gives me more flexibility for longer afternoon commitments like going on a run, going out for lunch, or volunteering in Lewiston.
When the weekends come, sleeping in feels like a luxury. Waking up at 10 A.M. on a Saturday with a clear schedule is especially satisfying.
I understand that 8 A.M.s are not for everyone. Many mornings when my alarm goes off I question my decisions. When balancing getting my first choice of classes, enjoying a relaxed lunch, and having free afternoons, to me, the early mornings are worth it.
If you are on the fence about taking an 8 A.M. next semester, I encourage you to give it a chance. With Bates new and competitive registration system, the 8 A.M. will always be there as a source or certainty. That said, if the shared hatred of the 8 A.M. continues, I definitely won’t complain about having less competition for my favorite classes.

title: Florida man creates massive Halloween display
text:
Florida man creates massive Halloween display
Florida man creates massive Halloween display
Joshua Kreppel has created what he describes as the biggest haunted house he has ever built in his front yard, offering a free and spooky experience for the community.
"This is the biggest haunted house. I've been doing it since I was a kid. I've been doing Christmas lights, Halloween stuff, and honestly, this is the biggest one. And next year I definitely want to go bigger and bigger," said Kreppel, a Delray Beach, Florida, resident.
Kreppel shared his love for the sense of community the event fosters.
"This I love, a group gathering with the community," he said.
He also expressed his enjoyment in seeing visitors' reactions.
"I love watching people get scared. I like watching people have coming in the community all being friends. I like seeing people in front of my house, shaking hands, hugging each other and being friendly and stuff," Kreppel said.
Video below: The science of being scared: What happens to your brain and body when fear strikes?
Visitors to the haunted house shared their excitement about the experience.
"There's not one person who did not go through that maze who did not get... it was because it was scary fun. Spooky," one attendee said.
"When you first come into the haunted house, you would never expect this is in someone's front yard," another visitor said.
Kreppel emphasized that the haunted house is free for everyone to enjoy.
"Guess what? You don't have to pay no money. It's free," he said.
Attendees described the event as "real fun," and Kreppel concluded with a festive message.
"Hey, listen, it's that month of October. I just want to say, 'Happy Halloween,'" he said.

title: Flash floods trigger evacuations in Arizona and Colorado amid heavy rains in southwest
text:
SEDONA, Ariz. (AP) — Flash flooding prompted mandatory evacuation orders in parts of the Southwest on Sunday as heavy rains in the normally arid region have already brought deadly flooding this fall.
Officials in the tourist destination of Sedona, Arizona, ordered residents in areas near Oak Creek to leave immediately as flood waters were rising rapidly and multiple people were already trapped in their homes.
In southwestern Colorado, officials in Pagosa Springs, also a tourist destination, warned in a Facebook post of potentially “catastrophic flooding” as the San Juan River is forecast to crest at more than 19 feet (5.8 meters) around 11:00 p.m. Sunday.
“To put the forecast into perspective, during the devastating 1911 flood that wiped out most of what existed as the town of Pagosa at that time, the San Juan River crested at approximately 17.8 feet (5.4 meters),” the Archuleta County Sheriff’s Office said in a separate Facebook post. “This is a potentially catastrophic flood event. Extensive damage is expected.”
The latest round of soaking rains started Saturday evening and were expected to bring flash flooding to already saturated areas through Monday. The National Weather Service estimates as much as 4 inches (10 centimeters) of rain could fall across the region, fueled by a series of Pacific storm systems.
The weather service issued flood watches for nearly all of Arizona and parts of southern Utah, southwestern Colorado, and western New Mexico, in addition to part of southern Nevada. That includes the sparsely populated Four Corners region where Arizona, Colorado, New Mexico and Utah meet.
Pagosa Springs officials said anyone in low-lying areas along the San Juan, Rio Blanco, Navajo and Piedra Rivers should head to a designated shelter at a local church.
They said residents should leave immediately, and not wait as emergency crews may be extremely limited during the worst of the storm. The highway entering the hot springs town also would be shut down to inbound traffic Sunday afternoon, town officials added.
Meanwhile in Sedona, local officials ordered residents living in affected areas to head to Sedona Red Rock High School. But they urged people not to attempt to drive across roads with rushing waters and to stay away from creek beds and washes.
Sedona Fire District Chief Ed Mezulis said in a short clip posted on Facebook that emergency crews from surrounding communities were coming in to assist as local fire and police officials were already responding to multiple reports of residents trapped in their homes due to the rising flood waters.
“Please stay at high ground, watch your alerts and be careful,” he advised.
A video shared by the fire department showed powerful flood waters inundating vehicles and rushing past homes and other structures. Other videos and photos shared on social media showed people standing on a pedestrian bridge taking photos and videos as churning, brown waters rushed underneath.

title: Patriots rally, then hold on to beat Dolphins
text:
MIAMI GARDENS, Fla. — Drake Maye was without a pair of top receivers and a running back Sunday against the Miami Dolphins.
No problem for the New England Patriots quarterback.
Star A.J. Brown (knee/ankle), Mack Hollins (calf) and running back TreVeyon Henderson (illness) were all sidelined. Still, Maye threw two touchdown passes and rushed for a score as the Patriots came back to beat the Dolphins 24-19.
“(If) you want to be a great quarterback in the National Football League, there’s not a whole lot of excuses,” Patriots coach Mike Vrabel said about Maye’s performance. “You go out there and find ways to win for your football team. That’s who he is and that’s what he wants to continue to be.”
Maye completed 16 of 20 passes for 199 yards and the Patriots (5-3) overcame a 10-point halftime deficit to take a 17-13 lead entering the fourth, then held on after a late Miami rally.
DeMario Douglas caught a pass and weaved through the Dolphins secondary for a 48-yard touchdown catch that put the Patriots up by two scores early in the fourth.
The Patriots hadn’t had a clean operation in the first half, but they took advantage of the young Dolphins’ mistakes in the second, outscoring Miami 21-0 until Malik Willis threw a 35-yard touchdown to rookie Kevin Coleman Jr. with two minutes left.
After an unsuccessful two-point try by Miami, Rhamondre Stevenson recovered Bradley Pinion’s onside kick, and New England kept the ball from there.
Stevenson had 19 carries for 82 yards, and Douglas caught three passes for 76 yards.
“We knew that once we settle in and get some drives together,” Maye said, “we had a chance of getting some points on the board.”
One week after leading Miami (1-6) to its first win of the season, Willis completed 21 of 32 passes for 211 yards. He threw for two touchdowns and had an interception while being sacked five times.
The Patriots pulled within three when Maye lofted a pass to Kyle Williams for a 43-yard touchdown that was initially ruled an incompletion after Williams’ knee appeared to jar the ball loose. Vrabel demonstratively launched the red challenge flag, and officials overturned the call to a touchdown after replays showed Williams crossed the goal line before losing possession of the ball.
“I was a lot more certain than the officials were the first time they called it,” Vrabel said.
Miami went three-and-out on the next drive, its momentum stalled after Ollie Gordon drew an unsportsmanlike conduct penalty after saying something to a defender following a 5-yard carry. Coach Jeff Hafley removed Gordon from the game for a play, and the second-year running back appeared visibly upset as Willis spoke to him on the sideline.
“Ollie is a competitor, and he cares about the game a lot,” Willis said. “And I was just letting him know that in that situation, that he’s … wrong. I mean, that’s the honest truth. And it would be wrong if I didn’t tell him the truth.”
On the next New England drive, Maye faked a pitch to Stevenson and ran it in for the 2-yard go-ahead score with 59 seconds left in the third — his fifth straight game with at least three total touchdowns.
Willis led the Dolphins on an 11-play, 70-yard two-minute drive that Malik Washington capped with a 1-yard touchdown to put Miami ahead 13-3 at the half.
Washington had briefly left the game after taking a hard hit from Patriots linebacker Christian Elliss earlier in the drive. Elliss was flagged for unnecessary roughness for the hit, and Washington, after a brief trip to the blue medial tent, returned five plays later to catch his first receiving touchdown of the season.
“I thought it was probably the best half that we played all year in the first half in some phases,” Hafley said. “But we had not had a lead like that going into a half. And there was great energy and we came out and I believe we held them to a three-and -out. And then those are the opportunities where you’ve got to learn to put people away.”
Zane Gonzalez, in his second game since re-signing with Miami, hit field goals of 31 and 52 yards, the latter of which doinked off the left upright and through. He missed a 43-yard attempt in the fourth.
Injuries
Patriots: TE Hunter Henry (foot) left in the second quarter and did not return. … Linebacker Gabe Jacas (knee) left in the third and didn’t return.
Dolphins: Edge rusher Malik Herring left in the second with a stringer but in the third.
Up next
Patriots: Host Green Bay next Sunday.
Dolphins: Host Detroit next Sunday.

title: Trump plays defense in red states amid Democratic rift in Senate battleground
text:
Trump plays defense in red states amid Democratic rift in Senate battleground
In the final weekend before Election Day, there is still significant uncertainty in the battle for Senate control.
Trump plays defense in red states amid Democratic rift in Senate battleground
In the final weekend before Election Day, there is still significant uncertainty in the battle for Senate control.
In the final weekend before Election Day, President Donald Trump is playing defense in two historically red states as a Democratic rift in another Senate battleground burst into public view, underscoring continued uncertainty in the fight for control of the upper chamber.
President Trump took a brief break from his campaign travel blitz on Saturday, opting to hold a series of tele-rallies in key states instead of in-person events. He returns to the campaign trail on Sunday with stops expected in Iowa and Kansas that were previously canceled and then rescheduled.
Explaining the pivot on Friday, Trump said, "I thought I could relax. Twenty-eight days in a row of this crap is a lot. It's a lot. My voice is operating at about 49.2%, and then they called me in Iowa, and they called me in Kansas, and they said, sir, would it be possible to do a little rally of about 50,000 people each? And I said, 'Does it matter?' They said, we just want to make sure that we win."
Kansas hasn't sent a Democrat to the Senate since 1932. Iowa hasn't voted blue in Senate races since 2008.
But now, those states are home to some of the most competitive Senate races of the season. Both are among seven contests rated "toss-ups " by the Cook Political Report.
It underscores the headwinds that Republicans are facing as the party tries to maintain control of both chambers of Congress, with major stakes for the president's agenda during his final years in office.
Democrats have expressed optimism about the chances of a "blue wave," like the one we saw at this point in Trump's first term, but the party is dealing with ideological divides that could complicate that mission. El-Sayed's campaign then disinvited Stevens from the planned appearance following a feud over his stance on Israel and past comments that have upset some Jewish voters.
That could complicate what is already a difficult path for Democrats to win the Senate majority.
Democrats need to flip at least four seats to take back control in the Senate. A potential loss in Michigan, where the Senate seat is currently blue, would complicate that path, requiring the party to pick up five seats to win a majority.
An Associated Press analysis going into the weekend found that early voting in states with key Senate races is significantly outpacing the last midterm election.
Turnout is also up nationwide, according to the UF Election Lab. As of Sunday morning, more than 52 million ballots had been cast, compared to nearly 46 million in the 2022 mi.

title: 1 killed, 8 injured in shooting after Alabama football game
text:
1 killed, 8 injured in shooting after Alabama football game
One person was killed and eight others were wounded in a shooting outside Legion Field in Birmingham, Alabama, shortly after the Magic City Classic ended Saturday night.
Shots were fired just before 8 p.m. on Graymont Avenue West, while tailgating was still underway.
CNN Video: Officials on scene after shooting in Alabama
One of the injured was in critical condition. The other seven were listed as stable, according to police.
One person was detained for questioning, but no arrests have been announced.
Tailgating was suspended after the shooting. Police asked people at the stadium to leave the property as soon as possible and not return.
The Birmingham Police Department is asking anyone who captured video of the shooting to submit it to investigators.

title: Obituary: Mary Ann Albert
text:
WINDHAM – Mary Ann Albert, 61, of Windham, passed away unexpectedly at home on Oct. 19, 2026. She was born in Westbrook on July 3, 1965, the youngest daughter of the late Roland Wilfred Albert and the late Janet Adeline (Rondeau) Albert.
Mary Ann was a 1983 graduate of Westbrook High School, where she was active in the Sock & Buskin Society. She worked at various careers, including running her own housekeeping business. In 2012 she graduated from a Certified Nursing Assistant course, and became a full time CNA at the Barron Center in Portland the following year. Later she became a Certified Medication Technician and continued her career at the Barron Center in that role. Mary Ann’s caring nature extended beyond her profession. She cared for both of her parents during their stays at the Barron Center. She cared for her father in the last months of his life, and she cared for her mother during the final years of her life, including through the pandemic.
Mary Ann’s friends and family remember her as vivacious, fun-loving and selfless. She made friends easily and maintained friendships dating back to grade school, as well as those formed at every place she worked. She was a natural caregiver who loved her job and the residents and staff at the Barron Center.
Mary Ann also had a special love for cats, from her first cat, Gus, to her last, Goatee, who recently passed away. Her favorite place was the beach, and she spent many happy days at Scarborough Beach and Pine Point Beach with her sisters, cousins, and friends. She loved music, especially the Beatles, Tom Petty, and Bruce Springsteen. One of her joys was watching her brother Peter play guitar, whether performing solo or with his various bands, most recently Legolas.
Mary Ann is survived by her sister Nancy Tarpinian and her husband Michael of Westbrook, her brother Paul of Harrison, her brother Peter and his wife Catherine of Westbrook, and her sister Becky of Tilton, N.H.; and several nieces and nephews who were very special to her. She leaves numerous friends, including longtime friends Susan Ledoux, Kristine Thuotte, and Judy Nelson Bouchard. She was predeceased by her parents.
Services will be held on Nov. 12, at Dolby, Blais & Segee at 35 Church St., Westbrook. Visiting hour will begin at 10 a.m., followed by a funeral service at 11 a.m., gathering to follow at Bruno’s Restaurant at 33 Allen Ave., Portland.
