title: Troy Jackson leads Susan Collins by 6 points in final NYT/Press Herald/Siena poll
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Troy Jackson led Sen. Susan Collins by six percentage points in a New York Times/Portland Press Herald/Siena poll of Maine voters — a big swing in a U.S. Senate race that, to this point, has been a dead heat.
Jackson, the 58-year-old Democratic nominee, had the support of 51% of respondents in the poll of 714 likely Maine voters, which was released Sunday but conducted over the past week. Collins, the five-term Republican senator, polled at 45%. The margin of error was 4.3%.
That was a nine-point swing from the September iteration of the Times/Press Herald/Siena poll. Behind that startling number was an apparently significant shift in Maine’s electorate in the past month and a half — in an election that could decide the majority of the Senate.
In the September poll, Collins held a three-point edge over Jackson. Collins, who has pitched herself as an experienced moderate, pulled substantial support from voters in Maine’s middle in that survey.
But this new poll suggests that may have changed. While in September, Collins had the support of 8% of the Democrats surveyed and Jackson drew 3% of Republicans, the new poll showed Collins with less crossover support than Jackson.
Jackson also had the support of more unenrolled voters, 52% compared to Collins’ 41%. That’s a big swing in Jackson’s favor — the September poll had the two tied among independents, each at 47%.
Voters also said they trusted Jackson slightly more than Collins on cost of living, while Collins had a one-point edge on tackling immigration. The economy was voters’ number one issue, the survey found.
Even Collins favorability was down: 48% of respondents said they had a favorable view of Collins, while 49% said they felt unfavorably. Collins had a 51% favorability rating in September, which matched her numbers in the heat of the 2020 campaign, when she defied polls and won with a nine-point margin over Sara Gideon.
Jackson was viewed favorably by 45% — a four-point jump since September — and unfavorably by 48%. Those figures came despite months of negative ads about Jackson from Collins and her allies, who held a large spending advantage throughout the race.
The Iran war has also been a major issue during the campaign. Jackson, whom Maine voters said they trusted more to handle foreign wars, by a three-point margin, has often pointed out Collins’ initial deference to the Trump administration in entering the war. The conflict has driven up fuel costs to record highs for the most heating oil-dependent state in the nation.
Collins has since voted several times to halt hostilities, and has touted deals with the Trump administration to release more fuel into markets.
She has also campaigned on her efforts to slow Trump’s trade war with Canada, on whom Maine is heavily reliant for bilateral trade. But Jackson has blamed Collins for not asserting congressional authority over tariffs.
That topic produced one of the more memorable moments of the campaign: Jackson telling Collins during an October debate that Mainers “can’t eat road salt,” in response to the five-term Senator pointing out that she secured its removal from the tariff list.
Another of the campaign’s most memorable moments came during the final debate between the two. Someone in the crowd at that Oct. 15 event stood up and began shouting about data centers, to which Collins said, “That’s obviously one of Troy’s supporters.” Jackson responded with “Oh, shut up,” and Collins’ allies have since spun the moment into a series of advertisements.
The campaign has been among the most expensive of this midterm cycle nationally, with nearly $50 million raised by the campaigns, and almost $150 million spent by outside groups, according to campaign finance tracker OpenSecrets.
But Maine may not see a winner in this competitive race Tuesday evening — or even this week; if neither candidate received 50% of votes, the count will proceed to a ranked-choice tabulation of those who wrote in a first-choice vote.
The NYT/Press Herald/Siena survey found that the vast majority of voters had settled on a candidate, with just 4% either refusing to say who they’d support, or responding that they didn’t know.
The New York Times/Portland Press Herald/Siena Research Institute poll of Maine voters was funded with support from the Maine Trust for Local News.

title: What to know about the Affordable Care Act open enrollment period now underway
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
What to know about the Affordable Care Act open enrollment period now underway
People heading into the Affordable Care Act open enrollment period with plans to sign up for insurance should expect a variety of changes in 2027, including higher premiums and fewer coverage options.
The sign-up window for the marketplace, also known as Obamacare, starts Sunday in most states and runs through Jan. 15.
Big changes to the exchange include expiring financial assistance, rising rates, potential delays in working with a broker, new restrictions on immigrants, and stricter enrollment checks.
Financial help, including premium tax credits and cost-sharing reductions, is now restricted for many groups of people who were previously eligible.
Across the board, healthcare experts predict less coverage and higher prices, with the average price of health insurance purchased through the marketplaces expected to rise by 13% in 2027, according to analysis of new CMS data by the healthcare research nonprofit KFF.
Increases are driven by multiple factors
Cynthia Cox, a vice president and director of the ACA program at KFF, said the increase is primarily driven by rising healthcare costs, hospital market concentration, and potential factors such as the No Surprises Act, which took effect in 2022 and bans surprise billing, or the rising availability of GLP-1 drugs.
The people who will be most affected by the new increases are those who do not qualify for a subsidy.
"They may or may not be able to afford to continue to keep their coverage into next year," Cox said, adding that "a lot of them have already moved into bronze plans, which are the cheapest plans."
A CMS fact sheet about open enrollment that was distributed Friday says “Americans using HealthCare.gov will have robust access to low-cost plans.”
The price of ACA insurance has skyrocketed for many people during Trump’s second term after Republicans opposed extending COVID-era subsidies that had helped offset the costs of health insurance for most enrollees during Democratic President Joe Biden’s administration.
That resulted in 1.2 million fewer people signing up for coverage in the exchanges.
Nearly 20 million people in US are actively enrolled in ACA plans
As of February, roughly 19.2 million people in the United States were actively enrolled in ACA marketplace health plans, according to the Department of Health and Human Services website. The number of enrollees grew during the COVID-19 pandemic when enhanced subsidies became available through the American Rescue Plan Act and Inflation Reduction Act, both signed into law by Biden.
New regulations starting in 2027 will also limit tax credits for certain lawfully present immigrants, which could result in an additional 1 million uninsured individuals over time.
Meanwhile, the Trump administration has been removing ACA enrollees from the program as part of the ongoing campaign against what it characterizes as waste, fraud and abuse.
In September, Vice President JD Vance and other officials in the Republican administration announced plans to remove 760,000 ACA enrollees from public healthcare exchanges, alleging the individuals were fraudulently enrolled in the program or simply did not exist.
Vance said the discovery of and canceled subsidy payments for hundreds of thousands of people from the exchanges, part of an administration-wide crackdown on fraud, would result in $2.2 billion in cost savings.
It's unclear how many more people will drop off of ACA coverage in 2027, Cox said. But with higher premiums, immigration eligibility changes and the anti-fraud efforts, “I think there’s going to be fewer people enrolled in this market, but it’s going to be harder to understand why.”

title: What’s on the ballot and how to vote in Bangor’s local elections
text:
Thanks to community support for our election reporting, this page is free to read as a public service. Help make free access possible when public service calls for it with a subscription ($1 for 3 months right now) or a gift today.
Beyond the myriad statewide races Mainers are facing during this year’s midterm election, Bangor voters have 12 candidates to choose from for City Council this year — the most crowded field the local office has seen in decades.
Election Day is Tuesday, Nov. 3. Here’s what you need to know about your polling place and the local candidates before you cast your ballot this year.
Where do I vote?
All Bangor voters are assigned the same Election Day polling place: the Cross Insurance Center at 515 Main St. Polls open at 7 a.m. and close at 8 p.m.
Can I register to vote on Election Day?
Yes. Maine allows same-day voter registration at your polling place. If you’re not yet registered to vote, or if you recently moved to Bangor, you can register when you go to the Cross Insurance Center on Tuesday. Bring proof of residence at your address, such as an ID or a utility bill.
Who’s running for City Council?
There are three open seats on the Bangor City Council. The Bangor Daily News has profiled all 12 candidates — you can read those stories here.
We’ve also published a story breaking down how each candidate would’ve voted on key measures that the council has decided in the last year, and videos where you can hear, in their own words, where each candidate stands on homelessness, public drug use and syringe litter, affordability and city spending, and how they’d work together to get things done.
Candidates are listed below in the order they appear on the ballot.
Joe Leonard is the only incumbent councilor running for reelection this year and has said his top priority would be implementing a wards-based voting system and a mayor. He works for an energy company and as a substitute teacher. A Democrat, Leonard also said he wants the city to invest more in housing and city staff and that he’s working to ban automatic license plate readers. He’s become a controversial figure on the council after three censures for his behavior, including one related to an outburst that cost the city nearly $100,000 when it caused a staff member to resign.
Michael Furrow is retired from the military and from a job at the U.S. Department of Veterans Affairs. His top priority is addressing drug use and he believes illicit substances are the root of many other issues in the city. He also wants to ban syringe exchange programs and automatic license plate readers and end the construction of affordable housing in the city, which he has said is “bringing in the wrong type of people.” Furrow is the chair of the Bangor Republican Committee.
Andrei Yermakov works for the Maine People’s Alliance, one of the state’s most prominent progressive political organizations, and said his top priority would be building community and addressing what he sees as a lack of civil discourse on the council. Yermakov is a Democrat and described himself as a “long-term union guy” with experience negotiating contracts on both the union and management sides. He wants to implement a rent freeze and ban automatic license plate readers in the city.
Anthony Cote owns a construction business and said his top priority as a councilor would be to make Bangor more business-friendly. He also wants to cut the city budget and further restrict the number of needles someone can get when visiting a syringe exchange program due to his belief that those programs enable addiction. Cote described himself as a centrist and declined to share his party affiliation in an interview with the BDN, although his campaign finance registration with the city, obtained through a public records request, lists him as a Republican.
James Gallagher, owner of Bangin’ Whoopie downtown, is running for council again after coming in as the runner-up last year. Gallagher is unenrolled in a political party and wants to declare a state of emergency around homelessness and quickly establish an emergency shelter if elected. He also wants the city to explore fundraising strategies, such as lemonade stands or car washes, to support its services. He’s in the middle of many other candidates on syringe service programs, saying he sees value in them but might consider restricting needle distribution to a one-for-one ratio.
Terry Dinkins is the pastor of the Mansion Church on Center Street, the chaplain at the Penobscot County Jail and a branch manager for an armored car company. Dinkins has run a winter warming center out of his church since 2020 and named reducing homelessness his top priority, with cutting down on drugs and needles a close second. He’d like Bangor to focus on improving mental health care and drastically reducing the number of needles distributed in the city. Dinkins is unenrolled in a political party and has drawn criticism in local circles online for counter-protests his church has held at LGBTQ+ pride events in the past.
Joseph Pratt oversees the wealth management group at Bar Harbor Bank and Trust and serves on the boards of several nonprofits, including the Bangor Public Library. He said his top priority would be to restore civility and decorum to the council. Pratt, a Republican, also wants to expand the tax base to ease the burden on property owners. He’s opposed to harm reduction programs like syringe services and said at a candidate forum that those programs are “basically perpetuating drug abuse.”
Adam Baker, a retail worker and a member of Bangor’s Advisory Committee on Equity, Inclusion and Human Rights, is running on a platform of making Bangor more affordable. They want to grow the city’s affordable housing supply and implement rent control measures. Baker, a Democrat, also wants to bring back weekend service for the city’s bus system and said they’d support strategies like a sanctioned encampment, the housing first model and expanding the city’s public health department to address Bangor’s homelessness crisis.
Dawson Nevells, a political science student at the University of Maine and the youngest candidate this year, said he’d prioritize implementing regional solutions to the homelessness crisis. He wants to build a regional service center combining shelter and other supports that would be funded by a bond and operated by the city and neighboring communities. He also wants to impose a one-to-one restriction on needle exchange programs. Nevells, a Democrat, made an unsuccessful bid for Bangor School Committee two years ago.
Katherine Devine works as a nanny and has been involved in conservative political activism in the state since she was a kid, including advocacy for a statewide referendum that would’ve barred transgender students from sports teams aligned with their gender identities. Devine, a Republican and the second-youngest candidate at 21, named changing the city’s approach to drugs and homelessness as a top priority, saying she wants to stop giving handouts and abolish syringe service programs. She’d like to see Bangor focus instead on improving its mental health facilities.
Jennifer McGinley Maskala is the programs director for the Wild Blueberry Commission of Maine and wants the city to “spend less, do more” by reducing the budget and focusing on what she sees as the most fundamental city services, like repairing aging sewer systems and school facilities. She also wants the city to require syringe service programs to tag every needle they distribute and then fine a provider if someone litters a needle obtained from that location. McGinley Maskala declined to share her party affiliation, and she left the field blank in her campaign finance registration with the city.
John King is a member of the city’s ethics board. He’s retired from the military and is currently pursuing a Ph.D. in business. If elected, he said he’d prioritize identifying duplications in the city’s budget to reduce spending, citing two homelessness-related positions in the public health department as a possible example. King is a Democrat and described himself as a moderate. He’s expressed some support for syringe exchange programs but also said he’d like to see more accountability measures for those programs.
Who’s running for School Committee?
Three candidates are running unopposed for three seats on the Bangor School Committee: Jamie Beck, Katie Brydon and Emily Tilton. You can read more about them here.
What else is on the ballot?
Bangor voters can also choose candidates for U.S. Senate, 2nd Congressional District representative, governor, the Maine Senate and the Maine House of Representatives.
Democrat Amy Roeder faces independent Steve Carey for Maine Senate, and there are two competitive state house races in Bangor: Republican Frank Casella versus incumbent Democrat Ambureen Rana in district 21, and Republican Brian Ames versus Democrat Victoria Kornfield in district 23.
Residents can also vote on a county-wide referendum about moving the Penobscot County Jail out of Bangor. All candidates for county-level positions are running unopposed.
You can view a sample ballot based on your address on the state’s voter information website and read more of the BDN’s statewide election coverage here.

title: Box Office: ‘You Can See Everything,’ 'Clayface' lead sleepy Halloween weekend
text:
The North American box office took a bit of a hit this weekend with the Halloween holiday drawing audiences away from theaters on Saturday. Ticket sales were led by the Elizabeth Holmes documentary “You Can See Everything” and the DC Studios movie “Clayface,” and aren’t likely to surpass $63 million, according to studio estimates on Sunday. That would make it the third-lowest-earning weekend of the year.
“You Can See Everything” had the slight edge over “Clayface,” with $10.6 million from 2,655 locations in its third weekend in theaters. The Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim-directed film has made $63.9 million to date against a reported production budget of $7 million and continues to generate the kind of buzz that’s hard to buy. This is the first time it’s hit No. 1, however.
“Clayface,” about the Batman villain, trailed “You Can See Everything” by only $200,684. The Warner Bros. release fell 57% in its second weekend in theaters. That brings its domestic earnings to $44.1 million against a reported $44 million budget.
Third place went to Laika’s animated film “Wildwood,” which added 150 screens in its second weekend, bringing its footprint to 3,100 theaters in the U.S. and Canada. The Fathom Entertainment release made an estimated $7.5 million, down 39% from its first weekend, bringing its running total to $25.9 million.
The comedic fantasy “Wicker,” in which Olivia Colman plays a woman who commissions a basket maker to build her a wicker husband (Alexander Skarsgård), landed in fourth place with $4.1 million. “Street Fighter,” now in its third weekend, rounded out the top five with $3.2 million.
In notable expansions, the acclaimed Sundance indie “The Only Living Pickpocket in New York” added over 1,000 locations in its second weekend and made $1.9 million, which landed it in the top 10.
Netflix also reported earnings from the theatrical release of its World War II film “The Mosquito Bowl,” which made $455,000 from 349 locations. “La Bola Negra” made slightly less, $418,000, from only 38 locations in its third weekend, bringing its running total to $1.2 million.
The domestic box office remains up over 17% from last year with nearly $8.5 billion to date.
Top 10 movies by domestic box office
With final domestic figures being released Monday, this list factors in the estimated ticket sales for Friday through Sunday at U.S. and Canadian theaters, according to Rentrak:
1. “You Can See Everything,” $10.6 million.
2. “Clayface,” $10.4 million.
3. “Wildwood,” $7.5 million.
4. “Wicker,” $4.1 million.
5. “Street Fighter,” $3.2 million.
6. “Resident Evil,” $2.5 million.
7. “Other Mommy,” $2.5 million.
8. “The Only Living Pickpocket in New York,” $1.9 million.
9. “Heart of the Beast,” $1.6 million.
10. “Sense and Sensibility,” $1.4 million.

title: 29-year-old influencer dies following motorcycle crash, girlfriend says
text:
'Difficult and heartbreaking': Influencer Liam Fitzgerald dies following motorcycle crash
A social media influencer, known for sharing posts about fitness, style, and finances to more than one million followers on Instagram, has died at the age of 29.
Liam Fitzgerald's girlfriend, Jamie Lyn Rinaldi, said the influencer died on Oct. 30 around 2 a.m. following a motorcycle accident.
Rinaldi said Fitzgerald suffered severe injuries.
"Despite the efforts of those who tried desperately to save him, they were unable to bring him back," Rinaldi said in an Instagram post. " There are no words to describe the heartbreak of this loss."
She continued, saying, "This is an incredibly difficult and heartbreaking time for everyone who knew and loved him. Please keep Liam's family, loved ones, and everyone closest to him in your thoughts and prayers."
According to People Magazine, Fitzgerald, who was based in Miami, Florida, had more than one million followers on Instagram and also served as a fitness coach, offering one-on-one training sessions.

title: Authorities rescue 10-year-old girl after she was abducted, found duct-taped inside home
text:
(CNN) - A SWAT team in Oregon rescued a child hours after she was kidnapped from her house, according to law enforcement.
The search for the 10-year-old girl started Wednesday morning.
Authorities said Vince Edgar Chavez got into the house and assaulted the girl. He was also accused of attacking her 12-year-old sister with a hammer.
By Wednesday afternoon, Clackamas County SWAT and Crisis Negotiation were led to a house where they found the girl, who was restrained with duct tape.
Chavez allegedly tried to run from officers by going out a second-story window but was captured and arrested shortly afterward.
Both girls received medical treatment, and their parents are working with the authorities. Police said there is a link between Chavez and the family but didn’t offer additional details.

title: All 9 people aboard a jet that crashed in Florida have died, transportation secretary says
text:
All 9 people aboard a jet that crashed near a busy roadway in South Florida have died
A business jet carrying nine people nose-dived into a South Florida neighborhood Sunday and erupted into a giant fireball that appeared to just miss homes near a busy roadway. Everyone on board was killed, the nation's transportation secretary said.
Video recorded by people inside their cars captured the terrifying moment the Bahamas-bound aircraft plunged from the sky before striking near the roadway and exploding. Flames flickered around chunks of pavement lining a crater as people milled about, expressing shock that it landed only feet from homes and inches from passing vehicles. Thick black smoke engulfed the crash site.
Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy posted on X that the Learjet 60 crashed in Palm Beach County at 12:50 p.m. and called it a “horrific tragedy.” The Federal Aviation Administration is sending a team to support the National Transportation Safety Board’s investigation, he said.
Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis said there were no immediate reports of anyone on the ground injured or killed.
“It was a cataclysmic plane crash,” DeSantis told reporters at the scene. “It looked like a missile going down and left a big crater on the side of the road.”
Rain pounded the region on Sunday. A flood watch due to excessive rainfall was in effect through Monday afternoon, the National Weather Service said.
The aircraft had departed Austin-Bergstrom International Airport in Texas and was headed to the Bahamas, according to the Federal Aviation Administration. Authorities did not immediately say what caused the jet to go down or who was on it.
The plane was heading east at 35,000 feet (about 11 kilometers) when pilots reported turbulence, icing and precipitation and requested to climb another 2,000 feet (about 610 meters).
Moments later, the plane entered a steep dive, first 10,000 feet per minute, then 20,000 feet per minute and up to 30,000 feet per minute, speeding the plane beyond its design limits, according to air traffic control recordings and flight tracking data.
A pilot declared an emergency and issued distress calls. The plane banked sharply to the right before it smashed into the ground.
Minutes before the crash, the pilot reported ice accumulating on the jet and turbulence that was jolting it by as much as 700 feet (213 meters), according to air traffic control recordings captured by LiveATC.net.
“We have light, clear ice that is manageable and moderate turbulence,” the pilot told controllers.
But the situation rapidly deteriorated. After encountering precipitation and requesting to climb, the pilot declared an emergency as the aircraft began losing altitude at an alarming rate.
“We’re descending 8,000 – mayday, mayday - we’re descending 10,000 feet per minute,” the pilot radioed.
“We are in an overspeed condition descending 20,000 feet per minute,” the pilot radioed, before delivering a devastating acknowledgment of what was about to happen. “We’re going to crash into the ground.”
Jim Reynolds, a spokesperson for Austin-Bergstrom International Airport, said the jet was a private aircraft. He could not immediately provide details about who was on the flight.
Palm Beach County authorities were evacuating about 600 people from a nearby mobile home community while federal officials investigate the crash. The road will be closed until further notice, county officials said.
The crash occurred in Greenacres, Florida, according to Palm Beach County sheriff’s officials. The city of 45,000 people is about 7 miles (11 kilometers) southwest of West Palm Beach.

title: What to know about the Affordable Care Act’s open enrollment period now underway
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
The sign-up window for the marketplace, also known as Obamacare, starts Sunday in most states and runs through Jan. 15.
Big changes to the exchange include expiring financial assistance, rising rates, potential delays in working with a broker, new restrictions on immigrants, and stricter enrollment checks.
Financial help, including premium tax credits and cost-sharing reductions, is now restricted for many groups of people who were previously eligible.
Across the board, healthcare experts predict less coverage and higher prices, with the average price of health insurance purchased through the marketplaces expected to rise by 13% in 2027, according to analysis of new CMS data by the healthcare research nonprofit KFF.
Increases are driven by multiple factors
Cynthia Cox, a vice president and director of the ACA program at KFF, said the increase is primarily driven by rising healthcare costs, hospital market concentration, and potential factors such as the No Surprises Act, which took effect in 2022 and bans surprise billing, or the rising availability of GLP-1 drugs.
The people who will be most affected by the new increases are those who do not qualify for a subsidy.
“They may or may not be able to afford to continue to keep their coverage into next year,” Cox said, adding that “a lot of them have already moved into bronze plans, which are the cheapest plans.”
A CMS fact sheet about open enrollment that was distributed Friday says “Americans using HealthCare.gov will have robust access to low-cost plans.”
The price of ACA insurance has skyrocketed for many people during Trump’s second term after Republicans opposed extending COVID-era subsidies that had helped offset the costs of health insurance for most enrollees during Democratic President Joe Biden’s administration.
That resulted in 1.2 million fewer people signing up for coverage in the exchanges.
Nearly 20 million people in US are actively enrolled in ACA plans
As of February, roughly 19.2 million people in the United States were actively enrolled in ACA marketplace health plans, according to the Department of Health and Human Services website. The number of enrollees grew during the COVID-19 pandemic when enhanced subsidies became available through the American Rescue Plan Act and Inflation Reduction Act, both signed into law by Biden.
New regulations starting in 2027 will also limit tax credits for certain lawfully present immigrants, which could result in an additional 1 million uninsured individuals over time.
Meanwhile, the Trump administration has been removing ACA enrollees from the program as part of the ongoing campaign against what it characterizes as waste, fraud and abuse.
In September, Vice President JD Vance and other officials in the Republican administration announced plans to remove 760,000 ACA enrollees from public healthcare exchanges, alleging the individuals were fraudulently enrolled in the program or simply did not exist.
Vance said the discovery and canceled subsidy payments for hundreds of thousands of people from the exchanges, part of an administration-wide crackdown on fraud, would result in $2.2 billion in cost savings.
It’s unclear how many more people will drop off of ACA coverage in 2027, Cox said. But with higher premiums, immigration eligibility changes and the anti-fraud efforts, “I think there’s going to be fewer people enrolled in this market, but it’s going to be harder to understand why.”

title: 48th Annual Halloween Art & Craft Show brings local artisans to Augusta
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
AUGUSTA, Maine (WABI) - The Augusta Armory was packed with local talent this Halloween weekend, where dozens of artisans gathered together to not only to sell their goods, but to keep a tradition alive.
Over 30 crafters took to Augusta Armory this weekend for the 48th Annual Halloween Art & Craft Show. Show Chairman Steven Taylor says he’s been carrying on the tradition for decades.
“My mom started this when I was 11 years old, and I have been part of the business since the beginning,” Taylor said. “When she was going to retire, I decided, you know, I really enjoy this. I enjoy the crafters, I enjoy the customers. So I decided that it’s something I want to keep going.”
Taylor added that the event offers variety for every visitor: “You can find sewing, there’s Haida boxes, let me see, body oil, photography — there is a little bit of everything for everybody.”
Crafters showcased one-of-a-kind goods, including personalized keepsakes and items made from upcycled clothing.
“I make all kinds of different types of bags,” said Bettilou Fielding of Betti’s Bags. “All of the jean bags came from jeans, and every pair of jeans is a little bit different. There are no two bags that are exactly alike.”
Janet Drienski, owner of The Salty Cowgirl, focuses on sentimental, custom pieces made with photos sent to her phone from customers.
“I can do custom Christmas ornaments, keychains, jewelry, charm bracelets, all kinds of really cool things,” Drienski said. “I hear stories all the time of someone who’s passed that they want to remember on their Christmas tree or have a special pendant that they can wear. Maybe a dog or a cat that’s passed or something special, grandchild, all of those things. It’s nice to hear the stories from the customers, too.”
For those who participate year after year, the show provides a venue to connect directly with the community.
“People like to see new and innovative ideas — anything from the gift card bags, the wine bags,” Fielding said. “I think the more it’s promoted, the more people would like to be part of supporting the crafters and the imagination that comes out of all of these products.”
“We enjoy each other. It’s a good crowd,” Taylor said. “We tend to be more like a family than competitors.”

title: 1 dead, at least 8 injured in shooting after largest HBCU football game, police say
text:
BIRMINGHAM, Ala. (WBRC/Gray News) – One person is dead and at least eight others are injured after two shootings Saturday night near the Magic City Classic in Birmingham, Alabama, authorities said.
The Magic City Classic is the largest historically Black college and university football game in the United States.
Birmingham Mayor Randall Woodfin confirmed Sunday that police were investigating two separate incidents that happened in the west city of the city.
Woodfin said the first shooting injured six people and happened outside of the Legion Field perimeter and outside of the Magic City Classic tailgate area. The mayor said the second shooting happened less than eight minutes later across the street from Legion Field in the Graymont Avenue area and had three victims. Police and fire and rescue responded to the scene around 7:50 p.m. Saturday night.
Investigators said multiple firearms were recovered at the scene.
Woodfin said a 17-year-old, who had a gun, is in custody in connection with the investigation; however, the teen is not the only suspect and the investigation remains ongoing.
Officials said seven people were taken to the hospital and the victims range in age from 19 to 30. Two are in critical condition and five are in stable condition, officials said.
More than 50 people were treated for minor injuries from the chaos of the shootings.
Birmingham Police Chief Michael Pickett described the shooting as a “senseless act of violence” and praised responding personnel.
“Everyone knows this is the largest event we have here in the city and it’s extremely taxing on our personnel. Other leaders in law enforcement recognize that and they quickly offered up support and we are grateful for that quick response,” Pickett said. “I’ll end with this.. our Birmingham police officer are true heroes. They are true heroes. Seeing the courage and resilience they displayed tonight, running alongside them in the direction of those gunshots, triaging people as we pass by them going in the direction of the shots to make sure they weren’t injured, or if they were injured rendering aid as we continue toward the gunfire.. that shows true courage, that shows the true dedication they have to actually saving lives. And I’m thankful that all of our police officers as well of others who were assistance are able to go home to their families tonight.”

title: Week Ahead in Washington: November 1
text:
WASHINGTON (Gray DC) - Election Day is Tuesday, Nov. 3, as Americans cast votes in local, state and federal races.
All 435 U.S. House seats and 35 Senate seats are up for election. Governor’s races are also on the ballot in 36 states.
The midterm elections will determine control of Congress. Republicans are looking to remain the majority party for the final two years of President Donald Trump’s second term, while Democrats are looking to flip both chambers to blue.
A number of key contests will be decided in critical states. Texas, Michigan and Alaska have some of the most closely watched races, with the latest polls showing the Senate races in those states are still considered “toss ups” ahead of Election Day.
Meanwhile, the Supreme Court is set to begin its November oral arguments session this week. The session includes seven hours of arguments over five days, Starting Nov. 2 and ending Nov. 10.
The highlight of the session is “St. Mary Catholic Parish v. Roy.” The case considers whether a Catholic preschool’s exclusion from Colorado’s universal preschool program counts as a form of religious discrimination.
Arguments in the case are set for Tuesday, Nov. 3.

title: Trump signals he'll give closing election pitch at the Reflecting Pool, a revamp plagued by problems
text:
Trump signals he'll give closing election pitch at the Reflecting Pool, a revamp plagued by problems
President Donald Trump signaled Sunday that he'll make his closing pitch of the midterm elections at the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool, pushing his slow, expensive and problem-plagued efforts to repair it back into the spotlight as Election Day looms.
In comments to reporters as he deplaned from Air Force One for a rally in Iowa, Trump said his speaking at the site would “show how beautiful it is.”
Related video above: Trump plays defense in red states, as Democratic rift widens in Senate battleground ahead of Election Day
“We might hold it tomorrow or something,” Trump added, without giving specifics. But in a post on his social media site before landing, Trump said that his Sunday evening rally in Kansas — which follows his stop in Iowa — “Will be my last stop.”
That would further suggest that, rather than using Monday to travel to key states and try to energize his “Make America Great Again” supporters as his Republican Party tries to maintain control of Congress, Trump would opt for an event at a Washington renovation project that has been embarrassing and contentious.
The unusual move would be a departure from Trump's month-long race to stage more than 25 rallies in largely conservative areas, hoping the GOP can overcome his own low approval ratings and polls predicting that the Iran war, high energy prices and cost of living increases could spell a strong election night for Democrats.
Trump spent a lot of time at those rallies talking about his second-term focus on molding the White House and the surrounding nation's capital in his own image, cramming the Oval Office with gold flourishes, demolishing the East Wing to construct a sprawling ballroom, converting the Rose Garden into a patio space reminiscent of his Mar-a-Lago estate and erecting a sprawling South Lawn helipad.
He also closed the Kennedy Center after failed attempts to add his name to the building, has planned a towering arch just outside the city and is pushing to revamp a century-old public golf course.
Trump has bristled at criticisms from former President Barack Obama and other Democrats that he's spent too much time focused on construction projects — insisting that renovations relax him and that he does them quickly and without requiring too much planning time.
Trump said the Reflecting Pool fix would be fast and inexpensive
His Reflecting Pool saga began in April when Trump said he wanted to change its color and would use contractors he knew to fix the monument in mere days and for about $1.5 million before Independence Day.
The repairs wrapped up nearly three months behind schedule and the budget ballooned to more than 10 times Trump's early estimate — and that's assuming no more additional work will need to be done in the future.
Trump had initially declared the work was complete in June. But after unveiling the overhaul, the pool was soon choked with algae blooms, and its “American-flag blue” liner began peeling off in sections. The pool was quickly drained anew for repairs in mid-July.
Trump has repeatedly blamed vandals, but the office of U.S. Attorney for the District of Columbia — former Fox News host and longtime Trump ally Jeanine Pirro — said the problems were caused by shoddy workmanship.
In his comments Sunday, Trump continued to insist that the Reflecting Pool “was vandalized badly.” He said that security cameras have since been added to stop that.
Still, a particularly ignominious moment came when the Justice Department charged former Olympian David Hearn with intentionally damaging the Reflecting Pool — then abruptly dropped the case this summer — determining he was not responsible.
A judge later permanently dismissed it.
That prompted Trump to fume that Pirro “choked,” and that he was "disappointed with Jeanine Pirro, really disappointed. She folded like an umbrella” — though he stopped short of firing her.

title: Maine High Court owes us a ruling: Who owns the rocks?
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
In 2019, the Maine High Court ruled that the seaweed hanging from the rocks on the shore belonged to the owner of the rocks. That court decision flew in the face of the long-established public right to harvest the marine resources from same place. The public’s right to “fish, fowl, and navigate” was established in 1647 and was included in Maine law in 1820.
I am one of the plaintiffs named in the follow-on case from June 2024 that argued that
the marine organisms found in the intertidal zone have always (and still) belong to the 
public because the intertidal zone is held in trust for the residents of Maine. 
It boils down to one question: Did the state of Maine ever legally transfer ownership of its intertidal zone to all the shore landowners?
There will be complex and likely heated discussions that will follow an eventual court decision. At the very least, its decision will trigger some deep title searching. Coastal tax assessors will be meeting. The current status of the Colonial Ordinance from 1647 will be considered. There will be surveyors buying boots and lawyers getting new cars.
In recent years, there have been numerous significant business investment decisions delayed or reversed for lack of clarity on this ownership question.
The Maine High Court needs to rule on this question. It’s been over two years.
George Seaver
Waldoboro

title: Police: Investigation remains active after 6 shot near University of Delaware campus on Halloween
Trump administration’s social media posts ahead of elections criticized for being inflammatory
text:
(AP) - The Trump administration’s online accounts are circulating images of a pumpkin carved with a sombrero design and a fake Halloween-themed background around a Black man apparently accused of food assistance fraud, in social media posts slammed by critics as inflammatory rhetoric.
Only days before the midterm elections, the posts coincide with the government’s sweeping campaign to show its aggressive immigration enforcement, and highlight efforts to crack down on fraud to save taxpayers money when rising healthcare costs and other economic stressors have made affordability a top voter concern.
Agriculture Secretary Brooke Rollins posted Saturday on the social platform X a photo of the Black man standing in front of stacks of what appear to be U.S. currency with the headline, SNAP FRAUDSTER, an apparent reference to the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program, formerly known as food stamps.
He is holding aloft what appears to be a bill set aflame.
“Some costumes come with a price tag. This one comes with a prison sentence,” it says to the backdrop of fake Spirit Halloween costume packaging.
Another photo posted by the White House on X on Thursday showed a pumpkin with the shape of a sombrero carved across it and the words “Spooky szn is here.”
The post by Rollins, who was nominated by Trump to serve as the U.S. Secretary of Agriculture in November 2024, appears to be taken from an Instagram post from September 2025 by an account under the name Shawty Dred.
Earlier this month, Mercedes Reshard New, identified by the Justice Department as a social media personality also known as “Shawty Dred,” was arrested on federal charges for fraudulently obtaining more than $4 million in Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program benefits in Georgia.
It’s not the first time the White House has been accused of posting inflammatory images on official government social media accounts.
Just over a year ago during the government shutdown, the White House revived a deepfake video posted by Trump of House Democratic leader Hakeem Jeffries in a fake mustache and sombrero to accuse the Democrats of acting on behalf of illegal immigrants instead of U.S. citizens. Jeffries described the meme as bigoted. They played it on repeat in the White House briefing room, though Vice President JD Vance promised that the “sombrero memes will stop” when Democrats agreed to end the shutdown.
The NAACP did not respond to an email seeking comment, nor did the White House or Rollins.
The Trump administration in recent weeks has ratcheted up its anti-immigrant rhetoric and accusations of fraud, including against U.S. Rep. Ilhan Omar whose Washington, D.C., home was searched by federal agents earlier this month. Federal authorities are investigating potential fraud in her family’s immigration paperwork. Omar, who was born in Somalia, is a naturalized U.S. citizen.
It also has taken a series of punitive steps linked to allegations of fraud in mostly Democratic-led states, including California and Minnesota whose governors accused the federal government of targeting their states for political reasons.
Federal prosecutors said in a news release Oct. 21 that the influencer, New, controlled more than 350 fraudulent SNAP accounts under stolen identities between January 2020 and July 2026. He allegedly applied for his company, Shawty Dred LLC, to become an authorized SNAP retailer and used EBT debit cards to extract about $4 million from the accounts.
New’s Instagram account, which has more than two million followers, has flaunted his extravagant lifestyle, federal prosecutors said. Posts depict him flying on private jets, posing with Rolls-Royce vehicles in front of his “super mansion,” and handling massive stacks of cash.
“Instead of this money feeding families in need, New, the social media personality known as ‘Shawty Dred,’ allegedly used the cash to bankroll a life of luxury,” Special Agent in Charge of FBI Atlanta Marlo Graham said in the release.
New was indicted by a federal grand jury Oct. 7 on dozens of counts of mail fraud and aggravated identity theft, and one count each of SNAP fraud and illegal transactions with access devices. He was arrested Oct. 13 and remains in federal custody.
According to Fulton County jail records, New has been arrested multiple times on suspicion of crimes including identity theft, insurance fraud, financial transaction card fraud, forgery and simple assault.
A federal defender listed in court records as representing New, Joseph Austin, did not return a phone message.

title: Obituary: Georgia Harriet Millett
text:
ELIOT – Georgia Harriet Millett, of Eliot, formerly of South Portland and Scarborough, passed peacefully on a beautiful fall morning at the home of her daughter Rhonda and husband James Newcomer, of Eliot. Georgia was born on Aug. 21, 1926, in Paris, Maine, to Herbert Scribner and Mary Cummings Scribner.
She attended schools in Paris and South Paris but attained her high school diploma from Portland Regional High School in 1977 at the age of 50.
Georgia was always a hard worker and held many diﬀerent positions throughout her long life. As a little girl she sold cottage cheese that her mother made. She performed ironing and cleaning at the Sigma Nu house at Bowden College along with various retail jobs. After moving to Portland in the early ’60s, she worked at Fairchild Semiconductor and then moved to Data General where she retired in 1990.
She enjoyed many hobbies, including sewing and quilting, Zentangle, paint by number and gardening. She loved bird watching and always had a dog or two.
Most of all she loved family and friends. She was a favorite “aunt” to many. Georgia was a long time member of Thornton Heights Methodist Church. “Be kind” was her motto and her faith was a source of strength.
She is survived by her daughter, son Kenneth Millett of Cape Coral Fla.; granddaughter Sharon Lunt of Greene, and grandson Kenneth Millett Jr. of Greene; five great grandchildren; and 11 great-great grandchildren.
She was predeceased by the love of her life, husband Linton of 76 years; grandson, Craig Millett; sister, Bertha Reny and brother, Leslie Scribner.
The family would like to thank the nurses and aides from Beacon Hospice for their care and kindness during Georgia’s final days. And special thanks to her best friend, Hazel Hollenbeck, for always being there when she needed anything.
Relatives and friends are invited to a time of visitation on Thursday, Nov. 5, from 12 p.m. to 1 p.m. at Thornton Heights United Methodist Church, 100 Westbrook St., South Portland, ME 04106. A memorial service will follow at 1 p.m.

title: Pierce Gorneault Wins State Title as County Cross Country Teams Shine
text:
Caribou’s Gorneault Wins State Cross Country Class B Title as County Runners Shine in Augusta
Aroostook County had plenty to celebrate at Saturday's Maine State Cross Country Championships in Augusta.
Caribou's Pierce Gorneault captured the Class B boys individual state championship, Emma Graves finished second in the Class B girls race, and the Houlton/GHCA boys came within 19 points of defending their Class C state title.
But the results went beyond individual performances.
Caribou earned both the boys and girls Class B Sportsmanship Awards, recognizing the Vikings for the way they represented their school and community.
Presque Isle also had strong performances in Class B, while individual runners from Houlton, Washburn and the Maine School of Science and Mathematics represented the County in Class C girls.
Here's how the local teams and runners finished at the state championships.
Class B Girls: Graves Takes Second as Caribou and Presque Isle Finish in the Top Six
Caribou sophomore Emma Graves was among the fastest runners in Maine on Saturday, finishing second in the Class B girls championship.
Graves covered the 5,000-meter course in 19 minutes, 28.70 seconds, finishing behind Lincoln Academy senior Karen Higgins, who won the state championship in 18:58.41.
Graves was joined in the top ten by Caribou freshman Jenna Strid, who finished ninth in 20:06.27.
That gave the Vikings two runners among the top ten finishers in the state.
Presque Isle also had a strong showing near the front of the field.
Junior Aleah Rideout finished 11th in 20:21.32, while freshman Lillian Johnson placed 13th in 20:31.24.
Caribou finished fifth in the team standings with 135 points, while Presque Isle was right behind in sixth with 144.
Freeport won the Class B girls team championship with 67 points, followed by Mount Desert Island with 81 and Yarmouth with 87.

His time was also the fourth-fastest among all classifications at the state championships.
It was a tremendous performance for Gorneault, who had already established himself as one of Northern Maine's top runners throughout the fall season.

title: Presque Isle, Fort Kent and Fort Fairfield Punch Tickets to Regional Soccer Finals
text:
Presque Isle, Fort Kent and Fort Fairfield Advance to Northern Maine Soccer Championships
Aroostook County is going to be well represented when the Northern Maine regional soccer championships get underway this week.
Saturday brought three more County teams into the championship picture, with Presque Isle's girls rolling to a shutout victory, Fort Kent's boys surviving a dramatic penalty-kick finish, and Fort Fairfield's girls winning a one-goal battle against Central Aroostook.
Not every County team was able to keep its season going, though. Presque Isle's boys fell to top-seeded John Bapst, while Madawaska's girls saw their tournament run end against Penobscot Valley.
With the semifinal round now complete, here's how Saturday's games played out and what's coming up on Championship Wednesday.
Girls Soccer
Class B North: Four Different Scorers Send Presque Isle to Regional Final
(3) Presque Isle 4, (7) Cony 0
Presque Isle's girls are heading to the Class B North championship after an impressive 4-0 victory over Cony on Saturday.
The third-seeded Lady Wildcats got goals from four different players, with Hailey Plant, Carrlyn Buck, Bridgid Schupbach and Willow Bugbee each finding the back of the net.
Cony came into the game after knocking off second-seeded Gardiner in the quarterfinals, but Presque Isle made sure the Rams wouldn't pull off another upset.
The shutout sends the Lady Wildcats into Championship Wednesday, where they'll face top-seeded John Bapst.
The Crusaders earned their spot with a 3-2 semifinal victory over Hermon, overcoming a halftime deficit to advance.
It's a matchup between the top seed and a Presque Isle team that's coming off back-to-back playoff victories, including Saturday's four-goal performance.
One more win would give the Wildcats the Class B North championship and send them to the state final.
Class D North: Fort Fairfield Edges Central Aroostook
(2) Fort Fairfield 1, (3) Central Aroostook 0
Fort Fairfield's girls are headed back to the Class D North championship after a hard-fought 1-0 semifinal victory over Central Aroostook.
It was another close game between two familiar County opponents, with the second-seeded Tigers finding the goal they needed and keeping the Lady Panthers off the scoreboard.
The shutout sends Fort Fairfield into Wednesday's regional championship, where the Tigers will face top-seeded Penobscot Valley.
Class D North: Penobscot Valley Ends Madawaska's Run
(1) Penobscot Valley 1, (5) Madawaska 0
Madawaska's tournament run came to an end Saturday with a narrow 1-0 loss against top-seeded Penobscot Valley.
The fifth-seeded Owls had earned their semifinal berth with an overtime victory over Ashland earlier in the week.
They gave the top seed a close game, but Penobscot Valley came away with the one-goal victory.
That sets up a Class D North championship between Fort Fairfield and Penobscot Valley on Wednesday at 4:15 p.m. in Presque Isle.
Both teams advanced through the semifinals with 1-0 shutouts, setting the stage for an interesting championship matchup.
Boys Soccer
Class B North: John Bapst Ends Presque Isle's Season
(1) John Bapst 5, (4) Presque Isle 0
Presque Isle's boys saw their postseason run come to an end Saturday against top-seeded John Bapst.
The Crusaders defeated the fourth-seeded Wildcats 5-0 to advance to the Class B North championship.
Presque Isle had reached the semifinals with a 4-1 quarterfinal victory over Erskine Academy, but couldn't find the same offensive success against the top seed.
While the boys' season comes to an end, Presque Isle will still have its girls team competing for a regional championship Wednesday.
Class C North: Fort Kent Survives Penalty Kicks at George Stevens Academy
(3) Fort Kent advances over (2) George Stevens Academy, 4-2 on penalty kicks following a 1-1 draw
Fort Kent's boys are headed to the Class C North championship, but they certainly had to earn it.
The third-seeded Warriors traveled to Blue Hill on Saturday to face second-seeded George Stevens Academy, and the semifinal turned into one of the closest games of the day.
James Wilson scored Fort Kent's regulation goal, with Dominic Cyr providing the assist.
The teams remained tied at one through regulation and overtime, sending the game to penalty kicks.
That's where Wyatt Daigle delivered the deciding kick for Fort Kent.
The Warriors won the shootout 4-2, securing their place in the regional championship.
And there's a pretty interesting storyline waiting for them.
Both the Fort Kent boys and girls will face Orono in their respective Class C North championship games.
The Lady Warriors advanced Friday with a 5-0 victory over Houlton, while the boys needed Saturday's penalty-kick finish to get past George Stevens Academy.
Now both Fort Kent teams are one win away from Northern Maine titles, and both will have to get past the Red Riots to bring those championships home.

title: In Maine’s 2nd District, Paul LePage’s name recognition is a blessing and a curse
text:
The towns were different, but the conversations in each place started to feel similar.
Since late August, the Portland Press Herald visited eight communities in Maine’s geographically vast 2nd Congressional District that stretches from Lewiston to the Canadian border to ask voters what they think about the race. More than 20 agreed to be interviewed.
But instead of offering strong takes on the contest, voters often began with a simple question.
Who’s running?
It is former Gov. Paul LePage — the 78-year-old Republican who grew up in Lewiston, previously served as Waterville mayor and who has moved between Florida and Maine since 2019 — against State Auditor Matt Dunlap, the 61-year-old Old Town Democrat who grew up in Bar Harbor and previously served as a state representative, secretary of state and Sportsman’s Alliance of Maine leader.
U.S. Rep. Jared Golden, the Democratic incumbent, decided last year to not seek reelection after first winning the seat in 2018.
With the basics out of the way, a reporter asked again, who would you prefer? The voters more often than not focused on LePage — though not always positively.
“Paul LePage? That’s just a no,” G. Carter, of Denmark, said one weekday morning in August while stopping at a convenience store in his Oxford County town.
“It would definitely be LePage,” another Denmark man said later that morning while quickly walking past, expressing familiarity with the Republican who led Maine from 2011 to 2019.
The conversations revealed the double-edged sword that is LePage’s strong name recognition. Endorsed by President Donald Trump, he has loyal supporters who appreciate his brash style and conservative views, and he has critics who have expressed deep reservations about those very same traits and pointed to his controversial rhetoric as governor that created both state and national headlines.
Dunlap, whose endorsers include U.S. Sen. Angus King and Gov. Janet Mills, is noticeably different with his soft-spoken demeanor and progressive platform. He is taking on the tall order of winning a politically peculiar district that has thrice backed Trump while electing Golden, a 44-year-old Marine veteran known for his moderate, party-bucking stances, to four terms.
The polarizing opinions from voters hint at why election forecasters had moved the 2nd District race in recent weeks from a “likely” LePage victory to the “lean Republican” category. Dunlap even narrowly led LePage in a University of New Hampshire poll in September that notably found just 3% of voters did not know enough about LePage to rate him. Some 20% said the same about Dunlap. (LePage won Tuesday’s mock Maine student election by receiving 52% of votes to 43.2% for Dunlap.)
The national environment — Trump faces low approval ratings and an unpopular war in Iran that has driven up fuel prices — has Democrats looking likely to retake the House in the midterms, even if LePage beats Dunlap. But setting aside the broader implications, talking with 2nd District voters ahead of Election Day is a reminder of what counts the most in rural Maine.
“People care more about who you are and (if) you know them than they care about whether you’re a Democrat or Republican,” said Tom Saviello, a Franklin County commissioner who previously served in both chambers of the Legislature as a Democrat and Republican and is now an independent, on a recent day while in his hometown of Wilton.
That sentiment can both help and hurt each candidate.
Richard Sherburne, an Augusta retiree, said he knows and likes LePage. He views the former governor as “more serious now” in terms of being prepared to serve in higher office. Maine taxpayers are “losing out” and need a candidate like LePage to help them in Congress, he added.
“He’s direct. I don’t know if he chooses his words right,” Sherburne, 68, said Wednesday while outside Augusta City Hall. “But it’s about the results.”
LePage has been more poised and relatively quieter during this 2nd District campaign, holding few events open to the press, and rarely publicly sparring with opponents. One notable exception came earlier in October, when LePage grew agitated during the race’s final televised debate after Dunlap brought up LePage’s years in Florida.
Dunlap’s supporters brought up his character and contrasted it with LePage’s style.
“I think that (Dunlap) is an honest, good person,” said Rolanda Nadeau, 69, who lives in Augusta and is retired from state government, where she had crossed paths with Dunlap when he was secretary of state.
In Androscoggin County, Dan Mastrogiorgio, of Auburn, said he’s quite familiar with LePage but does not feel the Republican has a plan to help lower heating oil costs in Maine. That’s a big issue for Mastrogiorgio, who said his annual heating oil bill may reach $1,700. He’s voting for Dunlap.
“We need some control on the federal government,” Mastrogiorgio, 41, said.
In 2022, when LePage mounted a gubernatorial comeback bid, Mills trounced him by double digits. LePage carried the 2nd District that year by about two percentage points.
Golden’s repeated victories since 2018, and the fact that his predecessor, former Rep. Bruce Poliquin (2014-2018), was the only Republican since Olympia Snowe (1978-1994) to hold the seat in recent decades, are signs of why the district “is more purple than red,” Saviello, 76, said.
The area also went to former President Barack Obama in 2008 and 2012 before backing Trump.
Wilton, a former mill town among the western Maine mountains and lakes with around 3,900 residents and a quaint Main Street, is one of several swingier communities dotted throughout the district.
Golden did well there over the years, though margins were close, such as when he beat former state Rep. Austin Theriault, a Fort Kent Republican, by 100 votes in Wilton in 2024.
That same year, Trump won Wilton over former Vice President Kamala Harris by a little more than 200 votes. Districtwide, Golden narrowly beat Theriault, a former NASCAR driver, by about 2,700 votes.
Saviello, the former state lawmaker from Wilton, said Golden did well at three things that he thinks good politicians possess.
“You have to not take (things) personally. You have to learn to count (when voting) and you have to know today’s friend is tomorrow’s enemy is tomorrow’s friend,” Saviello said.
LePage has not exactly followed norms when it comes to civil discourse over the years. When he and Saviello were both Republicans in 2018, he called Saviello “the most repugnant human” he had ever seen during a timber-related dispute.
LePage’s past behavior may cause him trouble with independent-minded voters, Saviello said. That proved prophetic when a Wilton man walking downtown said he is a registered Republican and did not want his name in the newspaper before proceeding to bash LePage’s temperament.
Other voters, such as David Heidrich of Augusta, exhibited Maine’s tough-to-characterize political nature by saying they are supporting LePage along with independent gubernatorial candidate Rick Bennett, a former state senator and Maine Republican Party chair who left the GOP last year.
The city that may ultimately render the verdict on LePage’s political future is Lewiston, his hometown. It is arguably the swingiest part of the district, and it is the largest by population. Lewiston supported him in his 2010 and 2014 gubernatorial races but then swung to Mills in 2022.
In downtown Lewiston on an August morning, Jonathan Diaz said he does not identity with either major party and that he had previously supported some of Trump’s policies, such as on child tax credits. But Diaz, 41, said he grew disillusioned with both LePage and Trump over the years.
“The things that Paul said he was going to do during his first run-through (as governor), I didn’t see them getting done,” Diaz said. “In fact, I only saw self-serving policies and things being proposed that would benefit rich people.”
Diaz said he did not know anything about Dunlap but was interested in learning more about him.
Lauren LePage, the former governor’s daughter who also serves as a spokesperson for his campaign, said in a statement that Dunlap is a “career politician” while the Republican nominee is someone who “pushed back against the political establishment, fought fraud and corruption and lowered taxes for working families and seniors.”
“It doesn’t matter who voters are choosing in other races and who they have voted for before,” Lauren LePage said. “What matters is who they choose on Tuesday.”
Dunlap knows LePage is a known figure and said in a statement that he has sought to put himself in front of voters by holding dozens of town halls throughout the district.
“We’re working hard to reach out to voters, and we’re running a stronger campaign because of it,” Dunlap said. “Everywhere I go I hear about high home heating oil prices and grocery costs that are breaking budgets. If elected, I’ll work hard to bring prices back to normal.”
For Dunlap, the real test may come in towns like Poland in Androscoggin County. Golden lost the town of about 6,000 residents that is home to Poland Spring and the bottled water giant’s resort to Theriault in 2024 by nearly 80 votes. Trump won the town by more than 400 votes.
State Rep. David Boyer, a libertarian-minded Republican from Poland, said Dunlap may struggle to win over the same voters who appreciate how Golden broke party ranks.
Still, Boyer said, “Mainers are ticket splitters” who will not always break the way political observers think. He echoed Saviello’s emphasis on personal ties.
“Some of these ballots, there’s no rhyme or reason,” Boyer said. “Maine’s one big small town.”

title: Northern Light Cancer Care highlights advanced therapies at Dana-Farber symposium
text:
On Oct. 15-16, Northern Light Cancer Care was represented at the 2026 Dana-Farber Collaborative Symposium and Cellular Therapies Symposium, held virtually and in person at Dana-Farber Cancer Institute in Boston. Organized by the Dana-Farber Collaborative Network, the symposium brought together oncology professionals to explore advances in cancer care, clinical research, and cellular therapies.
The symposium featured updates from Dana-Farber leadership, presentations by oncology experts, and opportunities for collaboration among participating institutions.
Sarah Sinclair, DO, medical director, Cancer Care and Clinical Research at Northern Light Eastern Maine Medical Center, presented alongside Megan Derba, Pharm.D. BCOP, MBA, director of Pharmacy for Northern Light Cancer Care. Their presentation highlighted efforts to expand access to advanced cancer therapies in rural Maine, including the implementation of bispecific antibody treatments at Lafayette Family Cancer Institute.
The presentation emphasized the multidisciplinary coordination required to safely deliver these innovative therapies, including collaboration among outpatient oncology, inpatient services, emergency medicine, intensive care and pharmacy. It also highlighted efforts to reduce geographic barriers to treatment through partnerships with regional oncology clinics, allowing patients to receive appropriate aspects of their care closer to home.
Looking ahead, the presentation introduced the Jim and Cathy Gero Center for Genomics and Advanced Therapies, established through a transformational $10 million gift from Jim Gero in memory of his late wife, Cathy. The Center aims to expand access to genomic medicine, precision oncology, clinical research, and advanced therapies, bringing innovative treatment options closer to patients throughout Maine.
Participation in the symposium provided an opportunity to share Northern Light Health’s progress in advanced cancer care while exchanging experiences and approaches with colleagues across the Dana-Farber Collaborative Network.
Learn more about Jim Gero’s generous donation and how it will help advance cancer care for Mainers for generations to come at https://northernlighthealth.org/News/2026/Northern-Light-Cancer-Care-announces-$10-million-g.

title: A cost-savings suggestion for Martin’s Point
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
So Martin’s Point is revamping its Medicare Advantage programs because of losing money. Well, I have a suggestion. It needs to stop mailing the multiple, pages after pages of information about what I have paid for, what meds I have ordered and what services I have had. I believe that most of us are quite aware of what we have purchased, especially the cost of them all.
Why are they not sending these in an email (I would think most members have email)? The cost of mailing — not to mention the paper alone — would be quite a savings if they are sending these to their tens of thousands members.
Louise Beaulieu
Ocean Park

title: USC stuns No. 2 Ohio State
text:
USC stuns No. 2 Ohio State with big plays from Jayden Maiava, freshman Trent Mosley
Jayden Maiava passed for 222 yards and a touchdown; King Miller and Waymond Jordan rushed for scores, and Southern California stunned No. 2 Ohio State 30-18 on Saturday night for the biggest win of head coach Lincoln Riley’s tenure.
Video above: Lawmaker pushes 21 age limit for paid fantasy sports
Freshman sensation Trent Mosley made a 69-yard TD catch on the second play from scrimmage and finished with five receptions for 101 yards for the Trojans (7-2, 4-2 Big Ten), who scored more points than Ohio State’s vaunted defense had allowed since 2024.
The USC defense didn’t allow a touchdown in the first 57 minutes by an Ohio State offense led by freshman quarterback Luke Fahey, who passed for 260 yards in his first career start in place of injured Julian Sayin for the Buckeyes (6-2, 4-1).
Jeremiah Smith finally scored on a 1-yard catch with 2:12 remaining, but the Buckeyes’ 2-point conversion attempt failed, and USC recovered the onside kick before making its third field goal with 1:46 left.
With a light, steady rain falling throughout Halloween night, USC beat a top-12 team for the first time in Riley’s half-decade in charge.
USC students and fans stormed the field after the Trojans beat a top-five opponent at the Coliseum for the first time since 2015.
Bo Jackson rushed for 121 yards and Smith had 10 receptions for 83 yards for the Buckeyes, who couldn't make it close despite racking up 464 total yards.
Ohio State hadn’t lost two games this early in a season since 2011, the year before Urban Meyer arrived in Columbus. The Buckeyes fell to 58-2 against unranked teams under coach Ryan Day, with this defeat joining their infamous home loss to Michigan in 2024.
Fahey got the start after Sayin injured his arm two weeks ago at Indiana. The freshman from nearby Orange County made several big throws, but went 21 for 38.
One week after the Trojans produced the fewest points ever from a Riley-led offense in an embarrassing 24-7 loss at Wisconsin, they shockingly surged to a 20-9 halftime lead while scoring the second-most points allowed by the Buckeyes' sturdy defense this season in an entire game.
On USC's second snap, Mosley caught a pass behind the line of scrimmage and sprinted through Ohio State's secondary for the sixth touchdown of his stellar freshman season. The Buckeyes hadn't allowed a play longer than 36 yards all season.
Later in the first, Mosley broke a 44-yard punt return and made an 18-yard reception to set up Jordan's 9-yard TD run.
Ohio State produced 192 yards, but only three field goals from its first five drives — even when the Buckeyes reached the USC 1 shortly before halftime.
Isaiah West then fumbled in USC territory in the second half, and the Trojans went up 27-9 when Miller punched it in following a spectacular 70-yard reception by freshman tight end Mark Bowman, who hurdled a defender and broke multiple tackles.

title: Police: 15-year-old charged after typing 'how to kill the president' on school account
text:
Police: 15-year-old charged after typing 'how to kill the president' on school-issued account
Florida authorities arrested a 15-year-old girl who they said typed "how to kill the president," followed by "just kidding," on a school issued account.
According to an affidavit acquired by Hearst sister station WESH, a school resource officer at Mainland High School in Daytona Beach, Florida, received a call at 11 a.m. on Oct. 30 after the principal received a Gaggle alert.
Gaggle, which describes itself as AI-powered student safety software, alerted multiple faculty, staff members, and law enforcement agencies to what the student had typed, according to the affidavit.
"It has been publicly known (that) President Donald Trump is coming to Daytona Beach. Her comments were made the same day the President is due to arrive. (Her) comments 'I'm just kidding,' shows that she knew any reasonable person would view her original comments as a threat," the affidavit stated prior to Trump's rally.
As the officer tried to detain the 15-year-old, she allegedly resisted by first attempting to exit their office, then by kicking and swinging her arms in an attempt to avoid being handcuffed, police said.
The officer reported they bear-hugged the teen, "redirected" her to the floor, and she continued to avoid being detained by lying on her arms.
"During the tussle with (the girl), my department issued taser broke off the holder depriving me the use of my equipment. (A school guardian) assisted, and (the teen) was eventually placed in handcuffs and physically detained," the affidavit continued.
The girl was arrested and taken to the Family Resource Center, police said. WESH did not identify the teen due to her age.
She faces charges of a written/electronic threat to kill, depriving police of means to protect or communicate, and resisting without violence, according to the affidavit.
News of the girl's arrest followed that of a 21-year-old woman elsewhere in the Daytona Beach area, who was charged for making similar threats towards President Trump.

title: Obituary: Peter John Curran
text:
RAYMOND – Peter John Curran, 83, of Raymond, passed away at his home on Oct. 24, 2026.
Peter was born on Feb. 25, 1943, in Portland to Edward and Phyllis Curran. He attended South Portland schools, graduated from University of Southern Maine and dedicated much of his career to education. He taught history at Westbrook High School for many years, where he also served as a soccer coach, tennis coach, and athletic director. In the final year of his educational career, he served as principal before retiring in 1999.
Throughout his life, Peter was committed to serving his community. He was active in the Kiwanis Club, local Boy Scouts, and Key Club. He was also a Fulbright Scholar and spent a year studying in Israel. His dedication to helping others led him to volunteer in the emergency room at Maine Medical Center, where he later worked for 10 years.
Peter also served in the Peace Corps for a year in Morocco and was a member of the Maine House of Representatives. His life reflected a strong commitment to education, public service, and community involvement.
After spending many Maine winters, Peter and his brothers moved to St. Cloud, Fla., where they lived for 17 years. Eventually, they returned to Maine and settled at the family camp at Little Sebago Lake, at Little Sebago Lodges, a place that brought them back to their roots.
Peter was predeceased by his parents, Edward and Phyllis Curran; and his brother, Edward Curran.
He is survived by his brother, David Curran; and many cousins.
Peter’s family would like to extend their heartfelt gratitude for the kindness and compassion expressed by the staff at Northern Lights Hospice.
In lieu of flowers, the family requests that donations be made in Peter’s memory to:
Westbrook Food Pantry or to:
the South Portland Food Pantry

title: Mexico comes alive during annual Day of the Dead celebrations
text:
MEXICO CITY (AP) — Bright orange marigolds, glowing candles and faces painted like the elegant skeletons known as catrinas fill the streets of Mexico every year during the country’s Day of the Dead celebrations.
Festivities begin in October and lead up to Nov. 1 and 2, when the souls of deceased loved ones are believed to temporarily return to earth to reunite with their families.
No one knows when the first observance took place, but it is rooted in agriculture-related beliefs from Mexico’s pre-Hispanic era. Catholic traditions were incorporated into the celebration after the Spanish conquest in 1521.
Today, celebrations are marked by massive parades running along Mexico City’s main avenue. Streets, businesses and markets are cloaked in orange Mexican marigold flowers, or cempasuchil, believed to light the path of the dead back to earth with their bright colors. Traditional pan de muerto, or bread of the dead, lines the display cases of bakeries.
Families decorate altars to their loved ones in their homes, placing treats, food and mezcal as offerings next to photos of their loved ones.
On the night of Nov. 1, families gather at cemeteries across the country to reconnect with their dead just as their ancestors have done for centuries.
But as the tradition and the Mexican capital have increasingly gained an international spotlight, and states like Oaxaca and Michoacan have seen an influx of tourists, some regions have experienced tensions around overtourism.
In Mexico City, many locals are skeptical of an annual parade featuring floats decorated with catrinas. The procession was created for the 2015 James Bond film “Spectre” and later incorporated into the city’s celebrations, though it was not previously part of the tradition.
In Janitzio, a small island on a lake in the central state of Michoacan, where celebrations were recognized by UNESCO as Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity in 2008, authorities closed the pantheon to tourists for the first time this year. The closure came after the island’s community council reported the collapse of damaged tombs, crosses and parts of the cemetery’s perimeter wall because of the flood of people.
Only local families and friends of those buried there would be allowed in.

title: Purrfect Pawty: Cat cafe celebrates one-year anniversary

text:
GARDINER, Maine (WABI) - One woman’s lifelong dream is marking a major milestone.
The Cat’s Familiar is celebrating its first year of operation — and the successful placement of 42 cats into forever homes.
Owner Bonnie Casperson said opening the space had been a lifelong dream, and her husband encouraged her to take the leap.
“I was tired of sitting behind a desk, and my husband said to me one day, ‘Why don’t you just try your cat cafe?’” Casperson said. “And I’m like, sure, if we can do it, let’s go for it.”
Patrons can spend time with 11 cats in the “cat haven,” check out the gift shop featuring local artists and grab a bite to eat in the cafe.
Nine of the 11 cats are available for adoption.
A new addition to the business is the pet pantry, a no-questions-asked food bank ensuring no neighbor has to worry about feeding their pets.
Looking ahead, Casperson hopes to expand the space while continuing to help feline friends find homes.
