title: 3 firefighters resign after drinking at a bar while on duty, police reports says
text:
NASHVILLE, Tenn. (WSMV/Gray News) - Three Nashville firefighters have resigned after they were seen ordering drinks at a Broadway bar while on duty, according to a police report.
Mayor Freddie O’Connell is calling for accountability after the incident happened around midnight on Monday night.
The police report said officers were called by the manager at Dierks Bentley Whiskey Row when a bartender reported she was concerned they were drinking alcohol on duty.
It identifies the three firefighters as Athams Davis, Griffin Hunter and Daniel Wrenn. They were wearing Nashville Fire Department T-shirts and carrying bright yellow radios while at the bar, police said.
Police report outlines reported bar visit
When police approached the firefighters, they told officers they were on duty but all denied drinking alcohol inside Whiskey Row, according to the report.
Officers continued to interview the bartender who served the group and other bar staff. They said the three ordered two vodka-Red Bulls and a water just after midnight.
While the bartender said she did not personally see the firefighters drink the alcoholic beverages, she provided officers with a receipt signed by one of them for the mixed drinks.
Police said they notified the area’s fire commander, who came to the scene and immediately placed the three on administrative duty.
The bar’s manager said they were working to obtain video footage to provide additional context.
Fire department launches investigation
The firefighters were placed on administrative leave before they resigned on Wednesday. It’s not clear if the internal investigation is still ongoing after their resignations.
The Nashville Fire Department simply said it was aware of an incident involving three employees, but would not release details of what happened or the names and positions of the firefighters.
The department said it would not provide any additional information because this is a personnel matter. A spokesperson did not respond to requests for a copy of the NFD employee rules and regulations for firefighter conduct.
“The Nashville Fire Department holds all personnel to the highest standards of professionalism, accountability, and conduct,” the department said in a statement. “Actions that compromise those standards are taken seriously and addressed accordingly.”
Mayor calls for accountability
The incident on Broadway comes just months after a firefighter was found unresponsive at his station with drug paraphernalia. The autopsy report said he died from cocaine toxicity.
O’Connell said he talked with Chief William Swann and was speaking with other leaders to make sure people know it is not acceptable for Metro employees to drink or do drugs on the job.
“I think (Swann) has demonstrated, within the fire department, that there is a zero-tolerance approach to this,” O’Connell said. “They are delivering internal accountability. But, I think also, what I am looking for is the assurance that we are doing the appropriate amount of retraining updates to ensure that all personnel are there.”
O’Connell said he is also working with the firefighter union, IAFF Local 140, to hold people accountable. The union said they do not have any comment about this incident at this time.
“Early indications are that our IAFF Local is wanting to ensure that a popular, successful fire department retains the confidence of Nashvillians, and their ability to execute on all fronts,” he said. “We have been having those conversations throughout the year. I think we will be looking to leadership in the Nashville Fire Department to give the public signs of the ongoing confidence we all need to have in them.”

title: Obituary: Bernadette “Bernie” Clancy
text:
WESTBROOK – Bernadette “Bernie” Clancy passed away peacefully on Oct. 28, 2026. She was 97 years old.
Born Bernadette Christman on July 13, 1929, to Napoleon and Lucienne (Melancon) Christman, she was a lifelong resident of Westbrook, Maine.
Bernie went to school in Westbrook, graduating from Westbrook High School in 1947. She was trained as a bookkeeper and held several positions, working for the City of Westbrook and as a bank teller.
Bernie married Gerald Clancy in 1952; they raised two boys, Paul, born in 1953 and Peter, born in 1960. Both boys went on to successful careers, Paul in business and Peter as a beloved teacher.
Bernie loved to play cards, especially cribbage. She loved golf, bowling, movies, popcorn and martinis, not necessarily in that order. More than anything, Bernie loved her family.
She is survived by Paul; four grandchildren, Jonathan, Christine, Joel and April; two great-grandsons; and she was a much-loved mother-in-law to Judi and Patty.
Private services will be held in Westbrook.
In lieu of flowers, please consider making a donation in Bernie’s name to any cause fighting Alzheimer’s

title: Sunday Photos: November 1st, 2026
Obituary: William “Billy” Duffy
text:
SCARBOROUGH – William “Billy” Duffy, 84, of Scarborough, passed away at home on Oct. 11, 2026. Born in Portland on May 8, 1942, he was the son of Frank “Hutch” and Helen (Murphy) Duffy.
Billy grew up in Portland on Munjoy Hill and graduated from Portland High School, where he met his high school sweetheart, Dorothy “Dottie” Murphy. He went on to attend Maine Maritime Academy, graduating in 1966. On June 11, 1966, he married Dottie, beginning a family that would become the center of his life.
Following graduation, Billy embarked on a long and distinguished career as an engineering merchant marine. For 40 years, from 1966 until his retirement in 2006, he sailed the world’s oceans as a chief engineer aboard tankers. Billy’s work took him around the globe and gave him a lifetime of stories from the sea. He was a man of remarkable intelligence and resourcefulness, with a wealth of knowledge and experiences that he was always happy to share.
Billy was also an entrepreneur. Together, he and Dottie owned and operated the Old Orchard House and Hotel and the Bastille Lounge in Old Orchard Beach. He later owned Duffy’s Pancake Kitchen & Bakery on Free Street in Portland from 1978 to 1992. No matter what he was doing, Billy brought his sharp mind, quick wit, and unmistakable personality to the table.
Known to nearly everyone as “Duff”, Billy was a man who could fix just about anything. He had a gift for woodworking and had his own shop in the garage, where he built birdhouses, decks, and countless other projects.
An avid golfer, Billy also loved music, especially Irish music, and enjoyed singing. He was a history enthusiast and a man with an impressive memory for details. He could recall the smallest parts of a story and had a deep understanding of the world around him. Intelligent, well-read, and an exceptional storyteller.
Above all, Billy loved his family. He took great pride in his family and cherished his time with them. Whether he was sharing a story, making someone laugh, or simply being there, Billy made an impression on everyone he met. His influence reached well beyond his immediate family; even those who were not related to him often called him Granddad.
Billy was predeceased by his beloved wife, Dorothy “Dottie” Duffy; his parents, Frank “Hutch” and Helen Duffy; and his brothers, Bobby and Jack Duffy.
He is survived by his children, Suzan Potito and her husband Ken, Kathy Pappas and her husband John, Bill Duffy and his wife Kristin, and Maureen Duffy; grandchildren, Alexia and her husband Cody, Kali and her husband Adam, Talia, Elizabeth; Nikko; Patrick; Kathryn, Mikey, Jack; Max, and Isla; and his great-grandchildren, Kitsis and Ella, who will be arriving in January.
Visiting hours will be held from 4 to 6 p.m. on Saturday, Nov. 7, at Conroy-Tully Walker Funeral Home, 1024 Broadway, South Portland followed by a service at 6 p.m. To view Billy’s Memorial or to share an online condolence, please visit http://www.ConroyTullyWalker.com.

title: Here’s the salary it takes to live comfortably in each US state in 2026
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
(SmartAsset) - As housing, grocery, transportation and other essential costs pressure household budgets, earning a six-figure salary no longer guarantees financial comfort in much of the U.S. A single adult now needs at least $80,000 a year to live comfortably in every state, while the threshold exceeds $100,000 in nearly half of states. For a family of four, the income needed to live comfortably is as much as $329,000.
SmartAsset used MIT Living Wage Calculator data to analyze the living wage in each state — what a full-time worker must earn to cover minimum basic needs — and adjusted it using the 50/30/20 budgeting rule. Under the rule, 50% of income goes to necessities like housing and utilities, 30% to discretionary spending and 20% to savings for retirement and emergencies. The resulting estimate represents the annual, pre-tax income needed to live comfortably in each state.
Key Findings
- In most states, a family of four needs at least $200,000 a year to live comfortably. That threshold applies in 40 states for households with two working adults and two children.
- Massachusetts and Hawai‘i are the most expensive states to live comfortably. Massachusetts is the most expensive state for a family of four, with an income requirement of $329,555. Hawai‘i is the most expensive state for single adults, who need $129,002.
- Montana had the largest increase in the income needed to live comfortably. For a single adult, that threshold rose 8.6% since 2025, the largest increase in the study.
- Mississippi and West Virginia are the least expensive states to live comfortably. Mississippi is the least expensive state for a family of four, with an income requirement of $187,533. West Virginia is the least expensive state for single adults, who need $81,245.
- In six states, the income needed to live comfortably has declined since 2025. Those states are Tennessee, Maryland, Louisiana, North Carolina, Mississippi and Texas. In each, a single adult needs less income in 2026 than in 2025.

title: Barefoot footprints led to rescue of man lost for days along snowy trail in Oregon
text:
Barefoot footprints lead to rescue of man lost for 4 days along snowy trail in Oregon
A man, who officials said was lost for four days, is receiving treatment after barefoot snow prints were found along a trail in Oregon.
The Marion County Sheriff's Office said a Forest Patrol Deputy discovered a set of footprints in the snow near Breitenbush Lake along the Pacific Crest Trail, which sits on a high plateau north of Mount Jefferson.
"Noticing that one of the tracks appeared to be barefoot, the deputy became concerned for the individual's safety and began following the trail," the sheriff's office said in a post on Facebook.
Related video: Royal Caribbean cruise passenger rescued at sea nearly a day after going overboard
After tracking the footprints for nearly five miles, the deputy located a man wrapped in a sleeping bag. He was taken to Detroit, Oregon, for immediate treatment. He was then taken to Santiam Hospital.
Officials said he is being treated for frostbite and hypothermia.
"We are grateful for the outstanding work of Forest Patrol Deputy Ramseyer, whose vigilance and commitment likely saved the mans life today," the post said. "This is also an important reminder to always be prepared when heading into the wilderness."

title: Shooting at Spirit Halloween store in California leaves pregnant woman dead and 6 wounded
text:
(AP) - A targeted shooting inside a Spirit Halloween store in Northern California left a pregnant woman dead and six other people wounded, police said.
Gunfire rang out at about 8:30 p.m. Friday inside the store, which sells Halloween costumes and decor, at the Solano Town Center in Fairfield, the city police department said Saturday in a statement on Facebook.
The shooting “stemmed from a targeted incident involving one suspect,” police said.
The woman who died was identified by police as Constance Hages, 31, and family members told authorities she was pregnant.
Three male victims, ages 16, 19 and 32, were in critical condition, and a 23-year-old man was hospitalized in critical but stable condition.
Two other men, ages 19 and 43, were treated for gunshot wounds and released from the hospital.
No arrests have been made. Authorities said they were reviewing video and other evidence “to identify the individual responsible for this heinous act of violence.”
The department said no additional information would be released at this time.
“We recognize the concern and uncertainty this incident has created throughout our community, particularly with the many Halloween events and celebrations planned for today,” the department said. “We understand that an incident of this nature is frightening and deeply unsettling. We encourage everyone to remain vigilant, look out for one another, and report any suspicious activity.”
Solano Town Center, which has 130 stores and restaurants, remained open but said it was canceling its planned trick-or-treating event scheduled for later in the day “in light of last night’s event.”
“We appreciate your patience and understanding during this time,” the mall said in a statement.
The FBI’s Sacramento office said it was assisting Fairfield police in the investigation.
Fairfield, a city of some 120,000 residents, is about 37 miles (60 kilometers) southwest of Sacramento and halfway between there and San Francisco.

title: Obituary: Christine (Card) Patton
text:
TOPSHAM – Christine Card Patton, a lover of history and of beauty, of the sea and shore, of trees, gardens, dogs, and birds, of her family and friends, of holidays and celebrations of any kind, and of giving back to her many communities, caring for all who entered her home or her life, died on Friday, Oct. 23, 2026, in Newburyport, Mass,, after a long illness. She was 93. It was a radiant autumn morning, of the kind she loved. She will be deeply missed.
Born in Medford, Mass. on Dec. 27, 1932, to Esther Bates (Lacount) Card, a French teacher and later parliamentarian, and Philip Weatherbee Card, a dentist, Christine grew up in Arlington, Mass. She was the salutatorian of the Arlington High School Class of 1950, where she met her future husband, Anthony Seavey Patton “Tony”, who would become a cardiovascular surgeon. She graduated from Wellesley College in 1954, going on to earn a master’s degree in social work from the University of Chicago in 1956. On July 14 of that year, Christine and Tony were married at the College Avenue Church in Somerville. Their union would last for 67 years until his death in 2023. She was a licensed social worker at Massachusetts General Hospital before she became a mother. During Tony’s medical residencies, she and her family lived in Devonshire, England and Salem, Mass. before moving to Danvers. There Christine blossomed into the person so many came to know and love.
While raising her three children (along with, over the years, a golden retriever, a bloodhound, two chocolate labrador retrievers, two cats, three bunnies, a half-moon parrot, a goat, and many gerbils and fish), Christine led the causes closest to her heart, especially local history. Her deep appreciation for her town’s pre-Revolutionary War heritage stemmed from her own home, a colonial farmhouse built by the physician Caleb Rea in 1756. For over 50 years, she and Tony lovingly restored the house, filling it with antiques from the period. For more than three decades, she gave thousands of volunteer hours to the Danvers Historical Society, providing support and leadership to many important initiatives, including the restoration of Samuel McIntire’s Derby Summer House on the grounds of the Glen Magna Farms. She also worked for numerous humanitarian causes, including mental health awareness and funding for Native American higher education. At Salem Hospital, she served in the Auxiliary and on the Board of Trustees. There, she championed investments in a renovated chapel and the hospital chaplaincy program, preserving the human element of healthcare amid an increasing industry focus on technology and efficiency. She also served as president of the North Shore Wellesley Club and as a corporator for Danvers Savings Bank. Adoring the natural world, Christine also created community ritual traditions such as the Winter Solstice celebration at the Unitarian Universalist Church of Danvers, where she was a devoted member since it was dedicated in 1967.
Christine’s ability to preserve and celebrate American history led to a professional career later in her life. In 1984, she became the Director of Marketing and Public Relations for the House of the Seven Gables and Settlement Association, serving there in senior leadership until 1995. The “Chris Patton Garden Fund,” established at her retirement from the Gables, has nurtured many blossoms on its grounds.
In 1984, Chris and Tony’s love of the coast of Maine brought them to Boothbay, where they built a summer home on Barters Island by the Sheepscot River. There, with characteristic energy, Christine dove into environmental conservation as a highly active member of the Board of Trustees of the Boothbay Regional Land Trust. She also worked as a contributing reporter for the Boothbay Register. Chris and Tony extended their retirement life in 2013 to Topsham, where she was an active fundraiser for the Maine Health MidCoast Hospital, while also vibrantly participating in the social life of the Highland Green residential community.
Christine’s energetic public service tells only part of her story. Through her gentle smile and conversational ease, she allowed anyone coming into her world to feel relaxed, at peace, welcomed, and loved. She was strikingly elegant, always “put together” in style, usually wearing her sunglasses on her head, even indoors. Even as the cruelties of her dementia slowly eroded her memory and in the end, even her ability to speak, her warmth, twinkle, and social grace held fast. At Port Healthcare, where she was skillfully cared for during the last two years of her life, she was known for introducing every visitor to her new friends — even if she had only met them only a few minutes earlier. And of course her visitors would invariably be complimented on their outfits.
Christine is survived by her children and their spouses, in birth order, Kimberley Patton and Bruce Beck of Newburyport, Mass., Geoffrey Patton and Karen Kent of Ashland, Mass., and Laurie Patton and Shalom Goldman of Shoreham, Vt. She also leaves her cherished grandchildren and step-grandchildren, Lee Patton and their partner Taylor Epperly, Caitlyn Patton and her wife Cat Kemmett, Christina Calfo and her husband Justin Calfo, Rosemary Beck; Daniel Shai Goldman, his wife Monica, and their three children.
A memorial service to honor her life will be held on Sunday, Dec. 27, at 2:30 p.m., on what would have been her 94th birthday, at the Northshore Unitarian Universalist Church at 323 Locust St., Danvers, Mass. To share a memory or leave a message of condolence, please visit Christine’s Book of Memories Page at http://www.bibberfuneral.com.
Arrangements are in care of Bibber Memorial Chapel, 67 Summer St., Kennebunk, ME 04043.
In lieu of flowers, donations in Christine’s memory may be sent to:
The House of the Seven Gables Settlement Assoc. or it’s Chris Patton Garden Fund (Salem, Mass.) or:
the Northshore Unitarian Universalist Church (Danvers, Mass.) or:
the Danvers Historical Society
(Danvers, Mass.) or:
the Boothbay Regional Land Trust
(Boothbay, Maine), or:
Wellesley College
(Wellesley, Mass.)

title: El-Sayed’s primary opponent, Haley Stevens, endorses Republican Mike Rogers in Michigan Senate race
text:
El-Sayed's primary opponent stuns Democrats by endorsing Republican opponent in Michigan Senate race
Michigan Democrat Abdul El-Sayed’s former opponent in the U.S. Senate primary, Haley Stevens, stunned party officials Sunday by endorsing Republican Mike Rogers as Democratic tensions boiled over days before the election that could determine the balance of power on Capitol Hill.
Stevens endorsed Rogers after attending a Detroit church service with him. The remarkable show of support for the President Donald Trump-backed candidate in the tightly contested race comes after she was uninvited to a joint event the same day with El-Sayed, who defeated the congresswoman by a slim margin in the August primary.
“Our Democratic nominee for Senate said I was no longer welcome in his campaign and that I should stay away," Stevens said in a video announcing the endorsement, which led her top aide to quit. “And he's right. And that's why I am endorsing Mike Rogers for the United States Senate today.”
El-Sayed dismissed the endorsement when asked about it by reporters later Sunday, saying he's focused on issues voters care about, such as the high cost of living.
“At the end of the day, I actually don’t think about Haley Stevens," he said, adding later: “None of this matters."
Michigan Democratic leaders were left shocked. With just less than 48 hours to go before Election Day, a party that had spent months trying to unite behind its Senate nominee was suddenly grappling with an extraordinary defection in one of this year's most important races.
Tensions between the two Democrats have festered since the primary. Stevens is a staunch supporter of Israel, while El-Sayed is a fierce critic of the U.S. ally. He has also been criticized by some in the community for past remarks regarding a Michigan synagogue attack and for appearances with controversial streamer Hasan Piker.
El-Sayed, a former Michigan public health official, is facing Rogers, an ex-congressman, for the seat held by the retiring Democrat, Gary Peters. Keeping Michigan in Democratic hands is vital to the party’s effort to win a majority for the final two years of Trump’s second term.
Stevens and El-Sayed were originally scheduled to attend church together, along with other Michigan and national Democrats, including South Carolina Rep. Jim Clyburn. Democrats hoped it would be a show of unity as they worked to boost turnout in the Detroit area, where concerns have lingered about enthusiasm among Black and Jewish voters in key Democratic strongholds.
Instead, Stevens swayed to gospel music alongside Rogers in the pews at Perfecting Church, while El-Sayed was a few miles away at a different house of worship campaigning alongside prominent Democrats, including Clyburn. The Associated Press attended both services as the dramatic split-screen unfolded.
Stevens' team resigns as Democrats are stunned by reversal
Plans for Stevens to join El-Sayed and Clyburn unraveled after a dispute over Israel and an outside group’s campaign advertisement escalated into a public exchange of criticism between the rivals.
After the church service north of Detroit, where Stevens and fiance Jason Turkish worshipped with Rogers and his wife, Kristi, the congresswoman told reporters, “I’m not turning my back on Democrats. It is this one vote.”
Rogers, standing beside her, said he was “honored” by her support.
Their appearance stunned Democrats, coming days after Stevens publicly reaffirmed she would vote for the nominee, and led her longtime chief of staff to resign with a number of staff members expected to follow soon, according to a person familiar with the developments who spoke on condition of anonymity to discuss internal matters.
“We are shocked and heartbroken,” the aide said in a statement.
The state party chair, Curtis Hertel, said Stevens' endorsement “shows that she has abandoned everything she claims to care about.”
“We reject the attempts by Stevens and bad-faith actors to divide our party and undermine our momentum, and will not allow these eleventh-hour distractions deter us,” Hertel wrote.
Among the Democrats who joined El-Sayed at church were U.S. Rep. Debbie Dingell of Michigan, U.S. Sen. Angela Alsobrooks of Maryland and state Sen. Mallory McMorrow, who dropped out of the Senate primary before voting began.
El-Sayed spoke for nearly 10 minutes at the service. He did not address the latest controversy.
“It’s in churches like this, in pews like the ones in which you sit, that the foundation of my life was built,” El-Sayed said.
Dingell says she disinvited Stevens after it became ‘distracting’
Dingell, a senior Democratic figure in the state who helped organize the planned joint appearance in hopes of bringing together Democrats in the final days before Tuesday's vote, said she asked Stevens not to attend and that Stevens told her she would abide by that.
“I'm the one who pulled it because it had become way too distracting," Dingell said in a telephone interview before Stevens appeared with Rogers. “This is not how I was going to spend my weekend before the election, to be perfectly frank.”
Dingell and other Democrats insist the party is united behind El-Sayed. Early voting has been underway since Oct. 24, before the latest tensions resurfaced, complicating efforts to deliver a unified closing message in crucial areas such as Detroit, where turnout could prove decisive.
Stevens defeated El-Sayed in Wayne County, which includes Detroit, and neighboring Oakland County, in the primary, drawing support from Black and Jewish voters who are important parts of the Democratic coalition.
Video below: Haley Stevens: "Personal" decision
How did we get here?
The Democratic primary was among the most bitter this year. Each candidate accused the other of making personal attacks. Tens of millions of dollars in outside spending poured into the race, including from the American Israel Public Affairs Committee’s affiliated super PAC, which backed Stevens. El-Sayed took particular offense to an outside group’s ad accusing him of disrespecting women.
Although Stevens pledged after the primary to help El-Sayed however she could, the two have not appeared together publicly since a unity breakfast two days after his summer win.
Their lack of joint appearances was particularly notable as some Jewish voters and leaders continued to criticize El-Sayed over his comments about Israel, past rhetoric and campaign appearances with controversial streamer Hasan Piker.
The divisions spilled into public view again Wednesday when Stevens’ fiancé told The Detroit News that he would vote for Rogers. Hours later, Stevens appeared on CNN to reaffirm her support for El-Sayed but urged his campaign to “shut out the hate and call it out.”
Dingell had been working to bring them together at church alongside Clyburn, one of the nation’s most prominent Black Democrats.
But on Friday, after The Associated Press reported on the planned joint appearance, Stevens released a lengthy statement calling on El-Sayed to condemn an ad by an independent left-wing group that linked U.S. support for Israel to high grocery prices.
“Abdul promises to get money out of politics,” Stevens wrote. “He can begin by getting Israel out of his explanation for everything Michigan cannot afford.”
El-Sayed then responded: “So while Congresswoman Stevens seems intent on relitigating a primary that ended three months ago, let’s all focus on the task at hand.”
He repeated Saturday evening that the ad was not made by his campaign and “I do not agree with the contents of that ad.”
Trump praised Stevens in a Truth Social post, saying she was “a Highly Respected Democrat” and that her support from Black and Jewish voters in Michigan is “virtually unprecedented.”
“Haley said what few people are willing to say. She showed great and almost unprecedented loyalty to the Great People of Michigan with what she did,” Trump wrote. “It’s a thing called bravery, and few people have it like just displayed by Congresswoman Haley Stevens!”
Appearing with Trump in Iowa for a campaign rally, House Speaker Mike Johnson said that he spoke to Stevens after she endorsed Rogers. Johnson said he “encouraged her to stay safe and keep speaking the truth.”
A spokesman for the Republican National Committee, Hunter Lovell, said Democrats who feel abandoned by El-Sayed “have a home” with Rogers.

title: Gabby Williams leads Valkyries to WNBA championship in second season, beating Dream 68-63 in Game 7
text:
SAN FRANCISCO (AP) — A fresh WNBA CHAMPIONS T-shirt over her uniform, Gabby Williams cradled the shiny MVP trophy in one arm and gave it a kiss. She held up a No. 1 with her left hand, then hugged and high-fived her supporters all the way to Golden State’s locker room where she pulled on some goggles for the celebration.
Williams made her way back to the Bay Area where she cherishes so many youth basketball memories exactly for a chance to do something like this — to win it all and be part of building something special.
And she has done that all right.
“I just walked into a group full of love,” Williams said. “And that just changed the entire trajectory of my career.”
Williams scored her team’s final 11 points of the third quarter and dazzled through the fourth on the way to 30 points, and the Valkyries captured a championship in just their second season by beating the Atlanta Dream 68-63 in a sensational first WNBA Finals Game 7 on Saturday night.
“Gabby is our closer she stayed patient, she stayed with it,” coach Natalie Nakase said. “Closing with 30, that is incredible!”
Williams joined Penny Taylor in 2007 for Phoenix as the only players in WNBA history to score 30 or more points in a winner-takes-all Finals game.
Jordin Canada scored 18 points, Allisha Gray 16 and Angel Reese had eight points and 12 rebounds for the Dream, denied another championship in the franchise’s fourth try.
Gray made two free throws with 11 seconds left then Atlanta forced a jump ball — Gray against Williams — and Veronica Burton corralled it and converted two free throws with 5.1 seconds to go.
“I’m just so blessed, this is insane!” said Burton, cut by Dallas two years ago.
Rhyne Howard’s layup tied it at 57 with 2:41 left only for Williams to answer once more with a clutch 3-pointer. She converted two free throws with 1:40 remaining, then Kiah Stokes scored a late basket. Stokes — now a four-time WNBA champion — pulled down 13 rebounds and blocked two more shots to cap her spectacular postseason.
Williams left Seattle with a great feeling about joining Golden State and its close-knit culture, returning to the Bay Area determined to prove herself as a WNBA star after all her international success — and now she’s a postseason icon. Fans chanted “Gabby! Gabby!” throughout the fourth quarter.
“All it took was good people,” she said. “All we heard last year was we don’t have no stars. We don’t have no talent. Yeah right! We got good people. We got good people. We got winners. We got people who are ready to put their bodies on the floor to win a game.”
When the final buzzer sounded, the violet-clad sellout crowd at Chase Center went into a frenzy as players sprinted onto the floor to hug and celebrate as confetti fell from the rafters.
“Ballhalla” had become “Boohalla” for this far-but-haunted Halloween night in the raucous arena. Now, with a women’s championship to its name right alongside the one earned by the Golden State Warriors in 2022.
“We gotta build a bigger trophy case,” co-owner Peter Guber said.
The team that led at halftime in the first six matchups had won every game so far, and the Dream were ahead 30-24 at the break. Atlanta also had been 16-0 this season when Reese made at least one 3. The Dream’s DeWanna Bonner became the first player in WNBA history to reach 600 career postseason defensive rebounds.
Nakase told Williams at halftime the game would open up for her.
“Nat told me to stay patient, I trust her with my life,” Williams said. “I stayed patient.”
Nakase changed her starting lineup in a move that paid huge dividends after Golden State fell behind 2-1, inserting Kaila Charles and Tiffany Hayes and bringing Kayla Thornton and Cecilia Zandalasini off the bench.
The 37-year-old Hayes, who came out of retirement two years ago and spent 10 seasons with the Dream, scored 11 points in the winner-take-all Game 7 and brought energy all series that made Nakase want to win for the veteran guard as much as anybody.
Valkyries owner Joe Lacob guaranteed a championship within the first five years for this franchise three years ago when the Bay Area was granted an expansion team, and in improbable, joyful fashion, his team accomplished it in Year 2. That after becoming the first expansion organization to reach the playoffs in its inaugural year in 2025.
During the victory ceremony, Lacob shouted out the team and its leaders, while Nakase, general manager Ohemma Nyanin and President Jess Smith hugged. And Lacob thanked the fans who have sold out Chase Center for every game since Day 1.
“Ballhalla!” Lacob hollered.
“These ladies deserve all the credit in the world for the incredible resilience, every last one of them, and our coach,” he said later. “I can’t even say how proud I am. I don’t care men, women, whatever, it doesn’t matter, that is an incredible year, an incredible performance, not only tonight but the whole playoffs.”

title: Coast to coast with Ford & Brinkley, part V
text:
Oklahoma is a broad state, with the longest section of the Mother Road, Route 66. However, the short section in Texas makes a huge impression, as the topography, and the feel of the old road begin to change.
We still have Route 66 paralleling us, along with busy railroad tracks, as we often hustle down I-40 to make some time. It is nearly impossible to drive every piece of the fabled old road, but we see the purists try, their red-mud splattered Jeeps testimony to the frequent off-roading necessary to relive the essence of those long-ago travelers heading west for a better life, or the servicemen and women trying to catch a bus, fetch a ride home before shipping overseas during WWII.

title: Harvest Festival of Crafts held at Augusta Armory to kick off crafts season
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Harvest Festival of Crafts held at Augusta Armory to kick off crafts season
This weekend, New England Craft Fairs kicked off its fall and holiday craft season with the Harvest Festival of Crafts at the Augusta Armory.
The event featured a variety of vendors and crafters from all over New England, with many from Maine.
Organizers of the event say it's a great chance for the crafters to show off and sell their products, while for visitors, it's an opportunity to get a head start on holiday shopping.
One of the vendors was Augusta-based Betti's Bags.
It's a business that began during the pandemic when Bettilou Fielding needed to get rid of several pairs of jeans. She turned them into tote bags, and the business just grew from there.
"I decided that not only did I want to put the jean bags out, available for people, I would like to create other bags of different qualities," said Fielding.
Fielding only sells her bags at craft fairs, and the ones hosted by New England Craft Fairs, she says, are unique in the connection the crafters hold.
"I haven't met a crafter I was not comfortable with. Everybody is very warm, welcoming, and they support each other," Fielding said.
New England Craft Fairs is holding several more events throughout the month here in Maine, including a few more in Augusta.

title: When law enforcement stops cooperating, public safety pays the price
text:
Eric Small is chief of police in Sanford, Maine.
When federal immigration agents enter a Maine community to conduct an enforcement operation, they may know who they are looking for. But do they know the community? Do they know the families, social workers or organizations that have spent years building relationships with its residents?
Maine’s local law enforcement officers often do.
After more than 25 years in law enforcement, I have learned that effective policing depends on training, communication, relationships and trust. That experience leaves me concerned about decisions by the state of Maine and certain municipalities to restrict cooperation with U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement, including Maine’s LD 1971.
I am proud that Sanford’s municipal government chose not to impose additional local restrictions, recognizing the importance of professional judgment and appropriate communication within the law.
Recent deadly force incidents involving federal immigration enforcement, including the July 2026 fatal shooting in Biddeford, have raised serious questions. Let me be clear: This is not a defense of ICE or its actions. I have no firsthand knowledge of those incidents and would never judge an officer’s conduct without examining the evidence. Nor can I claim local police involvement would have prevented a tragedy.
But I do know what Maine officers bring to difficult situations.
Our full-time officers complete 720 hours of basic training at the Maine Criminal Justice Academy. They learn constitutional policing, crisis response, professional judgment and appropriate use of force. Equally important, they spend years developing relationships with families, schools, housing authorities, mental health providers and community organizations.
Those relationships matter. An officer who knows a family member, understands someone’s circumstances or has an established connection with a social worker may have opportunities to resolve a dangerous encounter without confrontation. You cannot legislate those relationships into existence. They are earned over years of service.
These concerns are not mine alone. In February, Maine State Police Col. William Ross and Public Safety Commissioner Michael Sauschuck discussed communication problems surrounding federal immigration operations. Ross described the frustration of having little information about operations occurring in Maine communities.
I recognize that cooperation with ICE raises legitimate concerns within immigrant communities. If residents fear contacting police could expose their families to immigration enforcement, they may hesitate to report crimes or seek assistance. That damages public safety, too.
I am not advocating that local officers independently enforce federal civil immigration law or participate without limits in immigration operations. Constitutional protections, accountability and community trust must remain priorities. But there is a difference between enforcing immigration law and sharing appropriate information, expertise or assistance when lives may be at risk.
Federal immigration enforcement does not stop simply because Maine restricts local participation. Federal agents will continue operating in our communities, sometimes without the relationships or local knowledge our officers possess.
And when something goes wrong, who responds? Our police officers. Our firefighters. Our emergency medical personnel. We remain after federal agents leave, responsible for the consequences and for maintaining the community’s trust.
Distancing ourselves from federal operations does not necessarily make those operations safer. It may simply remove experienced local professionals who could help prevent dangerous situations from escalating.
Maine policymakers should examine whether existing restrictions allow meaningful coordination when public safety is threatened. That conversation should include law enforcement, emergency responders, immigrant communities and the organizations serving them.
As Sanford’s chief of police, my responsibility is to protect everyone in our community, regardless of immigration status, background or political beliefs. We can demand accountability from federal authorities while recognizing the value of local expertise. We can protect immigrant communities while preserving appropriate communication between agencies.
The question is not whether Maine supports ICE. The question is whether we are making the best use of every responsible public safety resource available to save lives. When lives are at stake, that distinction matters.

title: 1-year-old boy dies after walking into road by home, troopers say
text:
JONESVILLE, Fla. (WCJB/Gray News) — A 1-year-old boy was hit and killed on a Florida roadway, according to the Florida Highway Patrol.
The crash happened in the Jonesville area Friday afternoon.
Investigators said a car was headed west on Newberry Road when the boy entered the road from a nearby home. The driver didn’t see the child and hit him.

title: What to know about the Affordable Care Act’s open enrollment period now underway
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
WASHINGTON (AP) — People heading into the Affordable Care Act open enrollment period with plans to sign up for insurance should expect a variety of changes in 2027, including higher premiums and fewer coverage options.
The sign-up window for the marketplace, also known as Obamacare, starts Sunday in most states and runs through Jan. 15.
Big changes to the exchange include expiring financial assistance, rising rates, potential delays in working with a broker, new restrictions on immigrants, and stricter enrollment checks.
Financial help, including premium tax credits and cost-sharing reductions, is now restricted for many groups of people who were previously eligible.
Across the board, healthcare experts predict less coverage and higher prices, with the average price of health insurance purchased through the marketplaces expected to rise by 13% in 2027, according to analysis of new CMS data by the healthcare research nonprofit KFF.
Increases are driven by multiple factors
Cynthia Cox, a vice president and director of the ACA program at KFF, said the increase is primarily driven by rising healthcare costs, hospital market concentration, and potential factors such as the No Surprises Act, which took effect in 2022 and bans surprise billing, or the rising availability of GLP-1 drugs.
The people who will be most affected by the new increases are those who do not qualify for a subsidy.
“They may or may not be able to afford to continue to keep their coverage into next year,” Cox said, adding that “a lot of them have already moved into bronze plans, which are the cheapest plans.”
A CMS fact sheet about open enrollment that was distributed Friday says “Americans using HealthCare.gov will have robust access to low-cost plans.”
The price of ACA insurance has skyrocketed for many people during Trump’s second term after Republicans opposed extending COVID-era subsidies that had helped offset the costs of health insurance for most enrollees during Democratic President Joe Biden’s administration.
That resulted in 1.2 million fewer people signing up for coverage in the exchanges.
Nearly 20 million people in US are actively enrolled in ACA plans
As of February, roughly 19.2 million people in the United States were actively enrolled in ACA marketplace health plans, according to the Department of Health and Human Services website. The number of enrollees grew during the COVID-19 pandemic when enhanced subsidies became available through the American Rescue Plan Act and Inflation Reduction Act, both signed into law by Biden.
New regulations starting in 2027 will also limit tax credits for certain lawfully present immigrants, which could result in an additional 1 million uninsured individuals over time.
Meanwhile, the Trump administration has been removing ACA enrollees from the program as part of the ongoing campaign against what it characterizes as waste, fraud and abuse.
In September, Vice President JD Vance and other officials in the Republican administration announced plans to remove 760,000 ACA enrollees from public healthcare exchanges, alleging the individuals were fraudulently enrolled in the program or simply did not exist.
Vance said the discovery and canceled subsidy payments for hundreds of thousands of people from the exchanges, part of an administration-wide crackdown on fraud, would result in $2.2 billion in cost savings.
It’s unclear how many more people will drop off of ACA coverage in 2027, Cox said. But with higher premiums, immigration eligibility changes and the anti-fraud efforts, “I think there’s going to be fewer people enrolled in this market, but it’s going to be harder to understand why.”

title: All 9 people died on a jet that crashed into a Florida neighborhood, transportation secretary says
text:
FORT LAUDERDALE, Fla. (AP) — A business jet crashed into a South Florida neighborhood and erupted into a ball of flames, killing all nine people on board and leaving a fiery crater. The cause was not immediately clear, but federal investigators are expected to provide an update Monday.
Video recorded by passersby captured the terrifying moment on Sunday afternoon when the Bahamas-bound aircraft plunged from the sky before slamming into the ground and exploding in Greenacres, about 7 miles (11 kilometers) southwest of West Palm Beach. Flames flickered around chunks of pavement lining the crater as shocked residents looked on in horror. Thick black smoke engulfed the crash site.
“Debris was everywhere. Debris hit my house. Everything was on fire. The road was on fire,” Anthony Blackmon, who lives near the crash site, told NBC affiliate WTVJ. “I’ve always seen it on the news, never thought it would happen so close to somebody like how it happened today.”
Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis said there were no immediate reports of anyone on the ground injured or killed. Authorities have not released the names of the people who died.
Palm Beach County authorities evacuated about 600 people from a nearby mobile home community while the Federal Aviation Administration and National Transportation Safety Board investigate the crash.
Mother identifies one of the pilots
Authorities have not provided any information about what caused the Bahamas-bound jet to crash. NTSB officials planned to hold a news conference in West Palm Beach on Monday afternoon.
The jet began its journey at the Austin-Bergstrom International Airport in Texas. Airport spokesperson Jim Reynolds described it as a private aircraft but could not immediately provide details about who was on board.
Camila Corteleti told the New York Post and New York Times that her daughter, 20-year-old Nathalia Gadelha Filgueiras, 20, was one of the pilots. She earned her pilot’s license in 2023 while just a 17-year-old senior at West Boca Raton Community High School in Florida, local news reports said at the time.
Her pilot’s license showed she had the rating to fly that model of Learjet but not to be in command of the flight.
When reached by The Associated Press on Monday, Gadelha Filgueiras’ father, Allan Filgueiras, said he wasn’t prepared to speak about the crash.
Pilot reported turbulence and ice, then the jet’s rapid descent
The plane was heading east at 35,000 feet (about 11 kilometers) when the pilot started to report problems.
The pilot said ice was accumulating on the jet and that turbulence was jolting it by as much as 700 feet (213 meters), according to air traffic control recordings captured by LiveATC.net. Rain pounded the region on Sunday.
“We have light, clear ice that is manageable and moderate turbulence,” the pilot told controllers.
The situation rapidly deteriorated.
The pilot requested permission to climb another 2,000 feet (about 610 meters) then quickly declared an emergency as the jet lost altitude at an alarming rate.
“We’re descending 8,000 — mayday, mayday — we’re descending 10,000 feet per minute,” the pilot radioed.
“We are in an overspeed condition descending 20,000 feet per minute,” the pilot radioed, before delivering a devastating acknowledgment of what was about to happen. “We’re going to crash into the ground.”
The plane banked sharply to the right before crashing and exploding.
“It was a cataclysmic plane crash,” DeSantis told reporters at the scene. “It looked like a missile going down and left a big crater on the side of the road.”
___
Associated Press writers Amy Taxin in Santa Ana, California; Josh Funk in Omaha, Nebraska; Dave Collins in Hartford, Connecticut; and Philip Marcelo in East Meadow, New York, contributed.
___
This story has been corrected to show the crash happened in Greenacres, not Green Acres.

title: Selma Blair says ‘I am so sorry’ after arrest in alleged flight attendant assault
text:
(CNN) - Actress Selma Blair apologized Friday on social media for the alleged actions that led to her arrest last month.
Blair is accused of striking a flight attendant and biting another crew member during a flight. She also allegedly kicked a nurse who was involved with her transport.
In an Instagram post, Blair addressed the incident.
“Not one day ever have I intended to hurt or frighten anyone a day in my life,” Blair said. “And so to the people that I disappointed, that I hurt, that I frightened, alarmed, I am so sorry.”
Blair also spoke about what comes next.
“Right now, I’m going to be taking care of my health. And my son. And thinking of you all with gratitude and love,” she said.
Blair pleaded not guilty to assault on Oct. 12 and was released on bail.

title: Obituary: Wellington Oliver “Bud” Sawyer
text:
FALMOUTH – Wellington Oliver “Bud” Sawyer of Falmouth, died peacefully on Oct. 27, 2026. He was 94. He was born on Dec. 4, 1931, in Boston, Mass., a son of Wellington O. Sawyer and Edith Kelley of Boston, Mass. and Jonesport, Maine.
Bud graduated from Boston Technical High School and Boston University School of Communication.
In his senior year at Boston University, while producing a variety show for a local church group, he met his future wife, Janet, a rising senior in high school and member of the church group. Three years later they married.
Bud had a legendary career as a broadcaster in Southern Maine at WGAN, WLOB and WPOR. He entertained generations of Mainers, and became a part of their daily lives. He covered the Friendship Sloop Races, the Monhegan Island Race, and Lobster Boat Races in Casco Bay. He was a member of the Maine Broadcasting Hall of Fame. At WGAN and WPOR he teamed up with newsman Mike Audet, where they ranked at the top of the ratings charts year after year.
Bud was a family man and active in the community. He and his wife, Jan, were deeply involved in their children’s activities, including attending swim meets, and basketball, soccer, baseball and field hockey games. Bud also served as a baseball umpire. He supported a number of charitable organizations, including many years driving a snowmobile 50 miles for the Multiple Sclerosis Society, which honored him with its Hope Award. He was also honored as the Outstanding Older Worker at the National Prime Time Awards in Washington, D.C., and received the Ward L. Quaal Pioneer Award from the Broadcasters Foundation of America. He was a past member of the Falmouth Lions Club, the Portland Yacht Club, the Masonic Lodge, and the Portland YMCA where he was an active swimmer and squash player.
He is survived by, Jan, his wife of almost 70 years; his son Scott and his wife, Ellen, of Providence R.I. and Chebeague Island, his son David and his wife, Tammy, of Falmouth, his son Mark and his wife, Barbara, of Auburn, and his son-in-law David Vasconcelos, of Falmouth.
He was predeceased by his parents; and siblings; and his beloved daughter, Jennifer Vasconcelos.
He leaves nine grandchildren, Lily and Elizabeth Sawyer; Katlyn and Zachary Sawyer; Olivia and Camryn Sawyer; and Dayna (Vasconcelos) Bull, and Jack and Matthew Vasconcelos.
A celebration of life will be held at a later date. Please visit http://www.lindquistfuneralhome.com to leave condolences for the Sawyer family and share a memory of Bud.

title: Dozens injured, at least 6 dead in Halloween weekend gun violence at nightlife districts across US
text:
(AP) - Mass shootings over the Halloween weekend in nightlife districts across the U.S. left at least six people dead and dozens injured, officials said.
The deadliest violence occurred in Dallas, where a handful of shootings in the city’s Deep Ellum neighborhood, a center of music, restaurants and nightlife, killed four people and injured 15 others, police said.
Police in college towns like Fayetteville, Arkansas; Birmingham, Alabama; Newark, Delaware, and Bloomington, Illinois, also reported shootings in their nightlife districts.
Dallas Police Chief Daniel Comeaux said investigators were still trying to determine if three separate shootings Saturday night over the span of about an hour and 15 minutes were related, and it wasn’t immediately known why they started. Comeaux said some arrests were made but he didn’t specify how many or what charges were involved.
“This is a really big scene. It’s spread out,” Comeaux said.
The department had increased police presence in the district before the shootings. No police officers were injured.
One shooting happened after a football game in Alabama
In Birmingham, one person was killed and eight others were wounded in two separate shootings just outside Legion Field after the annual ‘Magic City Classic’ football game on Saturday night, Mayor Randall Woodfin said at a news conference Sunday.
Two were listed in critical condition Sunday, fire officials said.
Alabama State and Alabama A&M are archrivals whose annual contest has been played for more than 100 years. Nearly 70,000 fans attended Saturday’s game, won by Alabama A&M 31-28. The event draws some of the largest crowds in the country for games played in their college football division.
Michael Pickett, chief of the Birmingham Police Department, said most spectators and families had left the stadium property after the game. The first shooting happened nearby, where vendors were set up along Graymont Avenue.
The circumstances of the shootings were unclear, and it was also unclear where the fatality occurred.
Police spokesperson De’Rell Freeman said one person had been detained and that “multiple weapons” were found.
Shootings in other nightlife districts
In Newark, Delaware, six people were shot late Saturday near the University of Delaware campus, Newark police Lt. Greg D’Elia said.
All six were transported to hospitals for treatment and their conditions were not available. A university spokesperson said they would provide updates on the investigation online as they become available.
Video shared on social media showed people running for safety from the scene. One stretch of the city’s Main Street was closed for several hours after the shooting, police said.
A shooting early Sunday in Bloomington, Illinois, left a 19-year-old woman dead and another woman in critical condition. Six others had injuries of an unknown nature that were not life-threatening. The shooting happened near the campus of Illinois Wesleyan University. Bloomington is about 135 miles (217 kilometers) southwest of Chicago.
In Fayetteville, Arkansas, six people were taken to hospitals with gunshot wounds from a shooting early Sunday near the University of Arkansas. No arrests have been made, police said in a news release. A preliminary investigation indicates an altercation preceded the shooting.
Halloween stores were the scene of two attacks
On Friday, two people were killed in separate shootings at Spirit Halloween stores in California and Michigan.
Police said a shooting inside a store in Fairfield, California was a targeted attack. Family members told police that the 31-year-old woman who died was pregnant. Six other people were wounded, police said. There were no immediate arrests.
In Madison Heights, Michigan, just north of Detroit, a 21-year-old man was fatally shot Friday afternoon. A man who was assaulted by bystanders as officers took him into custody was hospitalized with injuries that were not life-threatening, police said.
___
Raby reported from Charleston, West Virginia. AP reporter Claudia Lauer in Philadelphia contributed to this report.

title: Augusta woman finds strength and purpose through bakery stand
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
AUGUSTA — Kalee Weatherwax has many titles: baker, small business owner, content creator, singer-songwriter, “momcologist.”
When her barely 2-month-old son was found to have a rare vascular tumor, life changed forever for Weatherwax and her husband, Joe. Now, seven years later, Weatherwax is finding ways to spend time with her family, give back to her community and earn money through a self-run bakery stand in her front yard.
Her charmingly comedic — and sometimes vulnerable — videos chronicle her day-to-day running the bakery and taking care of her sons, Alec, 7, and Everett, 4, while also showcasing her singing and songwriting skills to thousands of followers online.
To her kids, she’s a rock star in every sense of the term. And they’re not the only ones who think so.
A ‘momcologist’
Nobody plans to become a “momcologist,” a term often used by mothers of children with cancer to describe themselves, given the level of at-home caretaking cancer can require.
It started when Weatherwax discovered a bruise on her son Alec’s side not long after he was born; she rushed him to the doctor.
Her son underwent numerous tests and scans and a biopsy surgery before doctors determined he had an extremely rare tumor called Kaposiform hemangioendothelioma, or KHE for short, caused by an abnormal growth of blood vessels. While technically noncancerous, KHE spreads rapidly through veins, which can “strangle” and pierce through muscles and cause other complications.
Alec has taken oral chemotherapy medication twice a day since he was diagnosed as an infant to keep the growth of the tumor in check. Because of the medication, he has a weakened immune system and gets sick easily, often causing him to miss school, but it’s not all the time.
Weatherwax started lessons at home with Alec early, when she wasn’t sure if he was going to be able to attend school at all. Thanks to her efforts, despite his missed school days, she said he’s at the top of his class. On the October day Weatherwax sat for an interview at Barnes & Noble in Augusta, her next stop with her younger son Everett in tow was picking up Alec from school.
Watching her child go through so much at such a young age has been hard, she said, but throughout appointments, blood work and chemotherapy, Alec has always put up a brave face.
“That literally breaks my heart … that he’s just, like, used to this,” Weatherwax said. “But at the same time … he’s just that confident, strong kid that I just, I don’t have any doubts about that kid.”
Alec and his family hope for good news on the horizon. This month, he will undergo an ultrasound to see if he can wean off the chemotherapy without any new tumor growth.
A baker
As the Weatherwax family was figuring out life navigating Alec’s sickness, Kalee had to decide whether she would return from maternity leave to work as a state employee.
With her husband working at Central Maine Power, she decided to stay at home with Alec while exploring alternative ways to earn money to help pay for Alec’s treatment.
“Time has been a thief,” Weatherwax said. “And we haven’t gotten all of those normal experiences that a lot of other people have, and I’m grateful for every experience I get with my child, no matter what. But to me, I’m just like: how could I steal that time back? And that’s kind of why I wanted to start a home business.”
Weatherwax had worked as a restaurant manager and always loved baking in her free time. And others certainly loved her baking. When she brought baked goods to her husband’s CMP co-workers during storm duty, they always asked her why she wasn’t selling her delicious treats.
After years of selling candles and baked goods at craft fairs, she tried something new. Last summer her father built her a small, bright pink stand for her front yard where she could sell items regularly. Now every weekend, Weatherwax, with the help of her sons, stocks the stand with sourdough bread, cookies, sweet breads, muffins and seasonal treats for neighbors and community members to enjoy.
“The sourdough bread is my favorite,” neighbor Nancy Richards said. “I’ve had the muffins and and the cookies, and I’ve tried all of them. And I love them all, really.”
Weatherwax can bake up to 24 loaves of bread in one weekend, in addition to all the other goods. She always bakes banana chocolate chip muffins because they’re Alec’s favorite. They were one of the only things he liked to eat when dealing with painful mouth sores from chemotherapy.
Both her sons get excited to help her with the stand each weekend, and she often takes them to the grocery store so they can see what the money goes back into and how the business works.
Weatherwax said the stand has also helped in engaging with the community. With an immunocompromised child, many people were afraid or hesitant to visit because they didn’t want to get him sick.
“It was just so isolating,” Weatherwax said. “So I’m like: ‘OK, what can I do? What can I do? What can I do?’”
With thousands of followers online and many eager to purchase baked goods in person, Weatherwax is building community one loaf at a time.
A rockstar
Before she started selling baked goods, Weatherwax was looking for ways to occupy her time while staying home with Alec. Knowing she wanted to sing her kids to sleep, Joe surprised her with a guitar and lessons one Christmas.
She said music has always been a part of her life; when she was younger, she wanted to grow up to be a rock star.
Weatherwax started posting videos of her singing and her day-to-day life with her sons on platforms like TikTok under the username “weatheringthelife” several years ago, and now she has over 12,000 followers.
Weatherwax said watching her singing and guitar-playing progress in her past videos is encouraging. She’s hoping to host small free concerts at her house for the community.
Weatherwax also posts behind-the-scenes videos of her baking, many of which are creative or comical. The most recent videos feature Weatherwax in green face paint and a wig for Halloween.
Weatherwax said part of the reason she posts online is to be a role model for children about internet culture.
“If I’m gonna be online and perceived for online stuff, and everything else, for influencing these kids, I want it to be for something good that they can see exactly the work that goes into it and everything else,” Weatherwax said. “Nothing’s instantaneous.”
Weatherwax and her family’s impact on the community extends beyond her online presence or her baked goods.
Richards, the next-door neighbor, said when she was locked out of her house, Weatherwax let her use her phone and drove her to her daughter’s workplace to get a spare key. When Richards fell on the ice, Weatherwax’s husband helped her up and back into her house.
“They’re just a special family for sure,” Richards said. “And I love them dearly, just like they were my own.”
Weatherwax said her biggest takeaway from her son’s experience and running the stand is that you never know what others are going through.
“I mean, honestly, when people look at my family and look at my kid, they don’t immediately jump to: he’s on chemotherapy,” Weatherwax said. “You never know what other people are going through, and you should just always be kind and try and do what you can for the people around you. Because like I said, this is the way that I can give back to my community.”
Weatherwax’s stand is on the corner of Eastern Avenue and Pleasant Hill Road and stocked on Saturdays and Sundays.
This story was originally published by the Maine Trust for Local News. Sara Coughlin can be reached at scoughlin@metln.org

title: Judge dismisses lawsuit seeking to block certification of Alaska Senate race if GOP incumbent loses
text:
Judge dismisses lawsuit seeking to block certification of Alaska Senate race if GOP incumbent loses
A federal judge on Sunday dismissed a Justice Department lawsuit seeking to block certification of Alaska’s U.S. Senate race if Republican incumbent Dan Sullivan loses.
Sullivan, an ally of President Donald Trump, faces Democratic former U.S. Rep. Mary Peltola in one of the country’s most closely watched races, with Senate control at stake. Tuesday’s ranked-choice election also includes two candidates who have done little campaigning, one of whom shares the incumbent’s name.
The lawsuit, filed less than two weeks before the election and with early voting underway, called for an investigation into whether votes for retired teacher Dan J. Sullivan were intended for the senator. The state said the case lacked merit and argued there would be no way to determine that without violating voter privacy.
Shortly after the ruling, the Justice Department filed a notice saying it was appealing: “Alaskan voters deserve a fair election, not to be misled in an attempt to rig outcomes,” a department spokesperson said in a statement.
U.S. District Court Judge Sharon Gleason wrote in the order that the relief the United States seeks is “infeasible” because many voters have already cast their ballots. She said the cast ballots have been mixed together to the point where they cannot be matched to specific voters.
“More fundamentally, the United States provides no workable plan as to how it proposes to segregate ballots cast for Daniel J. Sullivan on Election Day and then conduct a court-ordered unspecified 'investigation' of those ballots in a manner that would preserve voter secrecy,” she wrote.
Attorneys for the state, Peltola’s campaign and the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee argued that the case lacked any legal basis and amounted to interference. The senator and his allies, including Trump, for months have portrayed Dan J. Sullivan as a sham candidate intent on confusing voters and helping Peltola.
The Justice Department, attorneys for the state and Peltola’s campaign did not immediately return messages seeking comment.
In the week before Election Day, The New York Times reported that Peltola’s campaign was involved in efforts to recruit the second Sullivan. Dan J. Sullivan in June, shortly after entering the race, said he’d had no contact with the campaign about running. He did not immediately respond to a request for comment on the report.
Peltola’s campaign responded by saying the campaign “has no involvement with either Sullivan campaign” — a statement similar to one it released after Dan J. Sullivan launched his bid.
“I am not interested in tricking voters,” she said during a recent campaign event.
State courts, including the Alaska Supreme Court, rejected Republican-backed efforts to block the retired teacher from the August open primary ballot on which he appeared as Daniel J. Sullivan Jr., with no party affiliation. The senator was listed as Dan S. Sullivan, Republican and incumbent.
Both Sullivans appear the same way on the general election ballot. Peltola placed first in the primary, followed by the senator. Dan J. Sullivan received about 2.5% of the primary vote, but that was enough to finish within the top four and qualify for the Nov. 3 ranked-choice election.
Attorneys for the Alaska Department of Law represented state elections officials in the case and asked Gleason, who was appointed by former Democratic President Barack Obama, to toss the lawsuit. They filed a scathing response to the federal government’s complaint, calling it “meritless.”
Alaska also said the state had taken “significant steps” to distinguish the two Sullivans on the ballot. Voters who still might be confused could ask for help or look up candidate biographies and other information in state-distributed election pamphlets.
Gleason wrote that the administration’s attempt to block certification ran counter to the Constitution, which gives states the authority to run elections. She also cited the Supreme Court’s Purcell principle, which holds that federal courts should generally not change election rules too close to an election.
Alaska’s ranked voting system also offers a solution to possible confusion, the state wrote, allowing voters to rank the Sullivans as first and second choices, if they choose.
“That way, if the voter’s first-ranked Sullivan is eliminated, his vote would transfer to the other Sullivan,” attorneys Rachel Witty, Margaret Paton Walsh and Laura Fox wrote. “The voter’s vote would not ‘be transferred to Peltola’ as the complaint asserts, unless the voter chose to rank Peltola as his next choice instead of the other Sullivan.”
Trump for years has railed against Alaska’s use of ranked-choice voting in general elections. Republican state leaders have said that while they don’t like ranked voting, they want voters to “rank every Republican” candidate on this year’s ballot, especially with a high-stakes governor’s race featuring one Democrat and three Republicans.
On Thursday, the Justice Department escalated a criminal investigation over the same-named candidates on the Alaska ballot, issuing a raft of new grand jury subpoenas, a person familiar with the matter told The Associated Press. The FBI also has begun contacting people who donated to Dan J. Sullivan, some of whom told the AP that the agents were asking if they had been misled about which candidate they were supporting.

title: Obituary: James “Jim” Wilson Sr.
text:
SCARBOROUGH – James “Jim” Wilson Sr., 92, died on Oct. 25, 2026, at Maine Veterans’ Homes in Scarborough, with his family by his side. Born on March 6, 1934, in Machiasport, Maine, he was the only child of the late Frederick and Claribel (Wood) Wilson.
Jim graduated from South Portland High School in 1952. After graduation, he served in the Air Force, Coast Guard, and Army National Guard, completing a combined 27 years of military service. A proud veteran, he enjoyed sharing stories of his service and travels abroad.
Jim met his wife, Mary, through his friend George Moberg, who was dating Mary’s sister and later became Jim’s brother-in-law. Jim and Mary married in 1960 while he was serving in the Coast Guard. They eventually settled in South Portland, where they raised their family. Married for 58 years until Mary’s passing in 2018, they were loving partners and wonderful role models throughout their life together.
He spent his career as an oil burner technician, working for Chevron, Harris, and Union Oil. Known for his strong work ethic and warm rapport with customers, he formed many lasting friendships over the years.
Jim was a loving and devoted husband, father, grandfather, and friend. He cherished South Portland and raised his children near his childhood home on Preble Street. He played an active role in their activities, and the family spent many summers at Ocean Park in Old Orchard Beach. Jim and Mary loved entertaining and hosted countless family gatherings, celebrations, and Sunday dinners.
He enjoyed sports, especially college athletics, track and field, and golf—as well as music of all genres. An animal lover, he provided a loving home to many pets over the years. He also treasured fishing trips with his sons and traveling with Mary.
Jim adored his grandchildren and remained involved in their lives, attending sporting events, dance recitals, and other milestones. He took great joy in watching them grow into adulthood and staying up to date in their lives.
He had a quiet, gentle spirit and valued hard work, independence, and, above all, family. A man of quiet strength and determination, he lived largely independently until just a few weeks before his passing.
Over his 92 years, Jim witnessed extraordinary changes in the world and nearly a century of transformation. Through it all, he moved forward with grace, humility, and resilience. His life reflected his ability to adapt, persevere, and navigate life’s many changes while remaining true to the values that meant the most to him and to his love and devotion to his family. He will be greatly missed, and his family will forever be grateful for the strong roots and blessings of a loving family that Jim provided.
Jim was predeceased by his parents; and his wife, Mary.
He is survived by his daughters, Lynn Aceto and her husband Vincent of Gorham, and Lisa Campbell and her husband James of Pittston, his sons, James Wilson Jr. of South Thomaston and Jeffrey Wilson and his wife Adrienne of South Portland; his grandchildren, Morgan and Joshua Cloutier, Jason and Alexandra Aceto, Tyler Wilson and his wife Grace, Conner Wilson, and Samantha Wilson; and his great-grandchildren, Arthur and Lyla Wilson.
Jim’s family extends heartfelt gratitude to the staff at Maine Veterans’ Homes in Scarborough for the compassionate care they provided during his brief stay there.
At Jim’s request, funeral services will be private.
To share memories of Jim or to leave the family an online condolence, please visit http://www.athutchins.com.
Those wishing to honor his memory may donate to: Maine Veterans’ Homes
