The U.S. House of Representatives passed a bill back in July that would make daylight saving time permanent. Since then, the Sunshine Protection Act has stalled in the Senate, meaning the clocks "fall back" an hour on Halloween weekend.
The Sunshine Protection Act passed the House 308-117. Making daylight saving time permanent would mean using the time zone year-round that people now set clocks to from March to November.
President Donald Trump has backed making the time zone permanent, writing on Truth Social in May, "It’s time that people can stop worrying about the 'Clock,' not to mention all of the work and money that is spent on this ridiculous, twice yearly production."
Daylight saving time occurs from March to November each year in the U.S. On the second Sunday in March, clocks spring forward. When it ends on the first Sunday in November, clocks fall back.
Use the tool below and search your ZIP code to see how your sunrise and sunset would change if the bill to make daylight saving time become law.
Daylight saving time was first implemented in 1918 with the passage of the Standard Time Act to conserve energy, but was repealed the following year.
It was then implemented once again during World War II, but was standardized in the U.S. with the passage of the Uniform Time Act in 1966, which established daylight saving time from April to October.
The act also allowed local exemptions. Neither Hawaii nor Arizona, excluding the Navajo Nation, recognizes daylight saving time. Both states follow standard time year-round.
The U.S. experimented with a trial of year-round daylight saving time in the 1970s. The effort, signed into law by President Richard Nixon, was to help with conserving gas.
At first, it had approval from most Americans, but that approval nosedived by the second month of the trial. One main concern was the safety of children leaving for school in the dark in the morning. The trial was reversed later that year by President Gerald Ford.
The length of daylight saving time has been expanded twice since the act's passage in 1966, once starting in 1987 and a second time beginning in 2007.

title: Aroostook County voters weigh choices in US Senate race
text:
Election 2026
Visit the BDN election page for our latest coverage of local, state and national races.
With the midterms just days away, Aroostook voters are weighing two of their own in one of the nation’s most watched races.
Republican incumbent U.S. Sen. Susan Collins and Democratic challenger Troy Jackson have both touted their working class heritage in Aroostook in their U.S. Senate battle. Collins, 73, points to her family’s longtime lumber business. Jackson, 58, touts five generations of logging roots.
But even in their home county, the race is too close to predict, with voter sentiment divided on who would best represent Aroostook residents’ interests. The Bangor Daily News talked to some of those people to gauge their feelings.
“To be honest, everyone I speak to is shell-shocked,” said Houlton Democrat Bev Chapman, noting she has knocked on 100 doors canvassing for the party. “One thing for sure, everyone is done with Trump except MAGA hardcore.”
Residents are weighing what each candidate has brought to Aroostook County.
Collins and her supporters laud her position as appropriations chairwoman, pointing to $428.6 million secured in 2026 for state projects spread among 16 counties. Eleven percent, or $46.4 million of the state total, is earmarked for 23 County projects, according to Collins’ office.
Of the Aroostook total, $20.3 million, or 44%, was secured jointly with Independent U.S. Sen. Angus King, according to funding data King’s office provided. Collins brought in about $390 per County resident this year. Joint projects between the two senators netted about $692 per person.
While he was Senate president, Jackson spearheaded bipartisan legislation in 2021 that provided free meals for all Maine schoolchildren, which passed unanimously in the Senate. In its first year, from 2022 to 2023, the state appropriated $34 million for approximately 173,907 students, according to the legislation’s fiscal report.
The program, which continues to grow, saves families about $160 a month per child, according to Gov. Janet Mills’ office.
U.S. Army veteran and Republican Roger Felix said he sees Collins pulling off another win.
“I would say definitely the 2nd Congressional District is going to be hands down for Collins,” the Caribou resident said. “She’s already proven that she can do the job. We’ve seen it happen. She’s not a stranger to Aroostook County by any means, and she doesn’t forget where she came from.”
Felix said it’s nothing against Jackson and he voted for him several times when he was in the Maine Senate. Jackson strongly advocated to keep the Maine veterans homes open in northern Maine, for which Felix gives him credit.
For Felix, it comes down to “deeds, not words” and Collins has already done the work, he said.
Bridgewater potato farmer Jim Gerritsen, who was an Aroostook County delegate in the Democratic nominating convention earlier this year, supports Jackson and said it’s time for Collins to retire.
Jackson has demonstrated a commitment to Maine’s working people, including efforts to control prescription drug prices and institute free school meals, Gerritsen said.
He criticized Collins’ votes in favor of the wars in Iraq and Iran, Supreme Court Justice Brett Kavanaugh’s nomination and her alleged trading of political favors with donors.
The claims arose in a ProPublica report that alleged a Collins fundraiser and Hawaiian government contractor Navatek engineered a $500,000 campaign donation in 2019. Collins has denied those claims.
“At the very least the conflict of interest is outrageous, so what that tells me is it’s more important to her to self benefit then be a good steward for taxpayer funds or the interests of working people in Maine,” he said. “It just demonstrates terrible judgment.”
Houlton resident Craig Harriman, 48, remains undecided.
“Susan Collins, being in the senate for nearly 30 years, is why we should consider term limits,” Harriman said.
But the independent was disappointed to find out that after Jackson said no billionaires were funding his campaign, recently released financials revealed at least four had contributed, he said.
Ludlow agricultural business expert Roxanne Bruce is not sure Jackson brings “enough change potential.”
“I know what Susan Collins has brought for years and I am hoping for change,” she said. “If we don’t change soon, a lot of what makes Maine great could be lost.”
Single mother of five, Lavinia Lengele, 39, an independent, said she believes politicians are out of touch with the communities they represent, especially rural communities. She doesn’t believe either Collins or Jackson is the answer, but voting on Nov. 3 matters more now than ever, she said.
“We’ve become so focused on left versus right that we’ve lost sight of what really matters,” the Houlton resident said. “We need people who care about their neighbors and are willing to show up for one another, because that’s what is actually making a difference in people’s lives.”

title: Man accused in crime spree with 17 victims, including three people stabbed
text:
TOPEKA, Kan. (WIBW/Gray News) - Ron Hubbard never expected fiction to become reality.
“I was thinking about a scenario I seen on TV where a delivery guy did the same when the police was chasing a guy who stole a car,” Hubbard said.
Hubbard said he was hanging with a friend Wednesday, Oct. 28, when they noticed something unusual.
“I happened to look up the street to my left, and I seen this strange guy,” Hubbard said.
The man, now identified as Adam Schwegman, also caught another bystander’s attention.
“We confronted him because the other guy had been up at the park, where this all took place,” Hubbard said.
Topeka police say an hour earlier, Schwegman stabbed two people along S.W. Fillmore. His booking charges also include an allegation of rape at that address.
TPD says Schwegman then moved up the same road, breaking into two homes -- four children were inside one of them, including a four-month-old. Officials say they were not hurt.
However, it didn’t stop there.
Police say a third victim was stabbed on a nearby street.
And finally, a 70-year-old woman was hurt when Schwegman attacked her at Ward Meade Park. Schwegman was running from there when Hubbard spotted him.
“I decided to step in, throw my leg out, trip him and he landed over here in the grass, and the knife fell in the grass,” Hubbard said.
Hubbard said he kicked the knife to the sidewalk, as the second person held Schwegman. He got away, but police soon caught him.
Schwegman was booked in connection with 16 charges, including aggravated battery and rape.
Hubbard says he was glad to step in to prevent further harm.
“Well, if you see something bad, try to help stop it. I wish we could have got to it before this happened,” Hubbard said.
Schwegman made his first appearance in court on Thursday, Oct. 29. The judge has set a total bond of $3 million.

title: Obituary: Christine (Card) Patton
text:
TOPSHAM – Christine Card Patton, a lover of history and of beauty, of the sea and shore, of trees, gardens, dogs, and birds, of her family and friends, of holidays and celebrations of any kind, and of giving back to her many communities, caring for all who entered her home or her life, died on Friday, Oct. 23, 2026, in Newburyport, Mass,, after a long illness. She was 93. It was a radiant autumn morning, of the kind she loved. She will be deeply missed.
Born in Medford, Mass. on Dec. 27, 1932, to Esther Bates (Lacount) Card, a French teacher and later parliamentarian, and Philip Weatherbee Card, a dentist, Christine grew up in Arlington, Mass. She was the salutatorian of the Arlington High School Class of 1950, where she met her future husband, Anthony Seavey Patton “Tony”, who would become a cardiovascular surgeon. She graduated from Wellesley College in 1954, going on to earn a master’s degree in social work from the University of Chicago in 1956. On July 14 of that year, Christine and Tony were married at the College Avenue Church in Somerville. Their union would last for 67 years until his death in 2023. She was a licensed social worker at Massachusetts General Hospital before she became a mother. During Tony’s medical residencies, she and her family lived in Devonshire, England and Salem, Mass. before moving to Danvers. There Christine blossomed into the person so many came to know and love.
While raising her three children (along with, over the years, a golden retriever, a bloodhound, two chocolate labrador retrievers, two cats, three bunnies, a half-moon parrot, a goat, and many gerbils and fish), Christine led the causes closest to her heart, especially local history. Her deep appreciation for her town’s pre-Revolutionary War heritage stemmed from her own home, a colonial farmhouse built by the physician Caleb Rea in 1756. For over 50 years, she and Tony lovingly restored the house, filling it with antiques from the period. For more than three decades, she gave thousands of volunteer hours to the Danvers Historical Society, providing support and leadership to many important initiatives, including the restoration of Samuel McIntire’s Derby Summer House on the grounds of the Glen Magna Farms. She also worked for numerous humanitarian causes, including mental health awareness and funding for Native American higher education. At Salem Hospital, she served in the Auxiliary and on the Board of Trustees. There, she championed investments in a renovated chapel and the hospital chaplaincy program, preserving the human element of healthcare amid an increasing industry focus on technology and efficiency. She also served as president of the North Shore Wellesley Club and as a corporator for Danvers Savings Bank. Adoring the natural world, Christine also created community ritual traditions such as the Winter Solstice celebration at the Unitarian Universalist Church of Danvers, where she was a devoted member since it was dedicated in 1967.
Christine’s ability to preserve and celebrate American history led to a professional career later in her life. In 1984, she became the Director of Marketing and Public Relations for the House of the Seven Gables and Settlement Association, serving there in senior leadership until 1995. The “Chris Patton Garden Fund,” established at her retirement from the Gables, has nurtured many blossoms on its grounds.
In 1984, Chris and Tony’s love of the coast of Maine brought them to Boothbay, where they built a summer home on Barters Island by the Sheepscot River. There, with characteristic energy, Christine dove into environmental conservation as a highly active member of the Board of Trustees of the Boothbay Regional Land Trust. She also worked as a contributing reporter for the Boothbay Register. Chris and Tony extended their retirement life in 2013 to Topsham, where she was an active fundraiser for the Maine Health MidCoast Hospital, while also vibrantly participating in the social life of the Highland Green residential community.
Christine’s energetic public service tells only part of her story. Through her gentle smile and conversational ease, she allowed anyone coming into her world to feel relaxed, at peace, welcomed, and loved. She was strikingly elegant, always “put together” in style, usually wearing her sunglasses on her head, even indoors. Even as the cruelties of her dementia slowly eroded her memory and in the end, even her ability to speak, her warmth, twinkle, and social grace held fast. At Port Healthcare, where she was skillfully cared for during the last two years of her life, she was known for introducing every visitor to her new friends — even if she had only met them only a few minutes earlier. And of course her visitors would invariably be complimented on their outfits.
Christine is survived by her children and their spouses, in birth order, Kimberley Patton and Bruce Beck of Newburyport, Mass., Geoffrey Patton and Karen Kent of Ashland, Mass., and Laurie Patton and Shalom Goldman of Shoreham, Vt. She also leaves her cherished grandchildren and step-grandchildren, Lee Patton and their partner Taylor Epperly, Caitlyn Patton and her wife Cat Kemmett, Christina Calfo and her husband Justin Calfo, Rosemary Beck; Daniel Shai Goldman, his wife Monica, and their three children.
A memorial service to honor her life will be held on Sunday, Dec. 27, at 2:30 p.m., on what would have been her 94th birthday, at the Northshore Unitarian Universalist Church at 323 Locust St., Danvers, Mass. To share a memory or leave a message of condolence, please visit Christine’s Book of Memories Page at http://www.bibberfuneral.com.
Arrangements are in care of Bibber Memorial Chapel, 67 Summer St., Kennebunk, ME 04043.
In lieu of flowers, donations in Christine’s memory may be sent to:
The House of the Seven Gables Settlement Assoc. or it’s Chris Patton Garden Fund (Salem, Mass.) or:
the Northshore Unitarian Universalist Church (Danvers, Mass.) or:
the Danvers Historical Society
(Danvers, Mass.) or:
the Boothbay Regional Land Trust
(Boothbay, Maine), or:
Wellesley College
(Wellesley, Mass.)

title: Mass shooting after Alabama football game leaves 1 dead, 8 wounded
text:
One person was killed and eight others were wounded in a mass shooting just outside Legion Field in Birmingham, Alabama, after the annual ‘Magic City Classic’ football game on Saturday night, police said. It was among several violent incidents nationwide on Halloween weekend.
Michael Pickett, chief of the Birmingham Police Department, said most spectators and families had left the stadium property after the game, but the shooting happened nearby, where vendors were set up along Graymont Avenue.
He said he was “very grateful that more people weren’t injured.”
The circumstances of the shooting were unclear.
Police spokesperson De’Rell Freeman said one person had been detained and transported to police headquarters for questioning, and “multiple weapons” had been found and secured.
Alabama State and Alabama A&M are historically Black universities and archrivals whose annual contest has been played for more than 100 years. Nearly 70,000 fans attended Saturday’s game, won by Alabama A&M 31-28. The event draws some of the largest crowds in the country for games played in their college football division.
The Magic City Classic has such a deep history that Alabama State coach Eddie Robinson Jr., a former NFL linebacker and alumnus of the school, proposed creating a Hall of Fame for the game.
In Dallas, police planned a news conference Sunday to address what it called “multiple” reports of overnight shootings in the downtown Deep Ellum neighborhood.
And in Newark, Delaware, six people were shot shortly after 11:10 p.m. Saturday near the University of Delaware campus, Newark police Lt. Greg D’Elia said. All six were transported to hospitals for treatment. Video shared on social media showed people running for safety from the scene. One stretch of the city’s Main Street was closed for several hours after the shooting.

title: Proposed solar project an economic opportunity for Jay
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
As the business development manager for Reed & Reed, a Maine-based construction company, I spend a lot of my time working on projects that create jobs, support local businesses and contribute to Maine’s economy. From that perspective, I believe the proposed Alden Mill Solar project in Jay represents a good opportunity for the community and for Maine’s construction industry.
A solar project of this size involves much more than installing panels. It requires a significant amount of engineering, site preparation, road construction, foundations, electrical systems and utility infrastructure. This work creates opportunities for Maine equipment operators, electricians, laborers, truck drivers, subcontractors and suppliers. These are good-paying jobs that support Maine families and businesses.
Jay has a proud history of industry and manufacturing. For generations, the Androscoggin Mill provided jobs and supported countless families. While no new development can replace what the mill once meant to the community, finding ways to put the property and its existing infrastructure back to productive use makes good sense.
I recognize that projects like this raise questions, and residents deserve to understand both the benefits and potential impacts. I hope the community will carefully consider the economic opportunities this project could bring.
Maine needs investments that put our people to work, support local businesses, and make good use of existing infrastructure. I believe the Alden Mill Solar project has the potential to accomplish all three.
Darryl Coombs
Business Development Manager
Reed & Reed Inc.
Woolwich

title: FBI blames North Korea for stolen billions from Binance in biggest hack in history
text:
FBI blames North Korea for stolen billions from Binance in biggest hack in history
The theft of billions of dollars from Binance within a matter of minutes, the biggest crypto heist in history, was orchestrated by North Korean hackers, the FBI said Saturday.
The bureau said in a statement that this week's attack was tied to “malicious cyber activity” by an entity known as TraderTraitor, the same actors behind a $1.5 billion Bybit hack last year.
The FBI asked crypto exchanges, blockchain analytics companies and others to block transactions linked to various addresses to make sure the money is not laundered to cover up its origins.
Related video: Ballot stacking: what is it and is it legal?
It also said its probe found that TraderTraitor was converting stolen assets primarily into a cryptocurrency called ethereum. The FBI expects that TraderTraitor will now attempt to convert the assets using DeFi and “instant swap services.”
Asked by reporters as he appeared on Saturday night during a Halloween party at his Mar-a-Lago estate in Florida, however, President Donald Trump suggested investigators weren't yet certain that North Korea was involved.
“I’m not concerned. We’re learning about it," Trump said of the case. “We don’t know if it’s North Korea.” Though he added that, it could yet be determined that it was.
Crypto expert Ari Redbord said he expects the hackers will break the stolen assets into pieces and try to launder them through smaller exchanges to evade detection, a process that could unfold over months.
“It’s bank robbery, in this case, at the speed of the Internet,” said Redbord, chief policy officer at blockchain intelligence firm TRM Labs. “However, we can also track and trace those funds in real time in order to build investigations, to disrupt and to seize back funds.”
He added: “It’s just this cat and mouse game.”
On Thursday, $6.3 billion in bitcoin and other digital currency was stolen from Binance, the world's largest crypto exchange, in what several crypto experts said bore the hallmarks of a North Korean hack.
The company said Saturday that it had enough set aside in the same digital currency that was stolen to cover 90% of the missing assets and promised that customers would be fully reimbursed.
___
Associated Press writer Russ Bynum in Savannah, Georgia, contributed.
